"An orator is a good man skilled in speaking." If he is evil, then even if he is skilled in speaking, he is still not an orator but a seducer. So was the one who said, to persuade: "You shall not die at all, but you shall be like gods." Rhetoric can do great things. She turns people from falsehood to truth. She gives comfort to the sorrowful and faith to unbelievers, and she makes the senseless sensible. Because this is so, she is very close to Philosophy, and so she wishes to heal this sick man with her power. And together with her, let Music, a servant born in our house, sing now lighter and now graver measures.

And together with Rhetoric, let Music, a member of my household, be fully ready and sing right after the prose: sometimes a heavier song, such as the heroic meter, sometimes a lighter one, such as the iambic, and other meters.

DESCRIPTION OF FORTUNE. What is it then, O man, that has cast you down into sorrow and grief? Well, dear man, what has brought you to this plight [?], into this sadness and into this weeping? You have seen, I believe, something new and unusual. Something new and strange has happened to you, I do not know what. You think that Fortune has changed toward you. You imagine that Fortune has turned against you. You are mistaken.
In that you are wrong. These have always been her ways; this is her nature.

These are her customs; this is how she is made. Rather, in her very changeability she has kept toward you her own constancy. She has shown you all the more her steadfastness in her very change. This is called an argument from the sign, that is, an explanation of the name. For what else is Fortune but the changeability of prosperity and adversity? Such she was when she flattered you. Such she was when she was most agreeable to you, when she caressed you, when she played up to you with the enticements of false happiness. When she played with you, it was with the lures of false happiness.

"You have discovered the two faces of the blind deity." Now you recognize the face of the one who hides herself, the deceiving demon. Or say: of the blind goddess, because the ancients held her to be a goddess and painted her blind. Why blind? Because her giving is such that it seems she does not see whom she gives to. She gives to the worse man and passes over the better. "She who still veils herself from others has made herself fully known to you." She who still hides herself from others has laid herself bare to you. "If you approve of her, accept her ways." If she pleases you, put up with her habits. "Do not complain." And do not complain.
If you shudder at her treachery, spurn her and cast her away as she plays her destructive games.

If you resent her faithlessness, then renounce her and cast her away, since she plays in an evil way. As long as she plays with you, for so long shun her, before she fails you. For what is now the cause of such great grief to you ought to have been the cause of your tranquility. What you are now sad about, you ought to be in good spirits about.
For she has left you. For she has now abandoned you, she whom no one can ever be sure will not leave him. No one ever becomes certain of her.
Do you really consider precious a happiness that is going to go away, that is, withdraw? Do you value a fleeting happiness as precious?
And is present fortune dear to you,
though it is not faithful in remaining, and will bring grief when it departs?

And shall she be dear to you while she is with you, she who is with you without faithfulness, and who at some time will grieve you by leaving? But if she cannot be held at will — if no one can keep her as he wishes — and if by fleeing she makes people wretched — and by going away she makes them sorrowful...
what else is a fleeting thing but a kind of sign of future calamity?

What is she, then, but fleeting, if she gives no sign of the sorrow to come? Such was Aeneas to Dido. That argument is called "ab eventu", that is, "from the end" or "from the effect", because we should look at the end within the deed that comes before it. As Virgil said: "While driving them, beware of running into the he-goat; he butts with his horn." Nor would it be enough to look at what lies before the eyes. Nor should anyone look only at what is before his eyes. Prudence measures the outcomes of things. Prudence considers the end of all things; she always thinks ahead. And the same changeability in either direction... And the same change in both, the good and the evil.
...makes neither the threats of fortune to be feared nor her caresses to be desired.
It does not let her, that is, prudence, fear the coming threats of fortune, nor love her present caresses.
A YOKE FREELY TAKEN UP MUST NOT BE BORNE IMPATIENTLY. Finally, once you have submitted your neck to her yoke, you must bear it with an even mind.

Whatever happens within Fortune's domain. In short: if you once bowed your neck beneath her, then you must calmly endure whatever is done to you in her court and whatever happens to you there. That is called the argument from related terms (argumentum a coniugatis). Cicero gave this example of it: "If the field is a common pasture, it is permitted to graze it in common." That means: if the pasture is shared, people may use it in common. This is like that: "If you put yourself under the yoke, you must bear the yoke."

If you wished to write for her a law of staying and a law of departing, her whom you freely chose as your mistress, would you not be unjust? Do you wish to set a law for your mistress, whom you chose willingly, about how long she shall be with you, or also when she shall leave? Do you not then deal with her improperly? And by impatience you would make bitter the lot which you cannot change. And with impatience you rage [?] against the lot, that is, you impatiently resent the fortune which you cannot change. That is rhetorical dissuasion: never to attempt what cannot be done.

If you committed your sails to the winds, you would move forward not where your will was aiming but where the gusts drove you. If you left your sail to the power of the wind, you would not travel where you wanted but where the wind carried you. If you entrusted seeds to the fields, you would weigh the fruitful years and the barren ones against each other. If you entrust your seed to the earth, you must of necessity take your chances with good years and bad. What was lacking in the bad year, you would make up with the good.
You have given yourself over to fortune to be ruled; you must obey the ways of your mistress.

You entrusted yourself to fortune so that she would take care of you; now follow her ways, for that is right. Those who are powerful in eloquence know how to bring forward such a pairing of paradigms, that is, of examples. For this reason rhetoric is also named among the Greeks from "copia fandi" (abundance of speech). But you are trying to hold back the force of the turning wheel? Are you striving to stop the spinning wheel that she drives? Yet, most foolish of all mortals, if she begins to stay, she ceases to be chance. Most foolish of men, if she begins to stand still, she is no longer changeable. That argument is called "a contrariis" (from contraries), because Aristotle says that motion is contrary to rest.
HOW MUCH SHE DOES WHILE SHE SHOWS HER STRENGTH. When she has turned the changes with her proud right hand,
She is swept along like the seething Euripus. And so when she overturns things with her proud right hand, she moves like the surging whirlpool. This figure is called parabole, that is, comparison.
Fierce, she tramples kings who were dreaded only a moment ago. And she cruelly tramples down the kings who were feared just a moment ago.
And, deceitful, she raises up the humbled face of the vanquished.
And on the other hand she deceitfully lifts up the head of the defeated. She does not hear or care about wretched weeping. She pays no heed at all to pitiful weeping.

And she even laughs at the groans that she, the hard one, has caused. And she gladly laughs at the sighing she has brought about. Through pride and cruelty she shows herself worthy of hatred, and through deceit worthy of contempt. This is what rhetoric teaches us to do to someone we want to make hateful to others.
So she plays; so she tests her strength. That is her game; in this way she tests what she can do.
And she shows her followers a great marvel:
if someone is seen in a single hour both cast down and happy. And she puts on this marvel for those who watch her: someone who, within one short while, becomes both happy and unhappy.

WHAT FORTUNE'S OWN ARGUMENT MIGHT BE. But I would like to discuss a few things with you in Fortune's own words. I would now gladly talk with you a little in her own words. So consider whether she is demanding what is right. Judge whether her demand is just.
Why, man, do you accuse me with daily complaints? Why must you [?] me every day with your complaints? What injury have we done you? What wrong have I done you?
Which of your goods have we taken from you? Which of your goods have I taken away from you?
Argue your case against me before any judge you like, over the possession of wealth

and of high offices. Summon me before whatever judge you wish, over your goods and over your office. And if you show that any of these things belongs to any mortal as his own, I will willingly grant that the things you demand back were yours. And if you show me any man who owns any of it as his own, then I too will grant you what you demand. That argument is called the argument from the general (a genere), because what is right for everyone is also right for one person. It moves from all to one. This type of issue (status), that is, the legal dispute, is called "absolute" (absolutum) in rhetoric. It applies when the accused person does not deny the deed but denies guilt, and says: "It was right to do so."
When nature brought you forth naked from your mother's womb, I took you in, naked and lacking everything,

and I fed you from my wealth. When you were born naked, I took you in naked and with nothing at all, and I fed you with my goods. And, which is what now makes you impatient with me, I was inclined to favor you and raised you too indulgently. That you are now ill-tempered comes from this: I gladly and willingly spoiled you. I surrounded you with plenty and with the splendor of everything under my control. I gave you your fill of everything that belongs to me, in abundance and in splendor.

Now it pleases me to withdraw my hand. Now I want to draw my hand back to myself. You owe me thanks, as one who has had the use of another's property. Now you should thank me for it, as someone who enjoys another's goods. You have no right to complain as though you had lost what was truly yours. You have no just complaint, as if you had lost what was your own.
Why then do you groan? Why then do you sigh?
We have done you no violence.

I have taken nothing from you by force. Wealth, honors and other such things are under my control. Riches, honor and things of that kind all belong to me. The servants know their mistress. They come with me, and when I leave they depart. They are my servants. They know me, they come with me, and they go away with me. This figure of speech is called homoeoteleuton, which means "ending alike." Cicero in the Rhetoric to Herennius calls it "similar ending" (similiter desinens), because it comes out in matching sounds, like poetry. I would boldly affirm. I dare to say this boldly:
If the things you complain of having lost were yours, you would never have lost them. If what you say you have lost were yours,

then you would not have lost it; then it would not be *alienum* (foreign) to you. This argument is called *a repugnantibus* (from contraries), because *proprium* (one's own) and *alienum* (another's) are contraries. What anyone has by nature is his own; he cannot lose it. What he gains from outside is *alienum*; that he can lose. Shall I alone be prevented from exercising my right? Must I alone not show my power? This is indignation mixed with rivalry, as Juno said of Minerva: "Could Pallas burn the fleet of the Argives and sink the men themselves in the sea?" The heaven is allowed to bring forth bright days and to hide them again in dark nights. The heaven may give bright days and dark nights by turns.
The year is allowed now to crown the face of the earth with flowers and crops, now to spoil it with clouds and cold.

The year may by turns adorn the earth with plants and grain, and at times also make it ugly with downpours and frost. The sea [?] has the right now to charm with a smooth, level surface, now to bristle with storms and waves. The sea, too, may be still, with a smooth, even surface, and at times also bristle up from wind and waves.
Shall the insatiable greed of human beings bind us to a constancy that is foreign to our ways?

Shall the insatiable greed of human beings make me constant, against my nature? That is rhetorical declamatio, that is, reproach and rebuke, just as acclamatio, its opposite, means praise. This is our power; this is the game we play without end. This is my power; this is the game I play. We turn the wheel in its spinning circle. I play with an ever-turning wheel; that is what I do. We delight in changing the lowest to the highest and the highest to the lowest. It pleases me to turn what is low upward and what is high downward.

Climb up, if you like. Sit up there, if it pleases you. But on this condition, that you do not think it a wrong to come down when the rule of my game requires it. On these terms: that it does not grieve you to get down when my game turns out that way. Or did you not know my ways? Was my custom not known to you? That is confutatio, that is, shaming, as if she said: if you are unwise, I will make you wise.

Did you not know that Croesus, king of the Lydians, who a little before had been feared by Cyrus, soon afterward became pitiable, was handed over to the flames of the pyre, and was saved by rain sent from heaven? Do you not know that Croesus,

who was king in Lydia, though he had just been fearsome to Cyrus, soon afterward became pitiable, and after Cyrus threw him into the fire he was rescued by a downpour? Because Croesus came to help the Babylonians against Cyrus, it happened that Cyrus drove him out of there, pursued and soon captured him, and threw him into the fire, from which God set him free. But when he did not thank God for this and boasted of his own good fortune, it came about that he dreamed he saw Jupiter pouring water over him and the sun wiping it off. His daughter interpreted the dream for him this way: that Cyrus would capture him again and hang him on the cross, and as the rain wet him, the sun would dry him. And so it happened afterward.
Has it escaped you that Paulus shed pious tears over the calamities of King Perses, whom he had captured? Is it hidden from you

that the consul Paulus Aemilius piously wept over the misfortune of Perses, king of the Macedonians, whom he himself had captured, because he thought the same could happen to him? Historians call him Perseus, not Perses. They also tell how often he had defeated other consuls before, and, when Paulus brought him captive to Rome, how he died in custody, and how his son learned smithing out of poverty and supported himself by it. What else does the outcry of tragedies lament but Fortune overturning happy kingdoms with an indiscriminate blow? What do tragedies lament but Fortune heedlessly destroying glorious kingdoms, since she regards no one more than another? Tragedies are mournful poems, such as those Sophocles wrote among the Greeks about the overthrow of kingdoms and cities, and they are the opposite of comedies,

in which we always hear a joyful and pleasant ending. But we do not know whether any Latin tragedians are to be found, as we find plenty of Latin comic poets. Did you not learn as a youth that two jars lie on the threshold of Jupiter, [?] two jars, the one evil, the other good [?] [garbled Greek quotation]. Did you not learn, when you were a child, what the poet Pacuvius wrote: that two jars lie full beneath Jupiter's doors, one of good and the other of evil? Who is there that does not drink of both, that does not taste both hardship and comfort? By this she shows that she could not spare him adversity. What if you have taken more abundantly from the share of good things? Why do you complain if you have drunk more of the better? As if she were saying: if I could not spare you altogether, still I have not struck you too hard.
What if I have not departed from you entirely? What if I have not yet wholly abandoned you? What if this very changeableness of mine is a just cause for you to hope for better things?

What if this fall rightly makes you hope for something better? Just as all those rightly hope for something better who suffer persecution for righteousness' sake, because they are all the more blessed. Yet do not waste away in spirit. Now do not be so sick at heart; let go of your heartache. And since you have been placed within a kingdom common to all, do not wish to live by your own law. Do not desire to live alone by your own law in a common realm. Now she has come to the commonplace (communis locus). In any argument, a commonplace is when someone attacks vices common to all without naming anyone, as these verses do.
THE COMMONPLACE.
If Abundance were to pour out from her full horn as much wealth as the sea, stirred up by the winds, churns grains of sand,

What more is there? Suppose Abundance (Copia), the handmaid of Fortune, were to shake out from her horn for people as much wealth as the sea, stirred up by the wind, swirls sand. Here the voice is held in suspense (suspensio vocis). The fables say that the river Achelous, which flows in Greece, turned into a bull and fought with Hercules. Hercules struck the horn off the bull and gave it to Abundance, who is Fortune's handmaid, so that she could hand out her mistress's goods with it.
or as many stars as shine in the sky, brought out on star-filled nights,
Or as many stars as shine in the sky at night, when it is starry. And the same goes here.
and did not draw back her hand. Nor drew her hand back to herself.
That is, she did not grow tired of it. And here as well.
the human race would not stop because of that
weeping its wretched complaints. Even so, people would never stop their wretched lamenting. Here the voice is lowered (depositio).
Even if God should willingly receive their prayers,
lavish with much gold,
and adorn the greedy with splendid honours,
what they have gained already seems like nothing. Even if God himself

gladly heard their prayers, was generous to them with his gold, and also gave them the honours they wanted in great abundance, what they had would still not seem enough to them. But savage greed, devouring what it has sought,
opens up other gaping mouths.

But great greed, having swallowed one thing, at once gapes for another. What bridles can now hold back headlong desire within a fixed limit? Who can restrain that greed, which always waits for more? When, though it overflows with generous gifts, the thirst for having burns all the hotter? As long as it has enough and still always wants to have more? He never lives as a rich man who, anxious and groaning, believes himself needy. He never becomes rich who, worrying and sighing, counts himself poor. Here the status [the issue under dispute] is concluded, because she [Fortune] has defended herself with argument against him as against an opponent. Therefore Philosophy now speaks to him
in her own person.

IN HER OWN PERSON. If, then, Fortune were to speak to you in her own defense with these words, you would certainly have nothing to mutter against it. If Fortune wished to defend herself in this way, you could not say anything against it. Or if there is anything by which you can rightly defend your complaint, you must bring it forward. Or if you can show that your complaint is just, then you should bring it forward. We will give you room to speak. I give you the opportunity to speak. Then I said: These things are indeed fair-seeming, and smeared with the honey of the sweetness of rhetoric and music. All these, I said then, are beautiful speeches, and as if honeyed, with rhetoric and with music. Since the sweetness of rhetoric is now mentioned here for the second time, and one cannot recognize its sweetness until one knows rhetoric itself, this should not be passed over here.
As much as can be said briefly, what it is.

WHAT RHETORIC IS. Rhetoric is one of the seven liberal arts, that is, of the seven book-arts, which few have learned but many can name. Of the seven, grammar is the first. It teaches us rectiloquium, that is, to speak correctly, which even children can learn, as we hear every day. The second is rhetoric, which leads us further, for it gives us the eloquence that is needed in court and in council, and wherever there is any assembly for common needs. For that, children are of no use, only wise people. Councils and court cases cannot take place without strife. Where is there such contention of words as in court and in council? Therefore an eloquent man is needed nowhere more than there.

Whoever can settle a dispute by speech, and has learned this in rhetoric, is an orator; in his mouth one finds the sweetness of rhetoric. But if he is unlearned and yet eloquent, he can carry out the office of an orator, but he himself cannot be an orator, because what comes from nature does not come from art. Who is there who knows that sweetness and would not gladly hurry to where he might hear it? When in Greece the two most learned men in this art, Aeschines and Demosthenes, agreed on a day to contend in court, did not many thousands from all Greece come there for that reason, as Cicero says? Why then should we be wholly ignorant of so delightful an art? Let us know, then, that this same science, which is called rhetoric, is threefold, for this reason:
because its subject matter is threefold.

ON THE SUBJECT MATTER OF THE ART OF RHETORIC. What is its subject matter but dispute? When a dispute arises, rhetoric has work. Without dispute it has nothing to do, just as medicine is idle when there are no diseases or wounds. If people dispute about right and wrong, as they do in court, that kind of dispute is called in Latin iudicialis (judicial), from iudicium (judgment). If people dispute about appointment to office, such as who is fit to be king or bishop, that kind of dispute is called demonstrativa (demonstrative), because the person's virtue has to be demonstrated. If people dispute about what is useful to do or to leave undone, as they disputed at Rome whether Carthage should be destroyed,

…or would not be. Because one must hold deliberationem about it, that is, resolution and common counsel, that kind of dispute is called deliberativa. After this we should know that each of the three kinds has two subdivisions. Of these two we call the one status legalis and the other status rationalis. When people dispute about the law (legem), and one wants to understand it in one way and another in another way, that status, that is, that dispute, is rightly called legalis. But when people dispute about how reasonable something is that one does or advises, then from the reason, that is, from the ratio, the dispute is called rationalis. It should also be known that people dispute about the law in five ways and about the reason in four ways. It should not weary us to hear about these ways.

WHAT THE LEGAL STATES ARE. One kind of dispute concerns the law, and it is called scriptum et voluntas (the letter and the intent). It works like this. The rule of the monks says: "After compline let no one speak." If a fire breaks out at night, whoever first notices it cries out to the others. If he is then accused on the grounds of the letter of the law, he defends himself by the intent of the writer. He says that the writer meant for an exception to be made in such a case. Another arises from contrary laws, where the laws are contrary to each other, such as: "Give to everyone who asks of you," and this one: "Ne aliquid cui nihil" [? "not anything to one who has nothing"]. The third arises from ambiguous laws, as in this Roman law: "If a harlot possesses a golden crown, let it be confiscated." Which should be confiscated, the crown or the harlot? The fourth is called definitio in Latin,

which means exact marking-out, or exact measuring. It is needed because the law uses a word that can be uncertain and disputed until its meaning is exactly measured. For example, there was a dispute in Rome about whether a man had been justly killed. He had been killed because he was going about at night with his pole. Roman law says: "Let one caught at night with a telum (weapon) be killed." So a definition had to be made of what a telum is. Telum is derived from the Greek word telon, which means longum (long) in Latin. The fifth is called ratiocinatio in Latin, which means establishing one thing from another. Take the man who flogged an exile: he argued that he was rightly allowed to do this because Roman law says: "It is lawful to kill an exile caught within the borders."

WHAT THE RATIONAL STATUSES ARE. Of the four rational statuses, the first is called coniectura, that is, conjecture. When the accused denies the charge, the matter is then worked out by conjecture, with signs and with arguments. King Solomon did this: "Bring a sword," he said, "and divide the living child into two parts." The second is called finis, definition. When the name of the crime is uncertain, it must be defined. This happens, for example, when sacred vessels are taken from outside the church, and it is in doubt whether that should be called theft or sacrilege. Judges cannot give judgment until the name of the crime has been defined. The third is called translatio, that is, change and misplacement. Change of what? Of place, time, person, crime, or punishment. They argue that it did not happen

where it should have, nor when it should have, nor before the one it should have. They also argue that the charges are not the ones the accused was charged with in writing, as often happened at Rome, where the charges were written up wrongly. It also happens that offences are punished more harshly or more lightly than is right. This dispute is called 'change' because it arises from change. For example, Gregory charged John of Constantinople with wearing the pallium when he should not have, and in the street, where he should not have. And Paul charged the faithful with bringing their lawsuits before unbelievers. And as we often say: why does one take only the property of a man whom one should have seized himself? Or why does one kill a man who has deserved a lesser punishment? The fourth rational status is called qualitas. It gets its name from the fact

that it examines the quality of the deed, I mean whether it is good or bad, right or wrong. Because qualitas has two parts, it is to be examined in its parts. What are its parts? They are negotiale and iuridiciale. Negotiale is the dispute that arises over custom. For example, merchants argue that a purchase made at the annual fair must stand, whether it is right or wrong, because that is their custom. Iuridiciale gets its name from the same source as the iuridici. At Rome, the men who declared the city law in court were called iuridici, and so a dispute in words that comes from this is called iuridicialis. Its parts are also two: absolutum and assumptivum. Absolutum means 'bare', because there is no excuse in it, except that the accused says plainly that he was fully entitled to do it.

…what he is reproached with. As Cicero says, the poet Pacuvius complained to him of the insult that an actor had dared to call him by name there at his house. The actor had no other excuse except that he was quite entitled to name him as he was called. Assumptivum is named from the assumption of a defence, that is, from putting forward a defence. This status has four parts. One is called relatio, that is, turning back, as Samson turned his guilt back on the Philistines when they accused him of burning their fields of grain. The second part is called remotio, that is, removal, as the woman removed the guilt from herself and laid it on another when she said: "The serpent deceived me." The third part is called comparatio (comparison).

An example is the man who excused himself by comparison: to free the army he gave the enemy arms and baggage, that is, weapons and provisions, and said that this was better than losing the army itself. The fourth part is called concessio, that is, confession. This dispute divides into deprecatio and purgatio, that is, into plea and excuse. Deprecatio is when the guilty person says, "I have sinned; forgive me," and does not contest the charge himself. The others who sit in judgement do argue, however, over whether he should be forgiven or not. Purgatio is threefold. One purgatio is called casus, that is, chance. A man excuses himself by casus when he says that another man's death, or his own sickness, or some unexpected event hindered him. The second purgatio is called necessitas, that is, necessity. This is the case if he pleads that he was captured, or overpowered by force, or put in chains. The third purgatio is called imprudentia, that is, ignorance. So Paul excused himself when he said: "I did not know that he was the high priest." These are the examples of the statuses that arise in court, that is, those that arise in the judicial kind of case. But those that arise in the demonstrative and deliberative kinds of case, where people deliberate, have the same names, though not such examples. From these examples one easily recognizes those others.

WHAT STATUS IS. Next it should be understood that status and constitutio are one and the same, and they take their name from the fact that the disputants set themselves against one another. Intentio and depulsio make the status. The beginning of the dispute is called intentio, and then depulsio; that is, charge and defense. For example, the accuser says to his adversary in court, "You did it," and he answers, "I did not." Or the accuser says, "You did it unlawfully," and he answers, "I did it lawfully." When the depulsio takes the form "I did it lawfully; I harmed him deservedly," it must at once give a ratio (reason) for this, such as: "For he harmed me first." The accuser then makes an infirmatio of this ratio, that is, a weakening of it, such as: "You ought not to have avenged your own injury." But if the accused says, "I did not do it; I did no harm," no ratio follows that depulsio, for what reason can someone give who admits to nothing? Then the accuser must turn to conjectures, so that he can convict the accused of lying. From these two, the dispute passes to the others who are present in court, so that they too begin to argue whether he did it, or, if he did it, whether he did it lawfully. The judges bring that dispute to an end, because it rests on their judgment whether he is to be held

guilty or innocent, and by their judgment he is either acquitted or punished. Before things come to that, the orator has to show the mastery of his speech and to bring forward everything that can help the case succeed. With it he can make credible to the judges whatever he wants them to hold as right or as wrong, and whomever he wants them to hold as guilty or as innocent. This means how he should proceed in the exordium, then in the narratio, then in the confirmatio, and finally in the conclusio; and in all of these, how seemly, how subtle, how playful where that fits, how wrathful,
how threatening, and how he should adjust his manner of speaking in every way. Cicero's books on the art of rhetoric are full of this.

ON THE PRESENT STATUS. Now let us also look in this dispute between Boethius and Fortune for the intentio (charge) and the depulsio (rebuttal). The intentio is Boethius's complaint: "Was Fortune then not ashamed at all?" and again: "We men are tossed on the sea of Fortune." The depulsio is when she says: "O man, which of your goods have we taken away? No violence has been done to you by us." The ratio (reason) of the depulsio is this: "Wealth, honours and the other things of that kind are under my law. The handmaids know their mistress. They come with me; when I go away, they depart." This reason is very strong.

…that Philosophy has charged him with: that he cannot answer against it straight away. As she says there: "If Fortune were speaking with you thus on her own behalf, you would certainly have nothing to mutter in reply." With these words she has charged him with weakness of reason. And because Fortune is in the right, and he cannot deny that this is her way, she now wants to instruct him by rhetoric: that he should not long so soon for her good, which is so unstable, and that he should desire only that good which, once it has come to him, can never again slip away.

IT FOLLOWS. "These things delight only while they are being heard." Such fine speeches are pleasing only for as long as one hears them. "But the wretched have a deeper sense of their ills." But the afflicted have more…

…of what weighs on them; they feel more of their sorrow. "And so, when these things stop sounding in the ears, the grief rooted within weighs down the mind." As soon as they stop hearing this, the pain struck into the heart weighs on them again. And she said: "So it is." "That is so," she said. "For these are not yet the remedies for your sickness." These are not yet the proper medicines for your illness. "They are only soothing applications for a pain that still resists cure." They are only poultices for your pain, which is unwilling to heal. "For when the time is right, I will apply those that go deep." When it is time, I will give you potions that go right through you. "Nevertheless, do not want to be thought wretched, that is, do not think yourself wretched." But meanwhile, take good comfort and do not consider yourself wretched.

ON THE GOOD THINGS RECEIVED. "Have you forgotten the number and measure of your happiness?" Have you forgotten your good fortunes, what kind they were and how many? "I say nothing of how, when you were bereft of your father, the care of the highest men took you in." I will say nothing about this: when you became an orphan, the most noble men took you into their care. "And chosen to be related by marriage to the leading men of the city…"

"…you began to be dear to them before you were their kin, which is the most precious kind of kinship." And you were chosen into the family of the noblest men in Rome, that is, chosen as son-in-law to your father-in-law Symmachus. You were dear to him before you became his kin. That is the best kind of kinship, when a man first makes sure [?] that he is loved.
"Who did not proclaim you most fortunate, with a father-in-law of such distinction,
with so modest a wife, and also with the blessing of male children?

Who did not call you blessed then, with such a father-in-law and such a mother-in-law, so chaste a wife, and such honorable sons? "I pass over the honors you received in youth, which are denied to old men." I will not speak of how, as a young man, you won the high office that old men could not win: you became consul while still young. "For I prefer to pass over what is common,

and I am glad to come to the unique peak of your happiness." What also happened to others I will pass over. I want to come to your great and special fortunes; it is of these that I will speak. "If any enjoyment of mortal things…"

…has no weight of blessedness. Can the memory of that light, that is, of prosperity, be wiped out by any mass of onrushing evils, however great? If human happiness amounts to any blessedness, can it then be robbed of [?] that shining glory by any misfortune that has happened? When you saw your two sons conducted together from your house, amid a throng of senators, amid the eagerness of the people. I mean: that you saw your two sons led together from your house with the whole multitude of the lords and with the joy of all the people, which brought them with those honours into the senate house, and both together received the consulship. When, with them seated in the senate house on the curule chairs, you, as the orator of the king's praise, earned glory for your intellect and eloquence. When they were sitting in the senate house

on the lordly seat, you, being the orator, were honoured for your intellect and your eloquence in the king's praise. It was the custom at Rome, when kings came back from war with victory, that the most eloquent man was entrusted with delivering the victory-praise in the Capitol before all the people, as was then done for him. But when he says 'seated on the curule chairs', he says it for this reason: because kings sat on the tribunal, where they held court or where they laid down laws for the people, but magistrates sat on curule chairs when they made civic law for the people. They were called 'curules' as if 'currules', because formerly the consuls, riding to the senate house in a chariot, sat upon it. When in the circus, in the middle between the two consuls, you satisfied the expectation of the multitude crowded around
with a triumphal largess. Then this also happened: that you, sitting in the middle between the two consuls, distributed the victory-gifts generously to the whole multitude.

ON THE TROPHY AND THE TRIUMPH. Of these victory-honours there were two, the lesser and the greater. The lesser was called in Greek 'tropheum'; that was when the enemy had been turned to flight. Then the victor came riding from the war on a white horse. On it he was received by the common people, without the senators; they led him, riding, to the Capitol, and sheep were slaughtered there as a sacrifice. For this reason that sacrifice was called 'ovatium' (ovation). But the greater victory-honour, of which he is speaking now, was called in Greek 'triumphus'; that was when the enemy had been slain.

Then the victor came from the war riding in a chariot drawn by four white horses. In it the senators, together with the common people, received him and led him to the Capitol, and there they sacrificed bulls. And for the common rejoicing, public treasure was taken out of the treasury and given to all the citizens; and palms were put into the victors' hands and a laurel crown on their heads, and the victory was glorified with praise, as was said above. He who was entrusted with delivering that praise or distributing the treasure was very greatly honoured. 'Sigo' (victory) takes its name from the 'signa' (standards): when the standards are taken from the enemy, that is called 'taking victory'.
ON THE INDULGENCE OF FORTUNE. You have, I think, cheated Fortune.

"While she soothes you, while she cherishes you as her darling." I think you deceived Fortune, so that she pampered you and cherished you so much. "Demulcet" means "strokes," as one does to someone one pampers. "Delitiae" are cherished things that we keep for pleasure, not for need, such as turtledoves and parrots. "You carried off a gift that she had never yet lent to any private person." You won from her what she has never yet given to anyone in particular, to none of your peers. When she says "private person," she excepts only the king. All who are not kings are called private persons.
Do you wish, then, to settle accounts with Fortune?

Do you want to reckon with her now? Has she now for the first time grazed you with a jealous eye? Only now, looking at you darkly, has she oppressed you? If you consider the number and measure of joyful and sad things, you still could not deny that you are fortunate.

If you count and weigh what you still have of both, sorrow and joy, then you will not yet deny that you are blessed. But if you do not think yourself fortunate because the things that seemed joyful then have gone, there is no reason to think yourself wretched, since the things now believed to be sad are passing away. If you think yourself unhappy because what gladdened you has gone, then what now grieves you will also go away. Therefore you should not think yourself wretched. This is called an argument from contraries.
"Or have you only now come here suddenly, a stranger, onto this stage of life?"

Are you such a newly arrived guest here on the stage of this life of ours? On the stage two kinds of stories were performed in turn: stories of happy things, as comedies are, and stories of sad things, as tragedies are. Because happy and sad things also come to us in turn, our life is like the stage. "Do you think there is any constancy in human affairs?" Do you think there is any steadiness in the affairs of men? "When a swift hour often destroys man himself?" When a short while often destroys even man himself?

For even if chance things rarely keep faith and remain, still the last day of life is a kind of death even for fortune that does remain. Even if there is seldom any constancy in anyone's fortunes, his end is always the end of those same fortunes, even if they had stayed fully with him until then.

What difference, then, do you think it makes whether you leave her by dying or she leaves you by fleeing? What difference do you see in this: whether you leave her by dying, or she leaves you by fleeing from you?
ALL WORLDLY THINGS ARE UNSTABLE. When Phoebus in his rosy four-horse chariot has begun to scatter light across the sky,
the star, dimmed, grows pale,
its white face overwhelmed by the pressing flames. When the morning-red sun, riding on its chariot, as the stories say, begins to shine, the stars grow dark, their pale faces covered by its rays.
When the grove has turned red under the breath of the warm Zephyr,
that is, the rose garden with spring roses,
let the cloudy south wind blow wildly,
and at once the beauty departs from the thorns.
When in spring, from the warmth of the west wind, roses spring up across the field, and then the cloudy south wind comes hot, the flowers must fall from the thorns. In calm, clear weather
the sea often gleams with unmoving waves;
often the north wind stirs up raging storms
and churns up the sea. At one time the sea is still and clear; at another it is churned and turns murky.
If the world's form rarely stays firm,
if it goes through so many changes,
go on, trust in the perishable fortunes of men,
trust in fleeting goods!
It is fixed and laid down by eternal law
that nothing born stays firm.

If the form of the whole world is unstable, and if it changes so often, then go and rely on transient fortunes and on the unstable goods of men! For it is certain and firmly established that nothing born is constant.
LIKEWISE: THAT HE IS NOT DEPRIVED OF ALL HAPPINESS. Then I said, I answered her: "What you recall is true, O nurse of all virtues. What you say is true, teacher of all virtues.
Nor can I deny the very swift course of my prosperity. Nor can I deny my prosperous course. But this is what burns more fiercely in one who recalls it.

That is what hurts me when I remember it. That burns me. For in every adversity of fortune, the unhappiest kind of misfortune is to have been happy. Among all misfortunes, no kind of unhappiness is as great as this: that a person remembers having been happy before. She said. Then she answered: But you cannot rightly blame things for the penalty you pay for your false opinion. It is not the fault of things that you suffer for your false belief. Know that you cannot blame them for it.
For if this empty name of chance happiness moves you,

you may reckon with me how many very great things you have in abundance. Since the bare name of happiness seems so weighty to you, then count with me and try to defeat me: you still have enough of many blessings. What you call blessings, though they are not truly so, have not yet escaped you.
Therefore, if what you possessed as the most precious thing in the whole wealth of your fortune is still preserved for you by God, unharmed and inviolate,
can you rightly complain, when you still keep all the better things?

Has God still kept for you, whole and unharmed, what you held dearest in all your treasure? Then by what right do you complain, when you have it, and have the best of it, as if you had nothing? Atqui (and yet) that most precious ornament of the human race lives unharmed: Symmachus, your father-in-law. Truly he still lives in good health, the honour of all men, Symmachus your father-in-law. And what you would not be slow to buy at the price of your life. And in him you have what you would gladly buy with your life.
A man made wholly of wisdom and virtues. He who is all virtue and wisdom. Secure about his own (that is, wrongs), he groans over the wrongs done to you.

And, [?] his own [?], he laments only you. Your wife lives, modest in disposition, excelling in chastity and modesty. Your wife lives, well brought up in every virtue, outstanding in chastity and honour. And to sum up all her endowments briefly, she is like her father. And to sum up all her dowry together: she is like her father. The goods that a wife brings with her to her husband are her dowry.

"She lives, I say." She lives, I say. "And weary of this life, she keeps her breath for you alone." And though she is weary of this life, she gladly keeps her breath in her only for your sake, so that she may see how things go with you.

"And she pines with longing for you, in tears and grief. In this one thing I would even grant that your happiness is lessened." And longing for you, she wastes away weeping and grieving. In this one thing I am even willing to grant you a lessening of your happiness.
What shall I say of your consular children?

What need I say about your sons who were consuls? Consulars are those who were consuls, or are worthy to become consuls. In whom already shines the likeness of their father's or grandfather's talent, as far as it can in boys of that age. In whom already shines the wisdom of their father and the understanding of their ancestors, as much as can shine at that age.

Since, therefore, the chief care of mortals is to keep their life, O how happy you are, if you recognize your blessings, you who even now have things that no one doubts are dearer than life. Since people hold nothing so dear as life, truly happy are you, then, if you know what is good for you: you still have what is dearer than life. In rhetoric, that persuasion is the most honourable and the most powerful which is made with the comparative, which can do more than the superlative.
So dry your tears.

Fortune does not yet hate all to the last one, that is, everyone without exception. Therefore wipe away your tears; Fortune does not yet hold them all in hatred. She is still gracious to your friends, though she oppresses you. Nor has too violent a storm fallen upon you, since the anchors still hold fast, which do not allow comfort for the present or hope for the future to be lacking. Nor has too strong a storm met you, since the sinking-hooks still hold fast, which do not leave you without comfort, now or hereafter. When the wind is moderate, anchors can hold a ship in place; when a powerful storm comes, they cannot. Anchors are heavy, hooked irons, named in Greek from the hand, because they hook themselves firmly onto the stones and the ground where one wants to moor the ship.

REPLY. "Let them hold, I pray," I said. "May they hold," I said. "For as long as they remain, however things may be, we shall swim out of it. As long as they stand in place, however things may be, we shall come through safely.
But you see how much has been taken from our honours." But what of our honours has gone from us, that you see."
AGAIN, PHILOSOPHY ON THE HUMAN CONDITION. But she said: "We have made some progress.

So it is already somewhat better with you now," she said, "if you are not yet weary of your whole lot. If you are not equally displeased with all of what has fallen to you by lot, if you still put your trust in your friends. But I cannot bear your delicacy, you who complain so mournfully and anxiously that something is lacking to your happiness. But it weighs on me that you are so pampered that you complain so wretchedly and so anxiously that anything of your happiness is missing.
For who has happiness so well arranged that he does not quarrel, in some respect, with the nature of his condition? Who is so fully happy

that he does not struggle somewhere over his affairs, over the way they stand? For the condition of human goods is an anxious thing. The nature of human good always leads toward anxieties. And it either never arrives complete or never lasts forever. And it is such that it never comes in full, or if it does come, it still does not last. A man never gets all his affairs in order, or if he does get them in order, it does not last.

DISTINCTION OF THE HUMAN CONDITION. One man has wealth in abundance, but his low-born blood is a shame to him. Some man is rich but is of low birth. Another is made well known by his nobility, but, hemmed in by the narrowness of his household means, he would rather be unknown. Some man is well known for his noble birth, but this grieves him because of his poor household means.
Another, who has plenty of both, weeps over his unmarried life.

[?]s, if perhaps he cannot find [a wife] worthy of his birth. One man has plenty of both, and yet he complains that he is unmarried. That man, happy in his marriage but without children, builds up his wealth for a stranger as heir. One man is well married and yet has no heirs; he hoards treasure for people who are not his heirs. Another, gladdened by a son or daughter, weeps in sorrow at their misdeeds. One man has plenty of children, and yet he complains that they are wicked.
Therefore no one is easily in agreement with the condition of his fortune. So there is no one who has come to terms with the condition of his life.
For in each person's lot there is something that the one who has not tried it does not know, and the one who has tried it shudders at. Things befall everyone that are unknown to them!

before they try them, and once they have tried them, those things displease them. Add to this that the most fortunate people are also the most easily hurt. Unless everything is ready at their command, they are cast down by the smallest things, because they are not used to any adversity. Add to that that some man who is blessed in every way is so delicate that if everything is not as he wishes, he is at once upset, even by a little thing, because he is so unused to hardship.
So very small are the things that take the height of happiness away from the most fortunate. Such small things deprive even those who are well blessed

that they do not become fully happy. How many do you suppose there are who would think themselves next to heaven if even the smallest part of what remains of your fortune came to them? How many do you think would consider themselves splendidly blessed if they had even a small part of your happiness?
This very place, which you call exile,
is a homeland to those who live in it.

This same place that you call exile is home to the people who live there. So true is it that nothing is wretched unless you think it so. And on the other hand, every lot is happy for the one who bears it with an even mind. So certainly there is no misery unless a person considers it misery. On the other hand, whatever lot falls to a person is happy if he bears it with an even mind.
Who is so happy that, once he has given himself up to impatience,

he would not wish to change his state? Who is there who gives himself up to impatience and does not want to change his situation, however it stands? With how many bitter things is the sweetness of human happiness sprinkled! Is this happy sweetness not mixed with much bitterness?
Even if it seems pleasant to the one who enjoys it,
"yet she cannot be held back from going away when she wishes." She is never so sweet to the one who enjoys her that he can make her linger so that she does not leave

when she wishes? "It is clear, then, how wretched the happiness of mortal things is." Now it is plain how miserable the happiness of men is. "It does not last forever with the even-tempered, nor does it fully delight the anxious." It never becomes lasting even with the even-tempered, and it does not please the troubled and anxious, even when they have plenty of it.

[ON] HAPPINESS. HE ARGUES THAT BLESSEDNESS IS NOT IN PRESENT THINGS. Why then, O mortals, do you look outside yourselves for the happiness that is placed within you? Why do you people go searching elsewhere for the happiness that you have within yourselves?
Error and ignorance confuse you.

You do not know it; you have mistaken it, and that leads you astray. I will briefly show you the hinge on which the highest happiness turns. I will show you what the greatest happiness consists in, and on what it turns. Is anything more precious to you than yourself? Is anything dearer to you than you yourself?
Nothing, you will say. No, you say. Therefore, if you are master of yourself, you will possess what you would never wish to lose,

and what fortune could not take away. If you will rule yourself so that you hold fortune in contempt, then you gain what you will never willingly lose, and what fortune cannot take from you either. By this both will be remedied for you, both the anxiety and the instability of which I spoke before.
And so that you may recognize that happiness cannot consist in these chance things,

Reason it out like this. And so that you may know that happiness does not lie in these uncertain things, consider it like this. If blessedness is the highest good of a nature that lives by reason, — If happiness is the foremost good of human beings, — Suspension [of the sentence]. and if that which can in any way be snatched away is not the highest good — and if that which one can lose is not the foremost good — And here.
Since that which cannot be taken away is superior,

For that alone is the highest which cannot be taken away from a man. And here: It is manifest that the instability of fortune could not aspire to the attainment of beatitude. So there is no doubt that unstable fortune cannot help a man at all to win blessedness. The argument says: because blessedness lies in the highest good, where that is lacking there is no blessedness. This argument is called 'from the cause', because the highest good is the cause of beatitude.

Furthermore. To this I tell you further: Whom this transitory felicity carries, that is, exalts, either knows it to be changeable or does not know it. There can be no third case: the one whom this fleeting fortune lifts up either knows that it lasts only so short a while, or does not know it. That is an argument from contraries. If he does not know, what happy lot can there be in the blindness of ignorance? If he does not know it, how can a happy lot have fallen to him in that ignorance? If he knows.
he must fear that he will lose what he does not doubt can be lost.

But if he does know it, then he must necessarily fear losing what he knows he can lose. Therefore continual fear does not let him be happy. Therefore the constant fear does not let him be happy. An argument of this kind is called in rhetoric comprehensio, that is, 'capture', because he cannot escape it without being caught. So now it says: whether he knows or does not know that fortune is unstable, he is never happy. So it is in the Gospel: 'Was the baptism of John from heaven, or from men?' Whether they said 'from heaven' or 'from men', they would have been caught. Or, if he loses it, does he think it should be disregarded? Or does he think that, if he loses it, he can console himself for it?

So too it is a very slight good that can be borne with a calm mind once it is lost. So it appears worthless and contemptible, so that it grieves us little when we lose it. All this is dissuasive speech, by which she turns him away so that he does not love fleeting felicity, because that is useless and not necessary.
And since you are the same one who, I know, has been persuaded and had it instilled by very many demonstrations that the minds of men are in no way mortal.

Suspension. And since you are the one to whom it has been made known, and in whom it has been instilled by manifold teaching, that men's souls cannot die. And since it is clear that fortuitous felicity is ended by the death of the body. And here: And since it is then plain that worldly fortune dies together with the body. It cannot be doubted, if this can bring beatitude, that the whole race of mortals slips into misery at the end brought by death. So there is no doubt, if it gives blessedness, that all men, in dying, go to misery. That is called an argument from antecedents, because if beatitude dies first [?].

then misery necessarily follows. But if we know that many have sought the fruit of happiness not only through death but also through pains and tortures, how can the present life make people happy, when its passing does not make them miserable?

If many have won happiness through death and through other sufferings, as the martyrs did, how can the present life make people happy, when its passing does not make them wretched? This is called an argument from contraries (argumentum a repugnantibus), since 'present' and 'past' are contraries. They are contraries because one tends away and the other tends this way.
HOW TRANQUILLITY IS TO BE KEPT.
Whoever, being cautious, wishes to set up a lasting seat. Whoever, for safety's sake, wishes to make his dwelling everlasting,
and stable,
and not to be laid low by the blasts of the roaring east wind. He who does not want to be thrown down by the roaring winds. And who takes care to scorn the sea
threatening with its waves. And who does not want to fear the threateningly surging sea:
let him avoid the summit of the high mountain,
let him avoid the thirsty sands. Let him build neither on the height of the mountain nor on the gravel of the shore.
The wanton south wind presses upon the one
with all its strength;
the others, being loose,
refuse to bear the hanging weight. There the wind seeks him out with all its might; here there is no firmness underneath that can bear the building.
Fleeing the perilous lot of a pleasant dwelling.
remember to build your house securely on a low rock. If you wish to flee a perilous place by building beautifully, then seek a low stone, on which you may build with confidence.
Although the wind thunders,
mixing the seas with ruin. Even though the roaring wind churns the sea and fells the forest,
you, happy, set within the strength of a quiet rampart,
will lead your life serene,
laughing at the angers of the sky. You will always lead your life in rest, happily lying hidden as if in a fortress, laughing at the weather's unruliness.

HERE SHE BEGINS TO ARGUE ABOUT THE THINGS THEMSELVES. But since the soothing remedies of my reasoning are now sinking into you, I think somewhat stronger (that is, remedies) should be used. Since my words, with which I have been bandaging you until now, are getting into you, I think it is now time to start on stronger arguments. Up to this point she has spoken with him by persuading and dissuading, according to the art of rhetoric, since the office of the orator is to urge what is honourable.

…useful, necessary, possible things; and, on the other hand, to dissuade from shameful, useless, unnecessary, impossible things. Now she wishes to dispute; that does not concern the orator at all, but the philosopher. To dispute means to treat of the natures of things, or of God, or of morals. Yet we should note that from here on she begins to do both: both to dispute and to persuade. Come now. Come, then, tell me what I ask.
If the gifts of Fortune were not fleeting and momentary,
What is there in them, that is, in the gifts, that could either ever become yours, or that, once looked into and considered, does not become cheap?

If these slippery and fleeting gifts of fortune were not so, what of these gifts could ever become yours if she did not grant them to you? Or what would you care for them, when you examine them closely? A man has no power to be rich unless fortune grants it to him; that very wealth is contemptible in its own nature.
ON MONEY. "Are riches precious through your nature or through their own?"

"Are they precious?" Are riches precious in themselves, or because of you? "Which of them is more so?" Which of the two is more precious? "Gold, or a great heap of money?" Do you think that gold and the gathered mass of treasure are more precious than men? "And yet"
"these shine better when they are spent than when they are heaped up." Truly.

they shine all the better if one gives them out rather than gathers them. Indeed, avarice always makes people hated, while generosity makes them renowned. That is evident from this: greed makes people loathed, while generosity makes them famous and spoken of.
But if what is passed on to another cannot remain with anyone,
then money is precious when it is passed on to others through the practice of giving and so ceases to be possessed.

If a man cannot keep for himself what he gives to another, then it is for that reason to be given, because the treasure becomes precious only when it is gone through spending. But if that same money, as much as there is anywhere among the nations, were heaped up with one person, it would leave all the others without it.

And your treasure is of such a kind that if one man takes hold of all of it, then whatever of it is in the world, the others go without. And the voice, whole, fills the hearing of many alike. Now the voice is a treasure such that all of it is in every man's ears at the same time. But your riches cannot pass to many unless they are broken up. But your wealth is not shared in any other way unless it is divided. And when that is done,
it must make poor those whom it leaves.

When it is divided, those who divide it and let it go are the poorer. O narrow and needy riches, which many may not have whole, and which come to no one without the poverty of the others! Truly, how narrow and how poor is that wealth which many cannot have, and which does not fall to one man without another growing poorer.
ON GEMS. Or does the gleam of gems draw (that is, entice and delight) the eyes? Do you like to look at gems? Is their glitter dear to your eyes?

But if there is anything outstanding in this splendor, that light belongs to the gems, not to men. And indeed I wonder greatly that men admire them. If there is any precious brightness in them, it belongs to them, not to men. And it is a wonder to me that anyone marvels at them.
For what thing that lacks the movement of a soul and the joining together (namely, of limbs) could rightly seem beautiful to a living, rational nature?

What lifeless and limbless thing should seem beautiful to a being with a soul, as man is, and with reason? What should seem beautiful to him is what is like him. Even if these things draw some of the lowest kind of beauty from the work of their creator and from their own distinctiveness, they are placed beneath your excellence and in no way deserved your admiration. Even if, by God's will and by their own colouring, they have something of the lowest beauty, they are still far removed from your high rank, and so they ought not to seem wonderful to you.
ON THE BEAUTY OF THE WORLD.
Or does the beauty of the fields delight you? Does the field seem beautiful to you?

Why not? Why should it not? For it is a beautiful part of a most beautiful work. It is a beautiful part of the beautiful world. So we sometimes rejoice at the face of a calm sea. So too the sea is lovely to look at when it is still. So we marvel at the sky, the stars, the moon and the sun. So we hold the heaven itself and all the stars to be a wonder. Does any of these touch you? Indeed? Does any of them concern you? Does it give you anything of its beauty?
Surely you do not dare to boast of the splendour of any such thing?

Do you dare to boast at all of their beauty? Or are you yourself made bright with spring flowers? Can you be made colourful like the flowers? Or does your fruitfulness swell into summer fruits? Or will you become the equal of the summer crops?
Why are you carried away by empty joys?

Why do you give yourself over to such vain delight? Why do you embrace outside goods as your own? Why is someone else's good dearer to you than your own? Fortune will never make yours what the nature of things has made foreign to you. Fortune cannot give you what nature has shut you out from.
ON FOOD. The fruits of the earth are, without doubt, owed to the nourishment of living creatures. The fruits of the earth shall serve as food for the living, without doubt.
But if you wish to fill the need of nature, which is enough, there is no reason for you to seek the abundance of fortune.

But if you are willing to be content with what nature needs, you will demand no excess from fortune. For the man who has enough is as well off as the man who has too much. For nature is content with few and very small things. With few and little things nature has enough. If you try to press more on its fullness with things it does not need, then what you pour in will become either unpleasant or harmful. If you give it anything beyond that, it will be to you either a displeasure or a harm.

ON CLOTHING. Now do you think it beautiful to shine in varied garments? Do you want to go about adorned in clothing of many kinds? If their appearance is pleasing to the eye, I will admire either the nature of the material or the skill of the craftsman. If it is pleasing to the eyes, then I praise either the skill of the maker or the material of the work.
ON SERVANTS. Or does a long train of servants make you happy?

Does the great number of your servants make you blessed? If they are vicious in their ways, they are a ruinous burden to the house and very hostile to the master himself. If they are of bad character, they are a danger [?] in the house, and a burden, and enemies to the master himself. But if they are honest,
How can another person's goodness be counted among your riches?
But if they are virtuous, how then can another man's virtues be your treasure and your wealth?

THAT THE GOODS HE LISTED BELONG TO OTHERS. From all of this it is clearly shown that none of the things you count among your goods is your own good. From all this it is evident that none of the things you take to be your good is your good.
"If they have no beauty worth desiring, why should you grieve when they are lost

or rejoice when you keep them?" And if they have no beauty that you ought to desire, why should it grieve you to lose them or gladden you to have them? "But if they are beautiful by nature, what does that matter to you?" If they are good by nature in themselves, what is their beauty to you?
For these things would also have pleased in themselves, separated from your wealth. Even if they were not yours, they would still be beautiful.

For they are not precious because they have come into your riches. Nor does the fact that they are yours make them precious. But because they seemed precious, you chose to count them among your riches. Rather, you thrust them in behind you because they seem precious to you.
THAT NEED IS NOT DRIVEN AWAY BY WEALTH. But what do you all want with such a great uproar of fortune? What do you all want to achieve with such a great abundance of your possessions?
You seek, I believe, to drive away need by means of wealth. You want to bring it about, I think, that you lack nothing. But this turns out the opposite for you.
Truly, it turns out quite otherwise. For more help is needed to guard the variety of precious furnishings.

Various more costly treasure also needs a great deal of equipment so that it can be guarded. And that saying is true, that those who possess a great deal need a great deal. And it is a true proverb, the one people say: whoever has much also needs much. And on the other hand, those need very little. But on the other hand, those need little who measure their abundance by the needs of nature,
not by the excess of ambition. These are the ones who make sure that they provide their means according to natural need, not according to the immoderation of greed.
ON ONE'S OWN NATURAL GOOD. Is there, then, no good

that is your own and implanted in you, so that you seek your goods in external and remote things? Are you then so lacking in yourselves that you have no good of your own, nor one implanted by nature, so that you seek it in other things?
Is the order of things so overturned that a creature made divine by the merit of reason
does not seem to itself to shine in any other way than by the possession of lifeless furnishings?

Shall the order of created things now be so overturned that man, who is more like God in the dignity of his reason, should not seem beautiful to himself except through the possession of a lifeless thing? And other things are indeed content with their own. The other animals are all content with their own good. But you, who are like God in mind,

seek ornaments for your excellent nature from the lowest things. But you, who are like God in your mind, want to seek adornment for your excellent nature in the lowest things. Nor do you understand how great an injury you do to your creator. Nor do you know how great a dishonor you do to God.
He wanted the human race to stand above all earthly things;
"you thrust your dignity down below even the lowest things." He wanted mankind to be the highest of all earthly things, but you make your lordship lower than the lowest things.

For if everything that is anyone's good is evidently more precious than the one whose good it is (that is, as God is the good of the just, so it is evident that God is more precious than all the just), then when you judge the vilest of things to be your goods (that is, not God), you subject yourselves to them by your own estimation. If each thing's good is more precious than the thing itself, and you consider your good to be the lowest thing, then you put yourselves beneath it; that is, you are lower than it, by your own estimation. This is called an argument from the greater: if riches are greater in value, then the rich are lesser in value. And this indeed happens not undeservedly. It happens to you rightly.
For this is the condition of human nature, that only when it knows itself does it excel other things. The nature of man is so made

that it is above other things only when it knows itself. Yet the same nature is reduced below the beasts if it ceases to know itself. And yet it is lower than the animals if it does not know itself. For in other living creatures it is natural not to know themselves; in men it comes from vice. That is because in animals it is their nature that they do not know themselves, but in men it comes from vices.
THAT NO ONE BECOMES BEAUTIFUL THROUGH OUTWARD ADORNMENT. But how widely this error of yours extends!

you who think that something can be adorned with the adornments of others. How far this error goes, and how many of you are deceived by it, in that you think that anyone is adorned by outward ornament.
But that cannot happen.

Now that cannot be. For if anything shines among the things added to it, it is the added things themselves that are praised. If anything bears something beautiful on it, people praise what it bears. But the thing covered and veiled by them still remains in its own foulness.

But whatever is concealed underneath keeps its ugliness in full. For my part, I deny that anything is good which harms the one who has it. I mean to say that what harms the person who has it is not good. Am I lying about this? Am I lying, then? Not at all, you say. You are not, you say. And yet

Riches have very often harmed those who possess them. Wealth has often harmed the one who had it. For every most wicked person, and therefore all the more greedy for what belongs to others, thinks himself alone most worthy to have whatever gold and gems there are anywhere.
I mean, when some wicked creature, all the more greedy for other people's goods, considers himself alone worthy to have all the treasure there is anywhere.
So you, who now anxiously dread the pike and the sword: if you had set out on the path of this life as a traveller with empty hands, you would sing in the robber's face.

So I tell you, you who now worry that someone will kill you: if you travelled through this life bare, you could even sing boldly in front of robbers. O splendid happiness of mortal riches: once you have gained it, you are no longer safe! Well, how precious the blessings of the wealthy are! They are truly so precious that once you win them, you are never safe again. This is called ironic mockery.
THAT THE ANCIENTS WERE CONTENT WITH LITTLE. Too happy was the former age. The earlier world was very happy.
Content with its faithful fields, that is, fertile ones. It was satisfied with what its land produced.
Nor was it ruined by idle luxury, that is, by the excess that makes people idle. It was neither ruined by immoderation nor corrupted by it.
It used to end its late fasts with acorns that were easily gathered. It was in the habit of eating late, and of simple food.
It did not know how to mix the gifts of Bacchus with clear honey. It did not know what [?] was; it had never learned to mix wine with honey.
Nor to mix, that is, to dye, the bright fleeces of the Seres [?, text garbled: 'servm!']

with Tyrian dye. Nor to colour the beautiful silk of the Seres with Tyrian juice. The Seres live far away in the east, next to India. They strip a kind of wool from their trees, which we call silk. It is spun into yarn, the yarn is dyed in various colours, and costly cloaks are made from it. But when people want to make purple, they look in the sea for the creatures that are called conchilia in Latin. These lie enclosed between two shells. The shells bleed when they are broken open, and the purple is dyed with that blood. Because the finest purple is made at Tyre, and that is also where it was first made, he says 'Tyrian'.
The grass gave them healthy sleep. In those days people slept healthily on the grass; they had no feather beds.
The gliding river gave them drink as well. The water gave them their drink.
The very tall pine gave them shade. Trees shaded them; they had no houses.
No stranger yet cut through the deep waters of the sea. Back then nobody yet travelled across the sea.
Nor with chosen goods
had seen new shores. Nor did he land, with merchandise gathered together, on an unknown shore.
Then the savage war-trumpets were silent. Then the perilous war-horns, with which men are now directed to battle, did not sound.
Nor had blood shed in bitter hatreds
stained the rough fields. Nor did blood that came from hostile wounds make the earth bloody.
For why would hostile fury want to be the first to take up any arms? Why should enmity come first? That is, why should anyone be the first to fight out of enmity?
When they saw cruel wounds
nor any rewards for blood. When they saw wounds

and no reward for the wounds? If only our times would now return to the ancient customs! Would to God that these times of ours turned back to the old customs. But the love of having burns fervently, fiercer than the fires of Etna. Now there is nothing of that; instead greed is now kindled, surging and boiling more fiercely than the fire in Etna. Etna burns in Sicily, as Vesuvius does in Campania, and Clemax [?] in Cilicia. Alas, who was he who first dug up the weights of hidden gold, and gems that wished to lie hidden, precious perils? Ah, all too grievously! Who was it ever who first dug gold and gems out of the earth, perilous treasures, which would still gladly have lain within
if they had been allowed.

WHAT THE DIFFERENCE IS BETWEEN RHETORICAL PERSUASION AND PHILOSOPHICAL DISPUTATION. Here you should notice what difference there is between rhetorical persuasion, with which she began at first, and philosophical disputation, in which she is now engaged. When she found him sick in his mind, and he blamed Fortune for it, as if he were pleading a case against her in court for having brought him to this, then she, being a physician, had first of all to heal his mind by clearing Fortune of what he accused her of. She did this with the defenses: that one should expect nothing better from her, nor ought anyone hope for anything better from her, and that she cannot become anything other than what she always was, and that if Fortune begins to be stable

…that she would not be Fortune [if she stayed constant]. And [she asks] to whom she has ever yet been constant, and [points out] that he has had her with him the longest. And since she has treated him better than others, why does he blame her? And [she says] that she has not yet actually failed him, and that what can be dearest to him has not slipped away from him. And, at the very least, that she has not carried off anything of his own from him; and that she was bound to grant him her goods only for as long as she wished, and was entitled to take her goods back to herself; and that he is sick more from his own impatience than from any injustice of hers. And [she says] he may call on whatever advocate he likes, and she will defend herself well against him in court. Who does not recognize that this speech, and everything connected with it, belongs wholly to the orator's office? And who does not know that this is the proper sport of rhetorical eloquence? With what are judges and legal experts occupied, if not with disputes like this? This kind of case is called forensic. Such controversies resound in the forum. In these there is persuasion and dissuasion. With what can one persuade or dissuade in court, if not with what is just and what is unjust? With what could she quiet him now, except by making him acknowledge that he has no just claim against Fortune? When one begins to show how just or how unjust it is that one person makes a claim against another, then persuasion and dissuasion succeed. And because she has now relieved him of his pain,

with the satisfactio [?], she therefore now steps down from persuasion to disputation, so that she may thereby fully heal his mind. Now let us understand well that in a speech where people sit in deliberation over whether this or that is to be done or left undone, persuasion and dissuasion must be carried out by means of the useful and the useless. As Livy writes, how great a dispute there was at Rome after the Gauls burned the city, over whether they should abandon Rome and move to the city of Veii, which was then wholly in their power, and settle there from then on, or not. Who could have spoken in that dispute about whether it was right or wrong? What had to be argued there was whether it was useful or useless. And all the persuasion

[the persuasion] that was involved in it hastened to make one of the two plausible: that the thing would be useful to do, or to leave undone [?]. But in the demonstrative kind of case, when people sit in contentious council over whom this or that should be entrusted to, then in persuasion one must name honorableness — I mean the honorableness of the person being recommended for it — and in dissuasion one must name his baseness, if he is being rejected. This is what happened with Cicero when he was made consul because of the emergency, since they trusted no one but him to defend them against Catiline and his associates.
