Some praised him for his wisdom. Others said, as Sallust relates in the Catiline, that the consulship was being violated because he had risen from the equestrian order, not from the senatorial. Questions of this kind are called civil, because they arise among citizens.

That is, 'belonging to the city' or 'belonging to the citizens.' As we have said, these involve persuasion and dissuasion, and these are what the orator takes on. Questions that are not civil, however, are philosophical; they are answered by disputation.

ON THE PARTS OF PHILOSOPHY. Philosophy is divided into divine and human. The divine part was taught by those who wrote for us in books about the nature of God himself and the truth of the Trinity. They are called theologians. The foremost of them was John the Evangelist. The human part is taught to us by the natural philosophers and the moral philosophers, that is, about natures and about morals. The oldest natural philosopher among the Greeks was Pythagoras; after him came Thales and his disciples Anaxagoras, Anaximander and Anaximenes.

They busied themselves with guessing where this world was created from. Some said: out of fire. Some said: out of water. Some said: out of the divine mind. They also inquired why the ebb and flow of the sea happens every day; why eclipses of the sun and moon happen from time to time; why the days of winter are short and those of summer long; where all the sources of rivers come from; whether the sun or the moon is greater; how big the earth is, what it stands on, and what holds it up. Later Ambrose wrote more truly about these and similar things in the Hexameron, and so did others. Bede learned it from them, and afterward he wrote it in his book On the Nature of Things. The ethici are those who teach us to have right morals. The first of these among the Greeks was Socrates. After him there were many Socratics.

Some of them then wrote books, as Panaetius did among the Greeks, and his son, and as Cicero did among the Latins in his book On Duties. In that book Cicero says he wants to complete what Panaetius left unfinished. They told what the society of human life should be like, which we call humanity. Cato also undertook to write about this in verse, in his little book that begins: "If God is a spirit, as poems tell us." But Terence the comic poet did not teach how morals ought to be. Instead he imitated how corrupt they are among people. That is why he said: "I have described the manners of men, of the young and of the old." That means:

I have imitated the manners of people. After that Ambrose also did not fail to write On Duties, that is, what each person's duty is to do and what is incumbent on him to do. From it one can learn integrity of life, which makes a person perfect and holy. This disputation bears on that point: riches cannot make a person blessed, and therefore they are to be despised.

THAT DIGNITIES AND POWERS ARE NOT NATURAL GOODS. "But what should I say about dignities and power?" What can I say about lordship and about power? "By which you make yourselves equal to heaven, ignorant of true dignity and power." These are the things that make you think yourselves as high as heaven, because you do not know the true lordship and the true might. What happiness can they give you?
But if these things should fall to all the most wicked, what fires of Etna with erupting flames, what flood could have wrought such great devastation?

What do they do when they come into the hands of a wicked person? What fire pouring out of Etna, or what flood, does such damage, that is, such destruction of the people? Certainly, as I think you remember, your ancestors wanted to abolish the consular power, which had been the beginning of liberty, because of the pride of the consuls, after they had earlier removed the royal name from the city because of that same pride. Indeed, as I think you remember, as you have read, your forefathers wanted to destroy the office of the consuls because of their arrogance, though that same office had been the beginning of liberty. They wanted to do this, just as they had earlier taken kingly power away from the city. Livy tells how Tarquinius Superbus, who was the seventh king at Rome after Romulus,

was driven out by Brutus and Collatinus and Tricipitinus and by other conspiring citizens because of his arrogance, from which he got his name; and how they agreed to have consuls instead of kings, who would be changed every year, so that they would not become arrogant by holding power for long. When these too, in the course of time, began to practise tyranny, they wanted to destroy that power as well and create new offices, which would be changed more than once a year, so that those who held them could not engage in any insolence in that span of time. If power were good in itself, it would not have become so hateful to them. Liberty is of two kinds. One is that which makes a man free, so that he is no one's slave.

The other is the one she is now speaking of, which releases them even from kingly power, so that a man is under no constraint except the common law. But if ever they are conferred on good men, which is very rare, what else is pleasing in them but the goodness of those who use them? If they also come into the hands of good men, which is very seldom, what can be pleasing in them then except the goodness of those who hold the power? So it happens that honour does not come to virtues from rank, but to ranks from virtue. So you can see that goodness is not adorned by the office, but the office is adorned by goodness.

But what is this power of yours that you so desire and that seems so splendid? What is this power that you pursue so eagerly and that you think so great? Do you not consider, you earthly creatures, who you are and over whom you seem to rule? Do you not know, you creatures of the earth, how lowly you are,
and those over whom you think you rule? Now if you saw among mice one claiming for itself, above the rest, right and power, how much laughter would it move you to?
Well then? If you saw one among the mice seizing power and might for itself, what a laughingstock would that not be to you?

But if you look at the body, what could you find weaker than a human being? If you consider the body, what do you then find more powerless than human beings are? Whom even the bite of little flies often kills, or the entry of creeping things into any of the inner parts. They often die, whether because flies bite them or because something creeps into them.
But over whom could anyone exercise any right except over the body alone, and over what is beneath the body?

In what can anyone show his power except in the body and in what is lower than the body? "I mean fortune": I mean his possessions. "Will you command anything of a free mind?" Can you force anything by threats out of a mind that is its own master? "Will you move a mind held together by firm reason from its state of rest?" Do you think you can stir any mind made firm by reason from its place and bring it out of its stillness? "When a tyrant thought he would force a certain free man, that is, the philosopher Anaxagoras, by tortures…"
to betray those who knew of the conspiracy made against him, he bit his tongue, cut it off, and threw it into the face of the raging tyrant. Do you not know this?

When the tyrant thought to force a man who was master of his own mind by torture to reveal to him those who knew of the conspiracy that had been made against him, he bit off his own tongue and spat it at the tyrant, before his eyes. In this way the tortures, which the tyrant thought were material for cruelty, the wise man made into material for virtue. In this way the wise man armed himself for defense with the very thing by which the tyrant meant to show his ferocity.
But what is there
that anyone can do to another that he cannot suffer himself from another? If a man is powerful, what can he do to another that he cannot suffer the same himself?
We have learned that Busiris was accustomed to kill his guests

was slain by his guest Hercules. We have heard that Busiris always slew his guests and sacrificed them to his gods; for that reason his guest Hercules did the same to him. Many Carthaginians captured in war
Regulus had thrown into chains,
but soon he himself gave his hands to the chains of the victors. Regulus imprisoned many Africans.

and bound those he had captured in war; afterwards he too was captured and bound just as tightly. Read Orosius. Do you think, then, that a man has any power if he cannot prevent another from doing to him what he himself can do to another? Do you think a man has any power if he cannot prevent the same thing he does to another from happening to him? Moreover,
if there were anything naturally and properly good in these ranks and powers themselves, they would never come to the worst men.

And besides, if there were anything naturally good in lordship and in power, they would never come to the worst men. For opposites are not usually joined together. For opposite things do not stay together. Nature refuses to let contraries be joined. Nature does not allow them to unite with each other. So, since there is no doubt
that the worst men very often hold high offices,

this also is clear: that things are not good by their own nature if they allow themselves to cling to the worst men. So it is evident, since the worst men come to offices, that those things are not good which can cling to the worst men.
This, indeed, can be judged even more fittingly of all the gifts of fortune,

which come more abundantly to all the most wicked. That is, one may confidently say this of everything that fortune gives, most of which falls to the worst men. This argument is taken from contraries.
Concerning these things I think this too must be considered: that no one doubts that a man is brave in whom he has seen bravery to be present.
And it is plain that anyone who has speed is swift.

Thus music makes musicians, medicine physicians, rhetoric rhetoricians. Concerning these things it is also to be observed that one knows that man to be strong in whom one recognizes strength, and that man swift in whom one recognizes swiftness; and music makes musicians, medicine physicians, rhetoric rhetoricians.
The nature of each thing does

what is proper to it. The nature of every thing works what it is its kind to work. These arguments are from cause, because qualities, such as bravery and swiftness, are causes, that is, the makings and workings of those who have these qualities, such as the brave and the swift. Nor is it mixed with the effects of contrary things. Nor does it mix itself with the contrary workings, as cowardice is to bravery and slowness to swiftness. And of its own accord it drives away what is opposed to it. And it readily defends itself against the things that are opposed to it. And yet

Nor can riches quench insatiable avarice. Truly, in the same way: just as fortitude takes cowardice away from a man, so riches cannot take away from a man his great greed. Nor will power make him master of himself whom vicious lusts hold bound with unbreakable chains. Nor does power make him master of himself whom his harmful desires bind with strong chains.
And dignity conferred on the wicked

not only does not make them worthy, but rather betrays them and displays them as unworthy. And dignities, which we call lordship, when they come into the hands of the wicked, do not make them worthy; rather, they reveal them all the more to be unworthy, and they make that plain. Why does it turn out so? Why does it go so? What they promise, why can they not do it?
For you delight in calling things by false names, when they are really otherwise.

It is because you choose to name things quite differently from what they really are. "These are easily refuted by the effect of the things themselves." Those misnamings are revealed at once by the working of the things whose names they are. "Therefore neither those riches, nor that power, nor this dignity can rightly be so called." Therefore none of them can rightly be called by the name they are given: not what you call wealth, not what you call power, and not what you call dignity.

"Finally, the same conclusion may be drawn about the whole of fortune, in which it is clear that there is nothing worth seeking and nothing of natural goodness." Finally, I will confirm the same about all worldly fortune: in it there is nothing to be desired, and plainly there is no natural good in it. "Fortune neither always joins itself to the good, nor makes good those to whom it has joined itself." It does not always join itself to the good, nor does it make good those it joins.
WHAT DISPUTATION IS. Reasoning carried out in this way belongs to the philosophers, not to the rhetoricians. Here one should not plead as in court, nor merely talk, but speak with wisdom.

This wise speaking is called disputatio. The name came about because the philosophers doubted about almost all questions, as they did about this one: what the highest good is. Some said wisdom, some virtue, some pleasure. And so disputare was first used to mean diverse putare, 'to think in different ways'. Now, however, we say disputare for affirming or denying with reason what is in doubt. At first the sick man's mind was not in a fit state for her to dispute with him, since disputation is always subtle and sharp. So she had to lead him by rhetorical persuasion, which is more delightful and plainer, to the disputation in which she is now engaged.
EXAMPLE OF THE ABOVE SENTENCE. We know what great ruin he brought about.
he who once set the city on fire and slaughtered the senators (the fathers),
who killed his brother,

and, savage, grew wet with his mother's spilled blood. We know well what great harm Nero did. He burned Rome and slew the lords of the senate. He slew his brother, and after that he grimly bloodied himself with his mother's life-blood.
And running his eyes over her cold body,
he did not wet his face with tears.

And he did not weep when he looked over her whole dead body. Instead he could be the censor, that is, the judge, of the extinguished beauty, that is, of the body. In other words, he could act as appraiser of his slain mother's limbs. Suetonius says that he often tried to poison his mother because she reproached him for his ways. When he did not succeed, since she had protected herself against it with antidotes, he ordered her to be killed with the sword. He was also curious about all her limbs. So he went over her when she was dead, felt her all over, examined her all over, and then said that some of her limbs were well shaped and some badly.
Yet this man ruled with his sceptre the peoples

whom Phoebus sees as he comes from the farthest east and as he hides his rays beneath the waves. He held power over all the peoples whom the sun shines upon, from its coming in the east to its going down in the west.
those whom the cold northern stars (the Septentriones) bear down upon,
those whom the violent south wind scorches with dry heat,
baking the burning sands again. He ruled over all the northern peoples, and over those to whom the hot south wind brings heat as it parches the sandy land.
Could lofty power at last turn aside the rage of wicked Nero? Could that high power turn Nero away from his wickedness at all?

"Alas, a heavy lot, whenever an unjust sword is added to cruel poison!" Ah, that grievously fallen lot, when the sword becomes the companion of poison, that is, when an evil creature becomes powerful.

CONFESSION OF BOETHIUS. Then I said: You know that ambition for mortal things had very little (that is, no) mastery over me. You know well, I said then, that no worldly greed ever took hold of me. But I wanted material for carrying out public affairs, so that my virtue would not grow old in silence. Rather, I always longed to do things in which my virtue would shine out and not grow old unnoticed. And yet this is the one thing
that can allure minds that are excellent by nature but have not yet been brought by the perfection of the virtues to the final finishing hand.

Truly, she said, I know well that this is the one thing that can entice noble minds. Noble ones, I say, not ones that have been brought through the perfection of all the virtues to the final polish. That is a metonymy: he names the agent in place of the agent's action. It is the custom of craftsmen, when they complete their work, to give it a final smoothing. Likewise, those whose virtues are perfect should polish them with their humility. Namely, the desire for glory. Their desire for glory is what entices them into public offices. And the fame of the best services to the commonwealth. And the reputation for great good deeds, which they perform in public.
How slight it is, and how empty of all weight, consider in this way. Consider for yourself in this way how meagre fame is and how weightless.

HOW VAIN EARTHLY GLORY IS, SINCE THE EARTH IS NOTHING IN COMPARISON WITH HEAVEN. It is established that the whole circuit of the earth has the proportion of a point to the expanse of heaven, as you have learned from astronomical demonstrations. It is well known to you, she said, that the whole earth, compared with heaven, amounts to the measure of a single point, as you learned in astronomy. That is, it would be judged to have no extent at all if it were compared with the size of the heavenly sphere. I mean that it has no size compared with the size of heaven. Aristotle teaches in the Categories

that the point is the beginning [?] and the end of a line, and that the parts of a line are divided by a point, and yet because it is so small the point is no part of the line. What can be smaller than something that has neither length nor breadth? Since it has no part in the line whose boundary it is, it is also no part of the circle whose center it is. In the same way the earth also has no size compared with heaven, whose point it is. Of this region, so tiny within the world, only about a fourth part is inhabited by living beings known to us, as Ptolemy proves and as you have learned. Of this same earth, so small compared with heaven, only the fourth part is inhabited by the people known to us. When she says "known to us,"

she says it in the person of humankind, because of the Antipodes, since they are unknown to us. We know that water surrounds the earth, and that the fourth part, toward the top, is laid bare, and on it people live. The heavens teach us that it is the fourth part. All who know astronomy recognize that the equinoctial zone divides the heavens exactly in two, and that from it to the outermost poles the distance is equal on either side, I mean to the northern pole and to the southern. So the earth is round, and we do not know whether it is laid bare on the underside. On the top, where it is bare, people live, from the Ethiopian Ocean to the Scythian Ocean. Those who live farthest to the south live in the Ethiopian islands; for them the sun is directly overhead

when it passes out of Aries in springtime, and when it begins to pass into Libra in autumn. For those who live farther this way, on the Ethiopian coast, it is overhead when it passes through Taurus and through Virgo. For those who live still farther this way, in Meroë, it is overhead when it passes through Gemini and through Leo. For those who live still farther this way, where Syene, a city of Egypt, lies, it is overhead at the solstice, when it passes into Cancer. From there human habitation extends northward as far as the island of Thule, which lies farthest out in the Scythian Sea. Those who live there live under the northern pole. This is clear from the fact that, as certain cosmographers write, there it is continuous day for six months, from the vernal equinox.

…until the autumnal [equinox]; and continuous night for the other six months, from the autumnal equinox until the vernal. This happens because six signs are hidden from them under the earth at all times; therefore it is night for them when the sun travels through those. The other six are always above the earth for them; therefore it is day for them when the sun travels through those. Since only the six northern signs are visible to them, it follows that the north pole is above their heads and is the highest point of all for them. One can see this well on the sphere that was newly made in the monastery of Saint Gall under Abbot Purchard. It shows the positions of all peoples, and so, when it is set so that the north pole points straight up, the six signs of the zodiac are visible:

the northern ones; the six southern ones are hidden. From this we know well that, from where people begin to live farthest in the south to where they live farthest in the north, it could well be the fourth part of the earth, if seas and marshes did not break it up. If in your thought you subtract from this fourth part as much as the seas and marshes cover, and as much as the vast region, that is, the desert, stretches out in thirst, that is, in dryness, scarcely the narrowest area will be left for people to live in. If you then consider how much water and fen and wilderness cut away from that same fourth part, then what remains is only a narrow homestead for humankind.

Do you then, fenced around and shut in within this tiniest point of a point, think of spreading your fame and advancing your name? Do you now, shut in and hemmed in within so small a part of a small part, think of spreading your reputation and your name far and wide?
Or what greatness and splendour can glory have when it is confined within such narrow
and small limits? Or what can glory have that is mighty and powerful when it is constrained within such tight boundaries? Add this: think of this as well.
That this very enclosure of a small dwelling-place is inhabited by many nations,

differing in language, in customs, and in the whole manner of their life. That in this same small settlement many peoples dwell, unlike one another in speech, in customs, and in the whole shaping of their life.
To these peoples not only can the fame of individual men not reach, but not even that of cities.

partly through the difficulty of travel, partly through the diversity of speech, partly through the unfamiliarity of trade. To these places not even the fame of certain cities can come, still less that of certain people: partly because of the hardship of the journey, partly because of an unknown language, partly because they are unused to trade and to all exchange. Indeed, in the time of Marcus Tullius, as he himself indicates in a certain passage, the fame of the Roman republic had not yet crossed the Caucasus mountains. Cicero says that even then, in his own time, Roman power had not become known beyond the Caucasus mountains. And at that time it was full-grown,
and fearsome even to the Parthians and the other peoples of those parts.

And yet it had grown so great by then that even the Parthians and other peoples there in that region feared it. Do you not see, then, how narrow, how cramped is the glory that you labour to extend and spread? Do you not now see how narrow and how tight the glory is that you want to broaden and plant far and wide? Will the glory of a Roman man go forward where the fame of the Roman name cannot pass? Shall the fame of any Roman man reach a place where there is no fame of Rome itself? That is an argument from the whole to the part.
What of the fact that the customs and institutions of different peoples disagree with one another?

What do you say to this, that the customs and laws of different peoples disagree with one another? Can that not also lead you astray? So that what is judged worthy of praise among some is judged worthy of punishment among others? So much so that what seems praiseworthy to some seems to others to deserve penalty and retribution. As a result, if anyone delights in having his fame proclaimed, it is of no use to him (that is, it does not fall to him) to spread his name among very many peoples. So it does him no good to spread his name among many peoples, the man who longs for renown. Each man, therefore, will be content with glory spread among his own people. So every man must be content with whatever glory he can have among his own people.
And that most glorious immortality of fame will be confined within the borders of a single people.

And that very weighty renown, as if it were eternal, will be confined within one country. But how many men who were most famous in their own times have been wiped out because writers forgot them? How many names that were famous in their own times have been destroyed because writers forgot them?

And yet what do writings themselves accomplish, when a long and dark old age buries them together with their authors? However I consider it, I cannot see what the writings themselves can do for this, since old age carries them away completely, together with the writers.

THAT TIME BEARS NO COMPARISON WITH ETERNITY. But you think you are extending immortality to yourselves when you think about fame in time to come. You think you will then gain something like immortality when you make yourselves famous forever.
But if you set it against the infinite spaces of eternity.
what reason do you have to rejoice over how long your name lasts?

If you stretch it out and extend it (I mean the fame spread abroad into future time) to the breadth of eternity, where then is the long duration of your name in which you rejoice? For if the span of a single moment is compared with ten thousand years, however small it is, it still has some share in them, since both spans are limited. If one hour is set against ten years, it has some share in them, even though it is small, because each quantity is measured with certainty and measured exactly.

But this number of years itself, and any multiple of it however large, cannot even be compared with a duration that has no limit. But ten thousand years, and many times as many again, cannot be compared in any way with a length of time that has no end.

For finite things can be compared with one another in some way, but the infinite and the finite never can. Things that have some end can be measured against one another in some way, but they have no measure at all against things that are without end.

So it happens that if fame lasting however long a time is set against inexhaustible eternity, it seems not small but plainly nothing. Hence it is that if long-lasting fame is measured against eternity, it is not small by comparison with it but nothing at all.
But you do not know how to act rightly except for the sake of the breezes of popular favour

and empty rumours. But you do not wish to act rightly except for people's praise and for vain reputation. And, abandoning the excellence of conscience and of virtue, you seek rewards from the petty talk of others. And paying no heed to the guidance of conscience — he who claims as his own, from himself, to have found what another found, and glories in it, goes about with vanity, not with virtue — you want to be thanked for words that came from others. He does not look to his conscience who [?] what another found, and glories in it. He goes about with vanity, not with virtue.
Hear how wittily someone mocked the frivolity [?] of such arrogance. Hear how merrily one man mocked another, who boasted so much and was so frivolous!
When a certain man had attacked with insults someone who had taken on the false name of philosopher, not to practise true virtue

but for proud glory, [Raising of the voice] and had added that he would now find out whether the other was a philosopher, namely if he bore the injuries inflicted on him mildly and patiently. And here [?]. The other put on patience for a little while and, having taken the insult, said as if gloating:

"Now at last do you understand that I am a philosopher?" [Lowering of the voice] It once happened like this. A man likewise claimed that he was a philosopher, out of vanity and not out of true virtue. Another man, testing him, greeted him with abuse and said that he would test well whether he really was one, namely by whether he was patient under provocation. Then the first man bore it somewhat patiently, but right afterwards spoke up again, as if mocking him: "Surely now you recognise me as a philosopher?" Then the other said, very bitingly: "I would have understood it if you had kept silent." When the one had said that, the other answered him: "Yes, by God," he said, very bitingly, "I would have recognised it if you had kept silent."
THOSE WHO ARE FAMOUS FOR VIRTUE RIGHTLY DESPISE FAME. But what is it that concerns outstanding men (for these are the subject of the discussion), who seek glory through virtue? What, I say, is it

What does fame matter to these after the body has been dissolved by final death? But what attaches to the most famous men — I mean those who wish to distinguish themselves by virtue, not by vanity — what attaches to them, what use is any reputation to them after death? For if men die entirely,
which our reasonings forbid us to believe,

there is no glory at all, since the one to whom it is said to belong does not exist at all? If a man dies entirely, in soul and in body — which my reasonings deny — where then is his glory, when he himself does not exist? As if she were saying: where is the accident, when the substance and the accident [?]. But if the mind, well conscious of itself,
once released from its earthly prison, freely seeks heaven, will it not despise every earthly concern, since it enjoys heaven and rejoices that it has been freed from earthly things?

But if the soul, secure, goes to heaven released from the prison of the body, what then is any earthly thing to it, since in heaven it rejoices that it has been set free from earth? What is earthly reputation to it? That is an argument from dissimilarity. Joy and prison are dissimilar, and so are heaven and earth.
THAT FAME IS NOTHING, HOWEVER WIDESPREAD, HOWEVER LONG-LASTING.
Whoever with headlong mind seeks glory alone and believes it the highest good,
let him look at the far-stretching regions of the sky
and the narrow place of the earth.
He who strives eagerly after glory, and to whom it seems the weightiest of things, let him look up at the breadth of heaven and down at the narrowness of the earth.

He will be ashamed of his enlarged name, which cannot fill even that small space. Then he will be ashamed of his famous name, which does not reach even to the end of the narrow earth, and the earth is a single point compared with heaven.
O, why do the proud long in vain to lift their necks from the mortal yoke? What [?] have the proud in mind? Why do they hope in vain to free their necks from the yoke of death?
Although widespread fame, travelling among far-off peoples,
may spread out tongues, that is, of other nations,
and although a great house may shine with famous titles,
death scorns lofty glory.

Though fame, surging, spreads itself far abroad among distant peoples and fills other languages too, and though many banners won in battle shine in the house and make the man famous, death has no regard for the glory of any of them. It envelops alike the humble and the lofty head. It takes the mighty just as it takes the lowly.
And it makes the lowest equal to the highest. And it brings the highest down level with the lowest.
Where now do the bones of faithful Fabricius lie? Where now is the grave of the faithful Fabricius? Who knows?

Where might it be? This is the man who answered the messengers of the Samnites when they offered him their gold and wanted to ransom themselves with it. He said that the Romans did not wish to have gold, but to rule over those who had gold. What of Brutus or stern Cato? Where now is Brutus, or the upright Cato? Brutus won liberty for the Roman people, as was stated earlier. Stern Cato stood with Pompey in defense of liberty against Julius Caesar. And when Julius won the victory, and Pompey, in flight, was slain in Egypt, Cato led the army from Egypt, with Caesar always pursuing, along the whole perilous road that runs from there to the city of Utica. There Cato killed himself so that Caesar would not capture him. From this he is called Uticensis.
A faint fame that survives marks
an empty name with a few letters. The reputation that has barely been left behind marks their name only, with a few letters.
But because we know the splendid names,
is it granted to know those who are consumed? Is it so? Because we know the names, can we from that know the men themselves, who passed away long ago?
You lie, therefore, wholly unknown,
nor does fame make you known. You truly lie in such a way that no one knows you. Nor does fame make you known. No one recognizes you, even though you are still spoken of.
But if you think that life is drawn out longer
by the breath of a mortal name,
when a late day snatches this from you too,

the second death now awaits you. Do you also think that your life is lengthened by the lasting of your name? What then? When the last day of the world takes that from you too, then eternal death lies upon you.

AGAIN, I HAVE TURNED MY STYLE FROM ARGUING TO PERSUADING. Now she turns back again from things that come by chance to Fortune herself. Everything she says about the things that Fortune grants, such as wealth, high offices and power, about how fleeting they are and why they deserve contempt for that reason, is all disputation. Reasoning of this kind belongs entirely to the shaping of morals and the correction of life, in the part of philosophy called ethics, as was also said earlier.

But what Fortune herself is like, as she is now about to say and also said earlier, is a civil matter, and it belongs to rhetorical persuasion, in the kind of case called demonstrative. When she defended herself against the charge Boethius had made against her, that defense was judicial, not demonstrative. Just as in the judicial kind one had to look to equity and iniquity, so here in the demonstrative kind one must look to praise and blame. When a controversy concerns particular, definite persons, it is civil; rhetoric takes it up and settles it by persuading and dissuading. But when it concerns things, it is philosophical, and then one must also settle it philosophically.

Cicero teaches us this distinction. I mean how we are to recognize, using these definitions, which questions are civil and which are philosophical. "A hypothesis is a controversy set out in speech that involves particular persons. A thesis, however, is a controversy set out in speech that does not involve particular persons." Hypothesis means "subpositum" (placed beneath), thesis means "propositum" (placed before). When people plead in court, when they sit in council, when they sit to make an election, that always concerns persons placed beneath [the eyes], that is, particular persons. But when people deliberate about morals and the ordering of life, or also about the hidden natures of things, that concerns "proposita", that is, things placed far from the eyes. That does not concern persons who can be placed beneath the eyes. From this you know

that everything she now intends to say in praise or blame of Fortune she must do rhetorically, since Fortune is a particular person, a kind of goddess. By persuading and by disputing one can instruct a person in all kinds of things. Philosophy therefore uses both in turn. That is why Luke says of Paul in the Acts of the Apostles: "disputing and persuading concerning the kingdom of God." He was disputing when he gave the reason for everything he taught. He was persuading when he said how good, how right and how blessed it would be to do what he taught.

FORTUNE: HOW MUCH BETTER ADVERSE FORTUNE IS THAN PROSPEROUS. "But lest you think that I wage implacable war against Fortune, there is a time when she, the deceiver, deceiving in nothing, deserves well of men." So that you do not think that I want to wage

a relentless war, as it were, against Fortune: she is deceitful, yet she is sometimes good to people, I mean when she is not deceitful. "Namely then, when she reveals herself, when she uncovers her brow and openly declares her ways." Then she is good, when she shows herself, when she bares her face and does not hide her ways. "Perhaps you do not yet understand what I am saying." Perhaps you do not yet know what I want to say. "What I am eager to say is a wondrous thing, and so I can hardly unfold my meaning in words." What I long to say is a wondrous thing; therefore I cannot say it readily either.
"For I think that adverse fortune benefits people more than prosperous fortune." I truly reckon that misfortune is sometimes better for people than good fortune.

For that one (good fortune), when she seems flattering, always lies with an appearance of happiness. As long as prosperity makes herself beloved with her kindness and seems good to a person, so long does she deceive him with the likeness of happiness.
This one (adverse fortune) is always truthful when she shows herself unstable by changing.

Adversity, however, is truthful when, by changing, she shows how unstable she is. That one deceives; this one instructs. The former deceives a person; the latter warns him and teaches him. That one binds the minds of those who enjoy her with a false appearance of goods; this one sets them free through knowledge of how fragile happiness is. The former fetters the minds of those who enjoy her with her splendour; the latter unfetters them with sure knowledge of transient good.
And so you may see that one windy and flowing,
"and always ignorant of herself; the latter sober, girded up, and prudent through the very exercise of adversity."

You can see the former exalting herself, unrestrained, not knowing herself; but this one moderate, restrained, and made wise by the constant exercise of hardships. Finally, happy fortune draws away from the true good, by her flatteries, those who stray;

adverse fortune for the most part draws them back with a hook, returned to the true goods. In the end, fortunate fortune with her charm makes people stray from the true good; but the unflattering one sets them back on the way and toward the true good, as if drawing them back with hooks.

Or do you think this should be counted among the least things, that this harsh, this horrible fortune has revealed to you the minds of faithful friends? Do you count it as little that the harsh and horrible fortune has shown you your friends in need, who are devoted to you out of true loyalty?
She has distinguished for you the sure and the doubtful faces of your companions. She has separated for you the faces of sure and unsure friends!

That is, what the former and the latter are like. Departing, she took away her own and left yours. In departing she took to herself those who were hers; those who were yours she left to you. At what price would you have bought this when you were whole and fortunate, as you seemed to yourself? How dear would that not have been to you, when you were in good standing and happy, as it seemed to you?

Stop seeking your lost wealth; you have found friends, which is the most precious kind of riches. Console yourself for your other, lost goods: you have found your friends, who are the most precious treasure.

ON THE OFFICE OF THE ORATOR. Here you can hear how one should persuade a person toward something that is hateful to us and that we therefore shun, as all people do, namely adverse fortune. One can entice us toward it if one begins to tell us of its many virtues and to promise us many pleasant things, as Philosophy now does about this same adverse fortune. She makes it dear to us in two ways: both by praising it and by reproaching prosperity. Who could expect anything good from adverse fortune? The very name of adversity makes it hateful. On the other hand, the name of prosperity makes itself pleasant; it is so called from the following wind, that is, 'a porro spirando' (from blowing from afar/forward). But since there is now nothing stable in prosperity, as she accuses it, nor anything certain, and it draws [?] people

and binds their minds. And she, acting very kindly, pretends to be what she is not. And when one expects everything one wishes from her, then she suddenly changes completely and thrusts the man away. To whom, then, should she seem good? But if adversity is the teacher of virtue, and leads people to God, and makes them perfect and worthy of heaven, as she [Philosophy] has praised it, should it not rightly seem good to us? What can be stronger for persuading than praise is? Rhetoric says that the office of the orator is to speak fittingly for the purpose of persuading; that means to speak persuasively. Is this not spoken persuasively? Who can do that as well as Philosophy? Therefore we should believe her that adverse fortune is better than prosperous fortune.

OF LOVE, WHICH MAKES FRIENDSHIPS FIRM AND BINDS ALL THINGS. That the world with stable faith varies its harmonious changes. Suspension. That the world, with firm faithfulness, varies the harmonious alternations of the four seasons. Summer and winter, spring and autumn, are different because none of them is like another. And yet they are alike, because none of them disturbs the other. That warring seeds keep a perpetual compact. And this. That the four discordant elements, which are the seeds of all bodies, keep an eternal agreement. They are opposed to one another, and yet they are together in all bodies. That Phoebus in his golden chariot brings forth the rosy day. And this. That the sun, riding in its beautiful chariot, brings forth the day. That Phoebe should rule the nights

which Hesperus has brought. And this. That his sister the moon, in turn, rules the night that the evening star brings. That the greedy sea (that is, greedy to go out) should hold back its waves within a fixed boundary, lest the wandering (that is, the waves) be allowed to stretch their broad bounds over the lands. That the sea too, which would gladly go out, turns back its unsteady waves at a fixed boundary and does not let them, I mean those same waves, go further out beyond the shores onto the land. Love binds this chain of things, ruling the lands and the sea and commanding heaven. Resolution. Love makes such an order of things firm. She rules the earth and the sea and

constrains them, and rules in heaven. Who is she? That is God himself. If she slackens the reins, whatever now loves mutually will at once wage war. If she lets go of the rein, whatever is now joined in love at once begins to fight. And the machine which they now drive with allied faith in beautiful motions, they will strive to break apart. And this worldly structure, which they now, being of one mind, make keep its course beautifully, they will hasten to shatter. She also holds together peoples joined by a holy covenant. The same love also holds human beings together with a holy covenant. She also ties the sacred bond of marriage with chaste loves. She also makes lawful marriage firm with pure loves. She also dictates their laws to faithful companions.

She also makes law for companions who rightly love one another. O happy race of men, if the love by which heaven is ruled should rule your minds. Truly, you race of mankind, how blessed you are if your mind is ruled by the love that rules heaven. HERE ENDS THE SECOND BOOK OF BOETHIUS.
Here begins the third book.
She had now finished her song. She ended the song. When the sweetness of the song had held me spellbound, eager to listen and astonished, with my ears still pricked up.

The sweetness of the song still made me listen to it; such eagerness and such wonder did I have for it. And so a little later I said. After that, after a while, I said: O highest solace of weary minds. Special comfort of the sorrowful. How much you have refreshed me, whether by the weight of your sayings or by the delight of your singing. How much stronger you have made me with the weight of your speech and with the pleasantness of your song. So much,
that I no longer think myself unequal to the blows of fortune after this. You have done so much that from now on I do not intend to think that I yield at all to the blows of fortune.
I can bear them well. And so the remedies which you said were rather sharp, not only do I not dread them, but, eager to hear, I earnestly demand them.

"And I do not shun the stronger remedies of your speech. I gladly hear them and ask for them." Then she said: "I perceived it when, silent and attentive, you were seizing upon our words." "Indeed," she said, "I noticed that when you were silent and listened so closely to my words. And I either waited for that disposition of your mind or, what is truer, I brought it about myself."
"And I waited until your mind became like that, or, what is truer, I made it so. For the things that remain are such that
that when tasted they bite, but when taken inside they grow sweet. The things still ahead are such that they bite when you taste them, but once swallowed down they seem sweet.
But as for your saying that you are eager to hear,
how greatly you would burn if you knew where we are setting out to lead you!

But as for your saying that you would gladly hear: oh, how earnest you would be about it, how you would burn, if you knew where I have begun to lead you! "Where, then?" I said. "Where, then?" said I. "To true happiness," she said. "To true happiness!" said she. "Which your mind also dreams of." Which you also dream of in your mind. "But because its sight is taken up with images, it cannot behold that happiness itself." But while it gazes at the image, it cannot see happiness itself. As long as you think of worldly happiness, you are thinking of the image of true happiness, not of true happiness itself. Then I said:

"Do it, I beg you, and show without delay what that true happiness is." "For God's sake," I said, "do that, and show me the true happiness without delay." "I will do it gladly for your sake," she said. "Now I will do that," said she, "gladly, out of love for you. But what is better known to you

I will first try to describe in words and give it shape, so that, once you have examined it, when you turn your eyes to the opposite side, you may recognize the pattern of true blessedness. But first I will depict for you worldly happiness, which is better known to you, so that afterward, when you have looked through this one, you may look over there and recognize the other all the better, and see what difference there is between them."
SHE IS ABOUT TO GIVE THE REASON WHY SHE DELAYS. Whoever wishes to sow a fertile field
first frees the land of roots. Whoever wishes to sow a good field first clears it of weeds.
With a sickle he cuts back brambles and fern,
so that Ceres may come heavy with new grain. He removes the fern and briars with the clearing-sickle, so that better grain may grow for him on the newly cleared land.
The labor of the bees is all the sweeter
if a bad taste has first consumed the mouth. Honey too is all the sweeter if the mouth has first tasted something bitter.
The stars shine more pleasingly
when the south wind ceases to make its rain-bearing sounds. And the stars shine more brightly when the rain-winds die down.
When the morning star has driven away the darkness,
the beautiful day, that is, the sun, drives, that is, brings forth, her rosy horses. And when the morning star drives the night away, the sun shows her red horses; she comes riding upon them.
You too, looking first upon false goods,
begin to draw your neck back from the yoke.

…true things will then enter the mind. So you too must do: first recognize false happiness and try to free yourself from it. Then the true things will come into your mind. Otherwise you will not succeed.

THAT ALL STRIVE TOWARD HAPPINESS, THOUGH NOT BY THE RIGHT PATH. Then, with her gaze fixed for a little while, and as if she had withdrawn into the august seat of her mind, she began thus. Then, looking a little toward the ground, and as if resting in her mind as on an imperial throne, she began thus.

All the care of mortals, which the labor of many different pursuits keeps busy, goes forward by different paths. The cares of all people have gone different ways, the cares that many kinds of struggle and many kinds of effort drive and stir up in them. Yet it strives to reach one end, that of happiness. Yet they all aim at one place, because they all aim at happiness.
And that is the good which, once someone has obtained it, leaves him able to desire nothing further. And that is the good: if anyone gains it,

then once he has gained it, he can desire nothing further. This is indeed the highest of all goods, and it contains all goods within itself. That is the foremost of all good, holding all good within it. If anything were missing from it, it could not be the highest. If it lacked anything, it would not be full. For something would be left outside it that could still be wished for. For apart from that, there would still be something a person could desire. That is an argument from the part: where one part is missing, the thing is not whole.

DEFINITION. It is clear, therefore, that happiness is a state made perfect by the gathering together of all goods. Therefore it is evident that happiness is the fullness of all good. If you wish to say 'the stable state of the fullness of all good,' that is the same thing. This, as we said,
all mortals try to attain by different paths.

That happiness, as I said, all people hasten to win. They all hasten toward it by various ways. For the desire for the true good is naturally implanted in human minds. That is because the human mind naturally desires the true good. But straying error leads them aside to false things. But mistaking the way misleads them to the false.

RICHES. Some of them, believing that the highest good is to lack nothing, labour to abound in riches. Some of them strive to become rich, because they consider it the best thing of all to be in need of nothing.

HONORS. Others, judging the good to be whatever is most worthy of reverence, gain honors and strive to be revered by their fellow citizens. Some, thinking that being worthy of honor is the good, hurry to win honors so that they may be held in awe by their fellow citizens.

POWER. There are those who place the highest good in the highest power. Then there are those who think power is the best thing. These people either want to rule themselves or try to attach themselves to those who rule. They want to become powerful themselves, or always to be with the powerful.
FAME. But those to whom fame seems something best,
these hasten to spread a glorious name, either by the arts of war
or of peace. Those to whom renown seems best want to make their name glorious with some of those skills which are needed at home or in the army.
PLEASURE. But very many measure the fruit of the good by joy and gladness. Some consider the best gain to lie in joy and in gladness.
These think it most happy to dissolve in pleasure. They consider it happy to live in delights and to swim in them.

ONE FOR THE SAKE OF ANOTHER. There are also those who exchange the ends and causes of these with one another. So there are also those who love this for the sake of that, and others who love that for the sake of this, and so have swapped them. Such as those who desire riches for the sake of power and pleasures,
or who seek power

either for the sake of money or to spread their name. That is how it goes when some seek wealth for the sake of power and pleasure, and others, on the contrary, seek power for the sake of wealth and fame. What a person uses to go further is the cause; where he wants to get to is the end. One can also say it this way: what he uses to aim at something is the cause, and what he aims at is the end.
WHAT IS ADDED TO THESE. In these things, then, and in others like them, the purpose of human actions and wishes is engaged.

These and similar things are what people's deeds and wills aim at. Such things are nobility and popular favour, which seem to win a certain renown. That is how nobility works, and the praise of the people, which serve to bring fame. Wife and children are sought for the sake of pleasantness. That is how wife and children work: people seek them for delight. But friendship, which is the most sacred kind of thing, is counted not under fortune but under virtue. What about the delight of friends? It is not of that kind. It is holy, so it belongs not to false happiness but to true happiness, which is where virtue belongs.
The rest, however, are taken up either for the sake of power or for the sake of pleasure.

What I named of other kinds is all acquired for love of power and for pleasure. Now it is plain that the goods of the body are referred to the higher ones. Now it is also clear that the body's advantages belong to those same five [ends].
For strength and size seem to provide power.

For strength and size give power. Beauty and swiftness [give] renown. Beauty and swiftness give fame. Health [gives] pleasure. Health gives delight. From all these it is clear that happiness alone is desired. All of these are desired for the sake of that one thing, happiness.
PROPOSITION. For whatever each person seeks above everything else, he judges to be the highest good. Whatever each person strives for most eagerly, he considers to be the best.
ASSUMPTION. But we have defined the highest good as happiness. And we have said that happiness is the best.
CONCLUSION. Therefore each person judges the state he desires above all others to be happy. So each person considers the state he seeks most eagerly to be blessed.

HOW GREAT THE FORCE OF THE SYLLOGISM IS. A syllogism does not deceive if it is properly constructed. It is properly constructed when, in dialectic, it has three members, two of which are so true that everyone can grant them, and which fit together so closely that they make the third true even without its being granted. For example: Jacob was the son of Isaac, and Isaac was the son of Abraham. Those are two members. If one grants these, one must necessarily grant the third: that Abraham was Jacob's paternal grandfather. So this syllogistic reasoning that we have come upon here is also evident: what each person most desires to obtain, that he considers the highest good.

And the highest good is happiness. Those are two members. Whoever grants these must grant the third, even against his will, which says: what each person most desires to obtain, that he considers happiness. From this let us understand that an argument is made either of one member or of two. Of one, as in this: if Jacob was the son of Abraham's son, then he was Abraham's grandson. That single member is called the proposition. It is made of two, as in this: if Jacob was the son of Abraham's son, then he was his grandson; and he certainly was so. That is a proposition and an assumption. But if it says instead: Jacob was the son of Abraham's son, and therefore he was his grandson.

That, then, is the proposition and the conclusion. So the argument is an imperfect syllogism. If you complete it to three members, it is a full syllogism. "You have, then, nearly" (that is, because there may be more) "the form of human" (that is, false) "happiness set before your eyes." Now I have shown you, very nearly, the image of human happiness: wealth, honours, power, glory, pleasures. I mean riches, honour, power, fame, delight.
"Considering these alone, Epicurus accordingly decided that pleasure was the highest good." Epicurus was one of the philosophers, and he went along with them in seeking the highest good.

He did not know God or spiritual goods. Thinking only of these five, he simply chose to take pleasure as the highest good. "Because all the other things seem to bring delight to the mind." He chose it simply because the other four, as it seemed to him, give delight to the mind, as pleasure does to the body. So he believed that those four were included in this one, and that in it alone he had found what he was seeking. "Epicuros" in Greek means in Latin "over pigs." The other philosophers gave him that name because he followed pleasure and lived like pigs with his followers.

THAT MEN DO NOT ERR IN THE END BUT IN THE WAY, AND THAT THE HIGHEST GOOD LACKS NONE OF THE FIVE THINGS WRITTEN ABOVE. "But I return to the pursuits of men, whose mind seeks its own good again, though with a clouded memory."

"Now I will tell again," she said, "what people strive for. Their mind always seeks after its good, even though it seeks it with a dim memory." "But like a drunk man, it does not know by which path it should return home." And yet it does not know, as if it were drunk, by which path it should go back home. It seeks what is to be sought, but it does not go rightly after it.
WEALTH. Surely those who strive to lack nothing do not seem to err?

Do you think those err in their minds who would gladly be without need of any good? No, they do not. And yet there is nothing else that could achieve happiness as well as a state abounding in all goods. Truly, nothing can fulfil happiness as well as an abundant state of every good. Lacking nothing from others, but sufficient in itself. That state needs nothing from others and has enough of itself.
HONOR. Surely those do not go astray who think that what is best is also most worthy of the respect of reverence? Do you think those err who regard the best as the most honorable?

Not at all. No, they do not. For what the efforts of nearly all mortals labor to obtain is not something worthless and contemptible. That toward which all people hasten could not be contemptible. They hasten toward the highest good; where they find that, there they have also found what is most worthy of reverence.
POWER. Or is power not to be counted among the goods?

Should power not be regarded as good? That is, should one not be certain that power goes with the highest good? What then? How does it seem to you? Is that which is clearly more excellent than all things to be thought weak and without strength? How could that which is foremost of all things, that is, the highest good, be without strength?

FAME. Or is renown to be counted as nothing? Should fame seem of little worth to a man? But can it be set apart? Whatever is most excellent must also seem most renowned. But how could it be otherwise, since what is also foremost is necessarily the most famous?
PLEASURE. For what point is there in saying that happiness is not anxious and sad, nor subject to pains and troubles, when even in the smallest things people seek what is delightful to have

and enjoy? What need is there now for me to deny that the highest good and happiness, toward which they strive, have any discomfort, since they desire even a paltry thing for the sake of pleasure? In the highest good nothing is more complete than pleasure. And yet these are the things that people wish to obtain. Without doubt these are the things that people desire. And for this reason they desire riches, high offices, kingdoms, glory, and pleasures: because they believe that through these they will gain sufficiency, reverence, power,

renown, and gladness. And for that reason they want wealth, high rank, power, glory, and pleasure, because they think that through these they will have abundance, honor, might, fame, and joy. What would wealth be to them, if they did not have abundance through it? What would lordship be to them, if it did not give them honor? What would power be to them, if it did not make them mighty? What would glory be to them, except for the sake of fame? And what would delights be to them, if they did not gladden a person?
It is the good, therefore, that people seek through such different pursuits.

That is always one thing, one good, toward which people strive in so many ways. In this it is easily shown how great the power of nature is: although opinions vary and disagree, they still agree in loving the goal of the good. From this one can easily see how strong nature is, when such differing ways agree on the goal of the good toward which they hurry.
ON THE POWER OF NATURE. How many reins of things
mighty nature steers,
by what laws, in her foresight, she preserves the boundless world
and holds it fast,
binding each thing with a bond that cannot be loosed: this it pleases me to set forth in clear-sounding song.
with pliant strings. How mighty nature turns her reins, by what law she preserves this world, and how she binds things with a firm bond, that I will sing aloud on supple strings.
Although Punic lions
they wear beautiful chains and take with their hands the food that is given them.

and, used to suffering blows, fear their harsh master. Although the bold lions wear chains on them, and although they are fed from the hand because they are tame, and although they fear their master because they are used to his blows,
if blood has stained their fearsome mouths,
their spirits, long dormant, return,
and with a deep roar they remember themselves. If they taste blood, their former fierceness rises up in them at once, and at once they remember what they are, gnashing their teeth after their kind.
They free their necks from the loosened bonds [?].
And the first tamer, torn (that is, lacerated) by the bloody tooth,
is the first to stain their raging wrath. At that moment they break the chains and attack the master first. He becomes the first victim, and as they tear at him with their teeth, their fury grows.
LIKEWISE. The chattering bird that sings on the high branches
is shut up in the hollow of a cage. And the bird that goes singing from tree to tree is caught and put in a cage.
Although human care may serve it cups smeared with honey
"and lavish feasts, playing with sweet zeal." Even if someone serves it with honeyed things and in full abundance,
as many people do, for pleasure and for play.
yet if, hopping out of its narrow shelter,
it sees the pleasant shade of the groves,
it tramples the scattered food with its feet;
sorrowful, it seeks only the woods;

it murmurs of the woods with its sweet voice. If it manages to escape from the cage to the wood, where it sees its beloved shade, then the earlier food means nothing to it. In the forest alone it wants to live; in the forest it wants to twitter.
LIKEWISE. A branch once bent by strong force
bows its top downward. The top of a young tree is also sometimes pulled down by force.
If the right hand that bent it lets it go,
it looks at the sky with its top held straight. If it is released, it straightens itself up again toward heaven.
LIKEWISE. Phoebus sinks into the western waves,
but turns his chariot again by a secret path
to his accustomed rising. The sun also goes westward in the evening to its setting. But in the morning it comes back by a hidden course to its rising.
LIKEWISE. All things seek again their own return,
and each thing rejoices in its return. Everything has its way back, and always strives toward the place it belongs to by nature.
Nor does any set order remain for anything,
unless it has joined its rising to its end
and made its own circle stable.

No other thing remains in its natural order unless its end reaches back to its origin and it makes itself stable in the manner of a ring. Therefore man keeps to his nature if he can find his way back to God, from whom he came.

THAT ERROR DRAWS BACK FROM WHERE NATURE TENDS. "yet your beginning. You too, O earthly creatures, dream, though in a faint image, of" You men do the same: however obscure the image may be, you still always see your origin, as if through a dream. The first transgression took this from men, so that although they seek their origin, they cannot recognize it clearly. "And you look ahead to that true end of happiness"

"with some sort of thought, though hardly a clear-sighted one." And you look straight ahead to the blessed end, even though you do it with a mind that cannot see through clearly. "And natural intention leads you there, to the true good, but manifold error leads you away from it!" That is, because nature is strong, it leads you straight, aiming at the highest good. And because nature has been corrupted, error leads you astray.

HE SAYS IT MUST BE PROVED BY ARGUMENTS WHETHER WHAT IS DESIRED CAN BE ATTAINED THROUGH THESE FIVE. For consider whether, through the things by which people think they will attain happiness, they can reach the destined end. Now consider whether, with those five things by which they trust to gain happiness, they can come to where they strive to go. For if either money
or honors and the rest bring something such that nothing good seems to be lacking, we too would admit that some people become happy by obtaining them.

If such things as treasure and honor can help anyone so that he lacks no good, then let us grant happiness to those who gain any of them. But if they cannot accomplish what they promise, and lack many goods, is not a false appearance of happiness clearly found in them? But if they cannot deliver what they promise, and they lack much good, then they are plainly a deceptive image of happiness.

FIRST PROOF, CONCERNING RICHES. First, then, I ask you yourself, who a little while ago abounded in riches. Now first tell me, you who were rich just recently: amid that most abundant wealth, did anxiety arising from some injury never trouble your mind? When you were at your richest, did anything distressing ever happen to you through anyone's fault, so that your mind was troubled?
"And yet," I said, "I cannot remember ever having been free in mind

…that I was not always anxious about something. "Truly," said I, "I was never, as far as I can remember, so free in my mind that I was not anxious about something." "Was it not because either something was absent that you did not want to be absent, or something was present that you wished were not present? Was it not because," said she, "you lacked something dear to you that you did not want to lack,

or had some grief that you did not want to have?" "It is so," I said. "That is so," said I. "Then you desired the presence of the one and the absence of the other." "Then you longed," said she, "for the presence of the one and the absence of the other." "I admit it," I said. "I confess that," said I. "But each person lacks," she said, "what he desires." "So a person is in need," said she, "of what he longs for."
"He lacks it," I said. "He is in need," said I. "But whoever lacks anything is not in every way sufficient for himself." "Whoever is in need of anything," said she, "is not sufficient in all things."
"Not at all," I said. "It is not so," I said. That is an argument from the part.

As if he were saying: a person who lacks some of the parts does not have the whole. "So you," she said, "suffered this insufficiency when you were full of wealth?" "Did you," she said, "suffer this want when you were very rich?" "Why not?" I said.

"How could it be otherwise?" I said. "Therefore wealth cannot make a person lack nothing and be sufficient for himself." "If this is so," she said, "then riches can never make anyone free from need or content." "And this was what they seemed to promise." "And yet they gave the appearance of doing so."

LIKEWISE. "Yet I think this too must be considered above all: money has nothing in its own nature that prevents it from being taken away from those who possess it against their will." This too must be carefully considered: treasure does not have the power in itself to keep people from taking it against the will of those to whom it belongs.
"I admit it," I said. "I confess that," said I. "Why would you not admit it? Why should you not confess it?" said she.
"When someone stronger snatches it away every day from an unwilling owner?"

"When every day whoever is more powerful takes it from another against his will? For where do the lawsuits of the courts come from? Where else do the legal complaints and the outcries in court come from, except that money taken from unwilling owners, either by force or by fraud, is being sought back? Except that treasures taken from unwilling owners by force or by treachery are being claimed back?"
"It is so," I said.

"That is so," I said. "Therefore," she said, "everyone will need protection sought from outside to guard his money." "So," she said, "everyone needs another man's help to protect and defend his treasure."

"Who would deny that?" I said. "Who," said I, "can deny that?" "And yet he would not need it (that is, protection) unless he possessed money that he could lose." "Now he would have no need of that help," she said, "if he did not have the treasure that he fears to lose."
"That cannot be doubted," I said.
"There is no doubt of that," said I. "So the matter has turned back into its opposite." "If this is so," said she, "then the thing is turned into its opposite."
For wealth, which people thought would make them sufficient to themselves, instead makes them need someone else's protection." I mean by this

that the riches that were supposed to make them sufficient on their own make them need other people's help. This is an argument from the outcome. As if she said: "Since [?] it turns out that the rich are in need, riches are the cause of need."
LIKEWISE. "But in what way is want driven away by riches? In what way, then, can needs be overcome by wealth?
Is it that the rich cannot be hungry? That they cannot be thirsty?

Can the rich not be hungry or thirsty, then? Do the limbs of the wealthy not feel the winter cold? Do the limbs of the rich not feel the frost? But you will say that the wealthy have the means to satisfy their hunger and to drive off thirst and cold. So they have the means, you say, to remedy hunger and thirst, and frost as well."
But in this way need can indeed be consoled by riches; it cannot be removed entirely. In that way, I say in turn, some comfort for need can come

from wealth, but [?] it cannot become a complete relief. For if this need, always gaping and always demanding something, is filled up with wealth, then there must remain something that can be filled. If need always gapes and always craves, and is stuffed full with things, then it necessarily lasts on and on until it is filled. Since being filled does not destroy it, as water destroys fire, but only quiets it, it always exists, and so it does not pass away. If it were destroyed by wealth, it would no longer exist. An argument from the lesser to the greater: for it is less to hold something down than to put it out.
Again. I say nothing of the fact that very little is enough for nature, and nothing is enough for avarice. I will keep silent about this:

that little satisfies nature, and that nothing is ever enough for greed. Hunger, thirst and nakedness make everyone needy. Wealth can remedy that need in those who are not greedy. But those who are greedy are always poor and always needy, because nothing ever seems full enough to them. Therefore, if riches cannot remove need, and even create need of their own, that is, add to it, why do you believe that they provide sufficiency? "So tell me," she said, "if wealth cannot destroy need and even creates need, what sufficiency can it give, do you think?" An argument from contraries. It is as if she were saying: how could riches, which produce need, produce sufficiency, which is its opposite?
THAT RICHES ARE USELESS TO THE AVARICIOUS.
Though the avaricious rich man, from a flowing flood of gold,

should heap up wealth that will never satisfy him. Though the greedy man, however rich he has become, as though the gold were flowing to him, should pile up his treasure, which never seems full enough to him;
and should load his neck with pearls from the shore of the Red Sea. And should load his neck with the gems of the Red Sea;
and should plough rich fields with a hundred oxen. And should go out to his fields with a hundred ploughs in fertile land;
still gnawing care does not leave him while he lives. For all that, he never lacks worries while he is alive.
And his fickle wealth does not go with him when he is dead. Nor, for all that, do his light possessions follow him when he is dead.
SECOND, ON HIGH OFFICES. But do high offices make honorable

...and worthy of reverence the one to whom they have come? But do the lordships make the man they fall to honourable and respected? Do magistracies have such power that they implant virtues in the minds of those who hold them and drive out vices? Is there such power in the offices,

…that they give virtues to the office-holders? Take away vices? Yet they are not accustomed to drive out wickedness, but rather to make it conspicuous. Truly, they are not accustomed to destroy a man's wickedness, but to reveal it. So it happens that we are often indignant that they have fallen to the most wicked men. It often happens that we are angry that they have come into the hands of the vilest men. And Catullus calls Nonius a 'goiter' (struma), although he sat in the curule chair. That is why Catullus called Nonius 'Goiter', even though he sat on the lordly seat. Catullus was a noble poet of Verona; therefore Nonius was contemptible to him, a man who had come from Gaul to Rome and climbed to the consulship with the support of the Goths.

Do you see how much disgrace dignities add to the wicked? Do you not see in this what dishonor offices and dignities bring to the wicked? Yet their unworthiness will be less evident if they are made famous by no honors. Truly, their unworthiness would show the less if no office or honor made them known.
LIKEWISE. Could you, too, be brought at last by so many dangers to think of holding a magistracy together with Decoratus, when you saw in him the mind of a most wicked buffoon and informer?

Could any dangers ever bring you to want to hold the consulship with Decoratus, whom you knew to be a buffoon and an informer? This Decoratus was a supporter of the Goths, and so he was an informer against the citizens. Because he also had the manners of a jester, Boethius would not become his colleague in the consulship, even though the king wanted it. That brought him danger with the king. For we cannot, on account of their honours, judge those worthy of reverence whom we judge unworthy of those very honours. We cannot regard as worthy of honour, on account of their office, those whom we regard as unworthy of the office itself.
But if you saw someone endowed with wisdom, could you think him unworthy

either of reverence or of the wisdom with which he is endowed? But if you saw someone wise, could you regard him as unworthy of honour and of his own wisdom? By no means. No, you could not. For virtue has its own proper dignity, which it immediately pours into those to whom it is joined. Virtue has in itself its own worth, which it at once gives to those to whom it is granted.

Since popular honors cannot bring this about, it is clear that they have no beauty of dignity of their own. Because worldly honors cannot do that, it is evident that they have no beauty of their own worth. The cause becomes evident from the end. If popular dignity were the cause of reverence, then whoever had dignity would lack no reverence. Therefore this argument is called 'from the end' (a fine).
In which this point is to be noted all the more.
In that place one must pay close attention to this: namely, of what the dignity of the wicked is the cause, since it is not the cause of reverence.
PROPOSITION. For if each person is the more despised the more people scorn him: if every man is the more rejected, the more people scorn him,
ASSUMPTION. since rank cannot make the wicked revered, though it does make them known: since office cannot make the wicked honoured, even though it makes them known.

CONCLUSION. Those whom it displays to more people, it makes more despised. In showing them, it makes them despised rather than honored. Here it is evident that for the wicked their dignity is a cause of contempt. But not with impunity. But not to their benefit either: they are repaid for it.
For the wicked pay back a like return to the dignities, which they defile with their contagion. For in return they do the same dishonor to the offices, which they besmirch with their wickedness.

LIKEWISE. And (namely, listen) so that you may recognize that true reverence cannot come through these shadowy dignities. And let me tell you more, so that you may recognize that no true honor comes from these false lordships. If someone who has held the consulship many times should happen to come among barbarian nations, will the office make him venerable to the barbarians? If someone who has often been consul should perhaps wander far away among foreign peoples, will his honor at home make him honored there?

And yet, if this gift (that is, reverence) were natural to high offices, then anywhere among the nations (that is, anywhere on earth) it would in no way fail in its function. If honour were inborn in offices, it would never fail them anywhere. Fire, for example, never stops giving heat anywhere on earth. In the same way, fire is nowhere without its heat.

But it is not their own power that attaches this (that is, the function of dignity) to them. It is the false opinion of men. So they vanish at once when they come to people who do not consider them dignities. Because honour is not given to them by their own virtue but by the false belief of people who consider them worthy of honour, they fail them as soon as they come to people who think nothing of that honour. But this happens among foreign nations. Now this happens among strangers.
FURTHER. But among the people where they arose, do they last forever?

Among the people where they first arose, do they stay steady? Yet the praetorship, once a great power, is now an empty name. Learn it from this: the praetorship was once a great power, and now it is only an empty name. And the senatorial census was a heavy burden. It was hard toil to manage the lords' treasure. Under Augustus there were a thousand senators, and as Suetonius says, the census they were to receive each year came to a total of eight hundred thousand. If the praetors had to pay out that treasure, it could not be done without toil. If anyone once had charge of the people's grain supply, he was considered a great man.
Now what is lower than that prefecture?

The man who once had charge of the citizens' food supply was powerful. But what office is more despised now? Up to the time of Augustus, the Romans had enough provisions for the year, gathered from Italy and Sicily. When Augustus made Egypt into a province, that is, a tributary land, he arranged a supply from there that gave them plenty for seven months. The man who had charge of so great a matter was necessarily powerful.

ON THE COMITIA. From Livy and from other historians we know that the appointments to office at Rome were called comitia, from 'comendo', and the offices themselves were called magistracies and dignities. Of these offices, after the kings were expelled, the consulship was the highest. The legate's dignity followed it, because what the consul undertook to do, his legate carried out. Just as kings wore a crown or diadem on their heads, so the consuls instead wore the fasces on their heads; these were the insignia of majesty.

That means adornment and a sign of the 'main-power' [majesty]. Just as in a house we call the greatest pillar the 'main-pillar', I mean the one that carries the ridge-beam, so the power of the consuls, or of the kings, or of the dictators was called 'main-power', because it was the greatest.
