Those who were disobedient to the majesty of the kings or of the consuls, and were condemned before them for that reason, had recourse to the people under Roman law, so that the people might help them in their danger. This recourse was called provocatio [appeal]. But because very great dissensions often arose from this, they appointed a dictator to put an end to those dissensions. His majesty was such that no one had an appeal to the people against what was judged before him. He was always followed by the magister militum [master of the soldiers],

whom he chose himself, as the consul chose his legate. After these came the tribunes of the plebs, who were the most powerful. Sometimes there were two of them, sometimes as many as ten, and they were often created in such a way that they had consular power, that is, power similar to the consuls'. They were called tribunes of the plebs because they took the judgments of the plebs upon themselves. After that there were praetors, censors and quaestors. The praetors went ahead of the consul in the army and set up his praetorium, I mean his tent, in which he sat ad iudicandum et contionandum, that is, to judge and to address the assembly. Hence he was called praetor, from 'going before' (a praeeundo), as if 'praeitor'. The censors controlled the public treasury,

which was kept in the aerarium. For that reason they were called censors, from census. The quaestors were the collectors of the treasury, so called as if they were quaesitores [seekers]. After that there were prefects, that is, overseers, who were in charge of various affairs. Then there were aediles, who guarded the buildings (aedes) and inspected them. Duumvirs and triumvirs were the officials who held court over crimes. That is why Suetonius accuses Augustus of having been most severe in his triumvirate. Later, governors (praesides) took the place of the duumvirs and triumvirs. The decemvirate was established only once, when the Romans chose ten men instead of two consuls, so that they carried the fasces one at a time and each in turn looked after the commonwealth. Proconsuls served in place of consuls. Pontiffs looked after religion. Emperors, dukes and counts
are well known.

ON THE ORDER OF ROMAN CITIZENS. In connection with this it is useful to know that the Roman citizens were divided into the patricians and the plebs. Of the patricians there were three orders. The highest order was that of the clarissimi (the most distinguished). Of this we read in the Passion of Saint Sebastian: "Daily he urged the most distinguished men Marcellian and Mark to reject the allurements of the world." The second was that of the illustres (the illustrious). Boethius belonged to that order. That is why the title of this book says: "Of Anicius Manlius Severinus, an illustrious man." The third was that of the spectabiles (the respectable). As blessed Agatha said of herself: "I am freeborn, and of a respectable family." Of the plebs there were two orders: the equestrian

and the pedestrian. A man was a knight (eques) if he could show that he had ten thousand of the heavy coins that were called sesterces. Those who had less had to go on foot. When it was time to fill the offices, they appointed the patricians through the votes of the plebs. The plebs' assent and their request were what were called suffragia (votes). Those who had come there from other cities had the same law, except that they could not cast votes. From this it is clear that those who were called patricians and senators had great dignity even without holding office.
LIKEWISE. For, as we said a little earlier, that which has no splendour of its own, through the opinion of those who make use of it,
now gains splendour and now loses it. As I rightly said before, dignity, which has no adornment of its own, gains it and loses it according to what the people it belongs to think.

CONCLUSION. If, therefore, dignities cannot make people worthy of reverence (suspension: the clause left open); if, moreover, they are soiled by contact with the wicked; and this: if they cease to shine as times change; and this: if they become worthless in the estimation of the nations; and this: what is there in them of desirable beauty, let alone (that is, not to mention) that they could give it to others? (Deposition: the clause brought to its close.)

If lordships cannot make people honourable; if, moreover, the wickedness of worthless men disgraces them; if they fade with age, that is, they fall into [?]; and if they are despised by distant peoples, then what desirable beauty do they have in themselves? I need not even mention what of it they could give to others.

LIKEWISE. Although Nero of raging luxury (that is, full of cruelty and luxury) proudly adorned himself with Tyrian purple and snow-white gems. Though the cruel and very lustful Nero proudly decked himself out with the costliest purple and with beautiful gems, yet he flourished hated by all. He was always hateful to all his people, not venerable. Yet the wicked man once gave unseemly curule chairs to the venerable fathers. Wicked as he was, he still bestowed unseemly offices on the venerable lords. Unseemly, because they came from a wicked hand.
Who, then, would think those honours blessed
which wretched men bestow?
Who then should suppose that honours are blessed when they are given by the wretched? This is an argument from contraries, such as blessedness and miseries.

THIRD, ON POWERS. Or can kingdoms and friendship with kings really make a man powerful? Can the power of kings, and the intimacy one has with them, make people mighty? 'Why not?' 'Why can it not?' you say?
'When their happiness lasts forever?' That is: since no one overthrows kings, and their good fortune continues with them? And yet
antiquity is full of examples, and the present age is full of them too, of kings who have exchanged happiness for calamity.

We have many examples of this, from old times and from new, of how many kings came to misery after good fortune. O splendid power, which is found not to be strong enough even to preserve itself! Truly, that is a glorious power which cannot even keep itself.
But if this power of kingdoms is the source of blessedness,

would it not reduce happiness and bring in misery wherever it was lacking in any part? If the power of kings makes blessedness, where is that blessedness now? For wherever that power is lacking, the lack must reduce the blessedness and bring in misery.
But however widely human empires may extend,
many peoples must still be left over whom any given king does not rule.

Even if earthly kingdoms extend far, there are still always many peoples over whom a king, however powerful, does not rule. But in whatever part the power that makes people blessed ceases, powerlessness, which makes them wretched, creeps in. Where the power that makes people blessed leaves off, the powerlessness that makes them wretched comes in. This is an argument from contraries. In this way, therefore, kings must have the greater share of misery. In this way it is necessary, that is, from this it follows necessarily, that more wretchedness than blessedness lies upon kings.
A tyrant who had learned the dangers of his lot, that is, of his high rank, depicted the fears of kingship by the terror of a sword hanging above the head. Dionysius, who ruled Sicily tyrannically,

and so he knew the terrors of his power. He compared the fears he suffered because of his kingdom to the fear of a sword hanging overhead. He hung it by a single thin thread over the head of the man who had told him that he was happy, and asked him: "How happy are you now?" "How happy can I be," the man said, "while I fear this sword?" "I am just as happy," said Dionysius, "since I fear the same thing." What, then, is this power, which cannot drive away the bites of anxieties or escape the stings of fears? What kind of power can that be, which cannot keep the bites of cares and the goads of fears away from a man?
And yet they themselves would wish to have lived securely, but they cannot. They would gladly live in safety, but they cannot. Yet they boast of their power. And still they boast of their power.
Or do you consider a man powerful when you see him wanting what he cannot accomplish?

Do you consider a man powerful who cannot do what he wants? Do you consider a man powerful who surrounds himself with bodyguards? Do you consider a man blessed who always surrounds himself with servants? He himself fears the people he terrifies more than they fear him. He dreads those whom he frightens. Whether he seems powerful lies in the hands of his servants. It rests in the hands of his men.
whether he is powerful. For why should I discuss the intimates of kings, when I show that kingdoms themselves are full of such great weakness?

What need is there for me to speak of the intimates of kings and how weak they are, since I have shown the kings themselves to be so weak? Royal power often brings them down, sometimes while it stands unharmed, sometimes after it has fallen. The power of kings overthrows them, sometimes while it stands upright, sometimes when it falls. When the king falls, his intimates fall; often he himself also brings them down. So they are even weaker. Nero forced Seneca, his intimate friend and teacher, to choose the manner of his own death.

This can be seen in how Nero drove his intimate and his teacher Seneca to choose his own death. When Nero wanted him dead, he presented it to him as a kind of honour, letting him choose his manner of death. After that he brought in the physician, who let his blood in the bath until Seneca grew so weak that he died of it. Antoninus threw Papinian, long powerful among the courtiers, to the soldiers' swords. That is, Antoninus, surnamed Pius, the twelfth emperor after Augustus, ordered his soldiers to kill Papinian, who had long held power there at court. And yet both of them wished to give up their power. Both of them would gladly have rid themselves of their power while they were still safe.
Of these, Seneca even tried to hand over his wealth to Nero

and to retire into leisure. Seneca even wanted to give all his wealth to Nero and live quietly at home. But the very weight of their position drags down those who are about to fall, and so neither of them achieved what he wanted. As always happens, their burden pulls down those who are sinking. Therefore neither of them escaped, and neither got what he wanted. They were overloaded, and that brought them down.
What then is this power

that is feared by those who have it? What kind of power is it, then, that is feared by the very people it belongs to? You are not safe while you want to keep it, and when you want to give it up, you cannot escape it. If you want to keep it, holding it leaves you insecure, and if you do not want it, you cannot get away from it.
Or are friends a protection, when they are won by fortune rather than by virtue?

Will friends help you here, so that you are not insecure, when they most often come from fortune rather than from virtue? But a man whom good fortune made a friend, misfortune will make an enemy. Do not trust in that. A man whom good fortune made a friend is soon made an enemy by misfortune.
And what plague does more harm than an enemy in one's own household? What sickness is more harmful than an enemy who is close to you?
WHAT TRUE POWER IS. Whoever wants to be powerful
must tame his fierce passions
and not bow his neck, conquered by lust,

to shameful reins. Whoever wants to be powerful must subdue his wanton mind, and must not let his neck be conquered by desire and made subject to its shameful bridle. That is, he must not give in to his desires.
For though the far-off land of India may tremble at your laws
and distant Thule may serve you. For even if the most remote lands fear your power, such as India in the east and Thule in the north,
still, to be unable to drive away black cares
and to banish miserable complaints
is not power. If you can never overcome harmful cravings and wretched complaints, that is, the sins that deserve lament, that is powerlessness, and it makes you powerless.

FOURTH, ON GLORY. But glory: how deceptive it often is, how shameful! But glory, how false it often is, and how shameful. It is shameful because it is false. Therefore the tragic poet rightly exclaims:

So the tragic poet among the Greeks can boldly cry: 'Glory, glory, for thousands of mortals you have become nothing but a great puffing-up of the ears.' (Greek, partly garbled: O doxa doxa myrioisi de broton … oden gagosen ei oton oggosas megan [?].) Yes: glory, glory, for a thousand people you have become nothing but a great swelling of the ears. The ears like to hear praise, and so they open themselves to it.

For many have often carried off a great name because of the false opinions of the crowd. Many have often won a great name from the false reputation they have among the people. What could be thought of that is more shameful than this? What then can be more worthless, or be imagined? For those who are falsely praised
must themselves blush at their own praises.

Those who are praised wrongly cannot help being ashamed of their praise. But even if that praise has been earned by merit, what will it have added to the wise man's conscience? Even if a good reputation is won rightly, what more virtue does the wise man then know himself to have? He measures his good not by popular rumour but by the truth of his conscience. He does not judge his worth by reputation, but by the truth his conscience knows.
But if it seems a fine thing to have spread this name widely,
it follows that he should not be judged to have spread a disgraceful [name].

If a man thinks it is a fine thing to have spread his name widely, then it is fitting that people should not think he has spread a shameful name, but a truly glorious one. But since, as I explained a little earlier, there must be many peoples whom the fame of a single man cannot reach,

so it happens that the one you think glorious appears without glory in the next part of the earth. But since it must be so, as I said before, that there are many peoples whom one man's fame cannot fully reach, it follows that the one you consider famous is unregarded in another land.
Among these things, however, popular favor

I do not even think worthy of mention. So I do not consider the praise of the people worth even thinking about. It does not come from judgment, nor does it ever last firmly. It does not come from careful choosing, nor does it hold firm.

ITEM. Now who does not see how empty and how futile the name of nobility is? The name of noble birth, which many take pride in: how vain and how contemptible is it? "Futile" is the word for a leaky vessel that has cracked open

or has become useless. A man who is worthless in himself and still wants to be called a nobleman is like such a vessel. If nobility is counted as renown, that renown belongs to someone else. That name should therefore not be counted as fame for him, because it belongs to another. For nobility seems to be a kind of praise that comes from the merits of one's parents. As this definition shows, nobility is praise that has come down from the worth of one's ancestors.
But if being proclaimed is what makes a person renowned, then the people who must be renowned are the ones being proclaimed.

Since praise makes people famous, the ancestors whose praise it is are the famous ones. So another person's renown does not make you illustrious if you have none of your own. Another person's fame does not make you illustrious if you have none of your own. But if there is anything good in noble birth, I think it is only this: that the noble seem to be placed under an obligation not to fall short of their ancestors' virtue. If there is anything good in noble birth, I consider this one thing alone to be good: that the nobly born feel obliged to take after their ancestors in virtue.
THAT ALL HAVE ONE ORIGIN. The whole race of men on earth springs from a like birth. From a like origin all people on earth have come.
For there is one father of things; one provides for all. Of all creatures there is one father; one cares for them all.
He gave rays to Phoebus and gave horns to the moon. He made the sun shine and the moon horned.
He also gave men to the earth and stars to the sky. He created men on earth and stars in heaven.
He enclosed in limbs the souls sought from the lofty seat. He shut the soul within the limbs, sent down here from heaven.
Therefore a noble seed brings forth all mortals. Therefore a noble seed has brought forth all men, because they are born from heaven.
Why do you clamour about lineage and ancestors? Why then do you boast of your kin and your forefathers? If your beginnings…
…and God your author you consider, no one stands out as degenerate.

If you look to the beginning and to God the creator, then no one is ignoble, unless, cherishing worse things through vices, he forsakes his own origin. Unless he chooses by sinning to renounce his origin: if he forsakes his creator, then he becomes ignoble.

FIFTH, ON PLEASURE. But what shall I say of the pleasures of the body? What can I say about the body's pleasure? Is not the craving for them full of anxiety, and having one's fill of them full of regret? A man is in great distress while he longs for it, and he grows just as weary of it once it is fulfilled.
How many diseases they usually bring on the bodies of those who enjoy them,
how unbearable pains, as a kind of fruit of wickedness!

How many diseases, how mighty pains they give to those who indulge in them, as if as the interest earned by wickedness? Therefore a poet said: "For in one way wine and Venus do harm." What pleasure their motions hold, I do not know. What delight there is in their craving, that I do not know. How can it be delight, when it is anxiety? But whoever is willing to remember his lusts will understand that the outcomes of pleasures are sad. And how sorrowful the outcome is, that he knows who is willing to remember his lusts.

If these can make people blessed, there is no reason why cattle too should not be called blessed. If they can make men blessed, then the beast too lacks nothing of being blessed. Their whole striving hastens to fill the bodily void. Their whole concern is to fill the belly.
LIKEWISE. Most honourable indeed would be the delight of a wife and children, but it has been said all too truly to nature that someone or other found his children to be his tormentors.

I would say that wife and children were chaste joys, except that it is said (which is far outside nature) that some children or other were the tormentors of their father. How biting any condition of theirs is, I need not remind you, who have learned it by experience elsewhere and are anxious now. However chaste their nature may be, I still need not remind you how full of care it is, since you have learned it elsewhere and are always anxious about your own children.

In this I approve the opinion of my Euripides, who said that a man without children is happy in his misfortune. For this reason I praise the saying of my dear Euripides, a Greek poet and philosopher, who said that the childless man is happy through his misfortune.
LIKEWISE. Every pleasure has this:
it drives the frenzied on with goads. All pleasures have this in common: they goad the eager and drive them on to the deed.
And like the flying bees. And they are like the bees.
When it has poured out its pleasing honey
it flees. That is, when pleasure has completed its sweetness, it shudders at what it has done. When pleasure has done the deed, it then makes it loathsome.
And it strikes the hearts it has wounded with a bite that clings too tightly.

And then it bites the hurt heart with a bite that holds fast. This is what happens to the bee: when it stings in revenge it loses its sting, and then it flees in fear because it has no defence. After that it is called fucus (a drone), that is, one that eats the honeycomb but does not make it.

HE RECAPITULATES THE FIVE ABOVE. There is therefore no doubt that these ways to happiness are certain byways. Since this is so, there is no doubt that these five ways lead away from the path to happiness,
Nor can they bring anyone to the place where they promise to bring him. Nor can they lead anyone all the way to where they promise.
I will show very briefly how many evils they are entangled in. I told at length before how many evils there are in the things that take away happiness; now I will sum it up briefly.
RICHES. What then? Will you try to gather money? But you will take it away from someone who has it.
What do you desire? Do you desire to gather treasure? Then you take it from someone else.
HONOURS. Would you shine in high offices? You will have to beg the one who grants them. Would you shine in office? Then you must plead with the one who gives it.
And you who long to go ahead of others in honour become cheap through the humility of asking. And by begging you become more despised than the others whom you long to rank above.
POWER. Do you desire power?
Do you want to become powerful? Exposed to the plots of your subjects, you will be subject to dangers. Then your own people lie in wait for you, and because of that you are in danger.

FAME. Do you seek glory? But dragged in different directions through every kind of hardship, you are no longer secure. Do you long for renown? Then you must live in anxiety, entangled in the troublesome affairs by which you wish to win glory.
PLEASURE. Do you choose a life of pleasure? Would you live a life of pleasure?
But who would not scorn and throw away being a slave of the body, a most worthless and most fragile thing?

Whom should it not shame to be the servant of the body, the most despised and the frailest of things? Those who serve pleasure are the servants of the body. Those who serve the spirit are spiritual and like God, who is spirit, and therefore they are free.

THAT IN BODILY GOODS MEN ARE NOT EQUAL TO THE BEASTS. Now those who carry bodily goods before them: how small, how fragile a possession they rely on! Those who put the goods of the body before the goods of the soul: how small a thing they hold on to! The phrase "carry before them" is said of the simiae, which we call apes. The ape always bears two young, and of those two, it loves one more

than the other. It always turns the one it loves more to face the front; the other follows it. When someone starts to hunt it, it lifts the one it loves more up to its breast; the less-loved one jumps up onto it and holds on by its hair. When it later finds itself in trouble, it lets go of the one it loves more and escapes with the one it loved less. Can you surpass elephants in size, or bulls in strength? Can you become bigger than elephants, stronger than bulls? Will you outrun tigers in speed? Or become swifter than tigers? Tigris means "arrow." It has that name from its swiftness, because no one can escape it. Saint Ambrose writes about this in the Hexameron.

Whoever steals its young from it while it is out hunting does not trust that he can escape it, and so he has provided himself with glass balls. Where it overtakes him, he throws one of them to it, as if he were giving the young one back to it. In the ball it sees itself and thinks the image is its young, and busies itself with suckling it. When it has no success at this and runs after him again, he deceives it with the second ball, and with the third, and so on, until he saves himself. Look at the expanse of the heavens, their firmness, their swiftness, and stop at last admiring worthless things. Consider how great the heavens are compared with elephants, how firm and strong compared with bulls, how swift compared with tigers, and let worthless things not be a wonder to you. Since the earth is great

and yet bears no comparison with the heavens, who then can know their breadth and their greatness? Since, wide as they are, they still turn round in twenty-four hours, what then can be so swift and so quick? Since even that immeasurable speed does not break them apart, what then is so firm? Yet the heavens are not to be admired for these things so much as for the reason by which they are governed. They are not so wonderful for the three things named as for the reason that drives them. That reason is God's wisdom. But the splendor of beauty: how swift it is, how fleeting, more fleeting than the changeableness of spring flowers! Consider also how hastily and how quickly it passes for you, the beauty of a man's appearance (I mean of his form), and how it is more changeable than the beauty of flowers.

But if, as Aristotle says, people had the eyes of a lynx. If people had lynx eyes, as Aristotle says. So that their sight could pass through what stands in its way. I mean that they could see right through a person. Once the insides were seen, would not the body of Alcibiades, most beautiful on the surface, seem utterly ugly? If they saw inside, would not even the body of Alcibiades seem badly made to them? He had the most beautiful body of all on the outside. We do not know who the beautiful Alcibias was, though many guess that she was the mother of Hercules, because he was called Alcides.
So it is not your nature that makes you seem beautiful, but the weakness of the eyes that look at you.

That you seem beautiful to men is not the doing of your nature, for inside you are dung, but of the weakness of the eyes. But value the goods of the body as highly as you wish, so long as you know that whatever you admire can be destroyed by the little fire of a three-day fever. Now value the body as highly as you will, since you know that the body that is so wondrously dear to you can be killed by a three-day fever.

From all of these one may bring it to a sum, that is, to brevity. From all these discussions I will bring it to the most concise statement: that these things, which can neither provide the goods they promise nor are made perfect by the gathering of all goods, neither lead to blessedness like certain paths nor themselves make people blessed. That is: these five, which cannot bring what they promise and are not perfect through the gathering of all good, are not paths to blessedness, nor do they make anyone blessed. The perfect gathering of all goods, that is blessedness.

Where that is lacking, there is no blessedness. For this reason the argument is called "from the cause," that is, from the efficient cause. How can the effect be present where the efficient cause is not? At one time she teaches him to infer the cause from the end, at another the end from the cause. Just as cause and efficient cause are one, so also end, effect and outcome are all one. With these two topics of argument, and in addition with clear examples, she has taught us, together with Boethius, that blessedness is not found in those five. All disputations have their strength in arguments, in syllogisms and in definitions,

and further in the examples of the ancestors and in divine authority. By what other means could one strengthen anything? Yet what the reasoning of syllogisms shows us is more certain than what arguments show, because some arguments are probable, that is, plausible, and these may sometimes be true and sometimes false. Others are necessary, that is, true by necessity. But syllogisms never deceive, if they are lawfully constructed. Therefore she has saved them until later, for a stronger disputation.
LAMENT OVER HUMAN BLINDNESS. Alas, what ignorance leads the wretched astray down a pathless track! Ah, how grievously! What ignorance misleads you wretched people and leads you so far off the road?
You do not look for gold in a green tree,
nor do you pick gems from the vine. Indeed, you do not think of looking for gold on trees, or of breaking gems off vines.
You do not hide snares on high mountains,
so that you may enrich your feasts with fish. Indeed, you do not set your nets on the mountains to fish.
Nor, if it pleases you to hunt roe deer,
…you seek the Tyrrhenian shallows, that is, the Tuscan sea. Nor, on the other hand,
if you want to hunt, do you set your snares around the sea-waves. Indeed, they even know its very recesses, that is, the secret places of the sea.
hidden by the waves.
which water is more fruitful in snow-white gems, that is, in large pearls,

or which in red purple, that is, in the purple-shellfish. They know well the familiar places of the sea: which are rich in the white large pearls, which we call pearls, and which in purple, that is, the blood of the purple-shellfish.
And also which shores yield tender fish

or rough sea urchins. And which shores are rich in tender fish, or in the rough echini. The echinus is a small, sweet fish, as rough as a hedgehog. Its nature is such that if it begins to cling to a ship, no storm comes great enough to move the ship.
But where the good that they desire lies hidden,
blind, they put up with not knowing. But where the good is that they go about seeking, that they do not want to know.
And what has gone beyond the star-bearing pole
they seek, sunk in the earth. And what has passed beyond heaven, they want to dig up out of the earth.
What fitting curse shall I call down on such foolish minds? What may I now rightly pray for on behalf of such foolish minds?
Let them strive after wealth and honors,
and when they have gained false goods with heavy burden,

then let them recognize the true ones. This is what I will wish for them: since they will not turn back, let them go after honors and after riches, which are false goods, and when they become aware of the burden, may God grant them by it that they recognize the true goods. This I wish for them; this I pray for them.
WHAT LEADS THE FOLLOWERS OF FALSE HAPPINESS ASTRAY.
Let it be enough to have shown the form of false happiness up to this point. Now let the image of false happiness be enough to have shown you.
If you see it clearly, the next step is to show what the true one is. If you understand it well, then it is time for me to show you the true one. "Yet," I said,

"I see that neither can sufficiency be gained through wealth, nor power through kingdoms, nor reverence through offices, nor renown through glory, nor gladness through pleasures." "I see well," I said, "that one gains neither sufficiency through wealth, nor power through a kingdom, nor honor through office, nor renown through glory, nor joy through pleasure."
Or have you also grasped the causes why this is so?

"Can you tell," she said, "what this means?" "I seem to make it out, as if through a narrow crack. It seems to me that I see it," I said, "as through a narrow slit. But I would rather learn it more plainly from you."

"But I would gladly learn it more clearly from you." "Yet the explanation is very easy." "Truly," she said, "it is a plain matter." "For human error separates what is simple and undivided by nature." Now hear it from her: what is truly simple and undivided by nature, people's error tries to separate. "And it moves it away from the true and perfect to the false and imperfect." And it leads it away from the true and the perfect to the false and the imperfect.
[Heading: Where there is one, none of these] "Or do you think
that what needs nothing [Heading, continued: five is lacking.] has need of power? Do you think that what is in need of nothing can be in need of power?"
"By no means," I said.

"No," said I. "If it needs nothing, how then can it need any one thing?" That is written in the Peri Hermeneias: if the universal negative is true, the particular affirmative is false. "You are quite right." "You are right in that," said she. "For if there is anything…"
that has weaker strength in any matter, in that matter it must need the help of another.

Whatever is powerless in anything, in that it needs the help of another. That is called an argument from adjuncts: weakness is always joined with the need for help. So it is, I said. That is so, I said. Therefore sufficiency and power have one and the same nature. Since it is so, she said, sufficiency and power are one nature. So it seems. So it must be, I said. That too is from adjuncts.
[Heading: Likewise.] "But what is of this kind,

do you think it should be despised, or on the contrary that it is the most worthy of reverence of all things? That in which there is sufficiency and power," she said, "is it contemptible, or worthy of all honors?"
"But this," I said, "cannot even be doubted."

"There can be no doubt of that either," said I, "but that the third follows those two." "Let us therefore add reverence to sufficiency and power, so that we judge these three to be one." "Now let us put together," said she, "sufficiency and power and venerability, so that we hold the three as one."
"Let us add it, if indeed we wish to confess the truth." "Let us do so," said I, "as we ought to, if we wish to acknowledge what is true."
Likewise. But what, she said, do you think this is obscure and ignoble, or most illustrious with all renown?

That in which those three are, she said, do you think it is without renown and ignoble, or the most renowned of all things? But consider whether what has been granted to lack nothing, to be most powerful, and to be most worthy of honour, would lack renown, which it could not supply for itself, and for that reason seem in some part more contemptible. Consider this for yourself: whether what is without need of anything, and mighty, and honourable, as you have admitted, could be without need and yet not be renowned [?], and whether for that reason it would be somewhat more contemptible than the others. I cannot, I said, but confess that this, as it is,
so too is most renowned.

I cannot admit anything else about it, I said, except what is so: that it is necessarily renowned. It follows, then, that we must admit that renown differs in nothing from the three above. If this is so, she said, then we must also admit that renown is not separate from the three above. It follows, I said. It is not separate, I said.

LIKEWISE. That which needs nothing outside itself, which can do all things by its own powers, and which is famous and revered: is it not clear that this is also the most joyful? "That which is without need of anything else," she said, "which is capable by its own strength, which is famous

and worthy of honour, is that not also the most joyful of all things?" "But I cannot even imagine," I said, "from where any sorrow could creep in on such a thing." "I could never conceive," I said, "from where sadness could come to such a thing." "So it is full of joy, if indeed the earlier points stand:

that must be admitted." "Therefore it must be admitted, if the earlier reckoning is true, that it is full of joy." "And by the same reasoning it is also necessary that the names of sufficiency, power, fame, reverence, and pleasure are different, but that their substance does not differ at all." "Therefore it is necessary," she said, "that the five have different names and yet are one being." "It is necessary," I said. "Truly necessary," I said. She has worked through all five with the same single argument she began with. That is the argument "from adjuncts" (ab adiunctis). Each of them is joined to the others, and therefore no one can separate them.

On the various choosing of the good. "This, therefore, which is one and simple by nature, human perversity divides." Now you have understood that human wrongness strives to split what is by nature one and is simple. "And while it tries to obtain a part of a thing that has no parts, it obtains neither the portion, which does not exist, nor the thing itself, which it does not seek at all." And by seeking a part of what is undivided, they lose the very thing which they ought to seek but do not seek.
"In what way?" I said. "In what way?" said I.

"He who seeks riches," she said, "in flight from poverty does not trouble himself about power; he prefers to be base and obscure. He who strives after wealth, fleeing want, does not seek power at all; to him it is dearer to be despised and unknown.

"He also denies himself many pleasures, even natural ones, so as not to lose the money he has acquired." And he takes from himself many of his comforts, even natural ones, such as sleep, so that he may keep the treasure he has gained.
"But in this way not even sufficiency comes to the one whom strength deserts,

whom trouble stings, whom lowliness casts down, whom obscurity hides." But someone who acts this way loses even sufficiency, since he loses even power. Discomfort stings him, contempt makes him an outcast, and obscurity keeps him hidden. Because he wants to have one thing without the others, which are its adjuncts, he loses that too.
LIKEWISE. "But he who desires only power squanders wealth, despises pleasures,
and counts honour without power, and glory as well, as worth nothing."

He who loves power alone squanders his goods, and cares neither for pleasures nor for honors without power, nor for glory. But you see how many things this man also lacks. There you also see what he is lacking. For it happens that sometimes he lacks necessities, that he is gnawed by anxieties. It often happens to him that he goes without his necessities and is goaded by anxieties.

And when he cannot drive these away, he ceases even to be powerful, which was what he sought most. And it happens to him, when he cannot defend himself against these things, that the power too, which alone he strove for, slips away from him as a result.
LIKEWISE. "One may reason in the same way about honours, glory and pleasures." I can say the same about honours,
glory and pleasures. "For since each of these is the same as the others, whoever seeks any one of them without the others
does not grasp even what he desires." Since they are one, he who desires one of them without the others does not get even that one.
Again. "What then," I said,

"if someone should wish to obtain all these things at once?" "But what," said I, "of him who wants to gain all five together?" "He would indeed wish for the height of happiness." "That is the one," said she, "who wants to gain the fullness of happiness."
"But will he find it in those things
which we have shown cannot bestow what they promise?" "But do you think he will find it in those things which I have shown you cannot do what they promise?" "By no means," I said.
"No," said I. "Therefore happiness is in no way to be sought in these things, which are each believed to supply some of the things to be desired."

"Therefore," she said, "happiness is not to be sought in those five, each of which can give something of what one desires, but by no means all of it." "I admit it," I said. "That is so," I said. "And nothing truer than this can be said." And nothing truer can be said than all of this.
"So you have," she said, "both the form of false happiness and its causes."
"Now," she said, "you have the image of false happiness, and with it the reason why it is false. It would not be false if people did not hasten to separate things that are inseparable."

TO TURN AWAY FROM FALSE HAPPINESS AND DIRECT ONESELF TO THE TRUE. "Now turn your mind's gaze in the opposite direction." SHE ADMONISHES. Now look toward what is opposite to it. "For there you will at once see the true happiness that we promised." There you will at once see the true happiness that I promised to show you. "And yet..."

"This," I said, "is clear even to a blind man." "Truly," I said, "even a blind man can see it. And you showed it a little earlier, while you were trying to reveal the causes of the false happiness." And you showed it earlier, when you showed where the false happiness comes from.
"For unless I am mistaken, true and perfect happiness is the happiness that makes a person self-sufficient..."
powerful, worthy of reverence, renowned

and joyful. Let my supposition not deceive me: that is the true happiness which makes a man rich, mighty, worthy of honor, renowned, and joyful. And so that you may know that I have inwardly understood: whatever can truly provide one of these, since they are all the same, I recognize without any doubt to be full happiness. And so that you may know that I understand it inwardly: whatever it is that can truly give one of these five, since they are all one, that I acknowledge to be full happiness."
"O my pupil, you are happy in this opinion," she said, "if indeed you add this to it. God bless you, my dear one, for this opinion," she said, "if you add this to it to make it complete.
"What is it?" I said. "Which one?" I said.

"Do you think there is anything among these mortal and perishable things that could bring about a state of this kind?" "I am leading you to this," she said. "Do you think there is anything among these transitory worldly things that can give a person this state?" That is what I wanted you to say by this. "I think not at all," I said.
"and you have shown this so fully that nothing more is needed."

"No, I do not think so," I said. "You have taught me this so well that there is no need for more." "Therefore these things seem to give mortals either images of the true good or certain imperfect goods." "They can give a person," she said, "what looks like the good, or what is imperfect good. But they cannot give the true and perfect good." "I agree," I said.

"I grant that," I said. "Since, then, you have recognized which happiness is the true one, and which ones falsely imitate it, it now remains for you to learn where you can seek this true one." "Since you now recognize the true happiness," she said, "and the things that falsely claim it for themselves, you now have to learn where you should go to get it, and whom you should ask for it."
"That indeed," I said, "I have long been eagerly wishing for. I have long been longing for that," said I. "But since even in the smallest matters," she said,
"...as our Plato holds in the Timaeus..."
"...divine help ought to be called upon, what do you think we should do now, so that we may be worthy to find the seat of that highest good?"

"But since Plato thinks, in his book the Timaeus, that one should beg for God's help even in small matters, what then do you think we must do so that we may find the chief seat of the foremost good?" "I think," I said, "that we must call upon the Father of all things, without whom no beginning is properly founded. I think," said I, "that we should call upon him without whom one can do nothing well." "Rightly!" she said, and at once she sang in measure thus. "You speak rightly," she said, and she sang thus in this metre:
PHILOSOPHY'S PRAYER TO GOD, THAT HE HIMSELF MAY SHOW THE HIGHEST GOOD. O Sower of the earth and heaven. You, Creator of heaven and earth,
You who govern the world by everlasting reason,

You order, shape and direct this world with your eternal wisdom. You who bid time go forth from eternity, that is, who commanded the times to begin at the beginning of the world. You bade the times begin their course together with the world, for before that there were no times, only eternity.
And, remaining unmoved yourself, you cause all things to move. And you yourself, steadfast, turn and change all things. For the heaven revolves and all things change.
You whom no outside causes drove
to fashion the work of flowing matter,

that is, matter formless and undistinguished. No other things drove you to make the shapeless material from which this world came. She means the undivided mass that he made first, in which nothing was yet distinguished. But, that is, nothing except, the form of the highest good planted within you, free from envy. Nothing but your own inward goodness, which has no envy. You, bearing the beautiful world in your mind,
you yourself most beautiful. You, who have always carried this beautiful world in your mind!

yourself more beautiful. You draw all things from the eternal pattern. You created it all according to the wisdom and the eternal image of your mind. And forming it in a like image, that is, you formed it. And you made it just as it was in your mind. No one made a model for you beforehand. And commanding ...
that is, you commanded the perfect parts to complete a perfect whole.

[Understand:] "work." And you commanded well-made parts to make a well-made work. For just as handsome limbs make a handsome man, so it also came about that every part of the world, being perfectly made, made the world perfectly made. If its parts were lacking, the world itself would be lacking. "You bind the elements by numbers," [understand:] "fixed ones." As if he were saying: you bind the four elements. You bind the four elements together in such a way "that cold things agree with flames,"

"dry things with liquid ones." That is, hot and cold, as fire and water are, and dry and wet, as earth and air are, do not fight each other. "So that the purer fire does not fly off." So firmly that the lighter fire, which has no murkiness in it, does not fly away upward because of its lightness, since it is uppermost.
"Or weights drag down the sunken earth." Nor does heaviness sink the earth downward.
"You join the soul in the middle and release it through harmonious members."

That is, you join the soul and release it through harmonious members. You fasten the soul to its beloved members and divide it among them. By this I mean the sun, which travels in the middle of the heaven and in the middle of the seven planets. The philosophers called it the world-soul, because it pervades everything that grows green and grows, as the soul pervades the limbs. "Of threefold nature." It is of threefold nature, because it shines, warms, and burns. Other fires also burn, but they do not warm. "Moving all things," that is, to grow. It quickens all things, as the soul quickens our body.
"Which, when it has rolled its motion, divided into two circles." That is, which, when it leads around its course, divided into two hemispheres,

"goes to return into itself," that is, to its rising. And when it bends its journey, divided into two arcs, one above the earth and the other under the earth, it goes back again to its rising. "And it circles the deep mind and turns"
that is, it illuminates heaven "with a similar image."

And by night it travels the hidden path under the earth, and in the same way by day it travels across heaven above the earth. "You bring forth," that is, produce, "souls and lesser lives by like causes," that is, by a cause: that there should be beings who would obey God freely. For the same purpose you created angels and humans, who are lower than they. What was the cause? That they should acknowledge you as their creator and honor you. Or another reading: with like gifts you have raised angels and humans above the other animals, I mean reason and understanding.
"And fitting them, lofty, to light chariots." And raising them up high on swift senses.
"You sow them in heaven and on earth." You place them in heaven and on earth: angels in heaven, humans on earth. "Which," [understand:] souls and lives, "you, with kindly mind, cause, turned back,"
"to be turned to you, led back by fire."

You make them turn back to you, turned toward you, by your goodwill. "Grant, Father, to the mind," [understand:] his, "to ascend to the august seat." You who do this, grant his mind that it may climb up to your imperial throne, so that it may understand heavenly things.
"Grant it to survey," that is, to find, "the source of the good." Make his mind find the origin of the good. "The light having been found." And when he finds the light,
Grant that it may fix the clear sight of the mind on you. So let him hold fast on you the clear eyes of his mind.
Scatter the mists and the weights of the earthly mass. Drive away the blindness and the sins of the earthly body.
"And shine upon them with your splendor." And shine upon them with your radiance. "For you are the clear sky." You are the clear brightness.
"You are tranquil rest for the pious." You are restful peace for those who mean well. "To see you is the end." When one sees you, that is the end.

You are also the beginning, the carrier, the leader, the path and the goal. You are the beginning. You are the one who carries us, that is, to the end. You are the guide, and you yourself are the way, and the end that we strive toward.

WHETHER THERE IS SOME HIGHEST GOOD. Since, then, you have seen what the form of the imperfect good is, and also that of the perfect. Since you have looked upon the image of both, of the imperfect good and of the perfect: namely, the form of the imperfect is the one that gives one of the five, and the form of the perfect is the one that gives all of them together. Now, I think, it must be shown
in what this perfection of happiness is established.

So now we must say where perfect happiness has its place and where its seat is. "In this, I think, the first thing to ask is..." In this account I think the first thing to ask is "whether any good of the kind you defined a little earlier can exist in the nature of things." That is, whether any such good can exist among all things, as you showed earlier when you said: "Unless I am mistaken, true and perfect happiness is the happiness that makes a person self-sufficient, powerful, worthy of reverence, celebrated, and joyful."

"So that an empty image formed by thought does not deceive us, apart from the truth of the thing that underlies it." So that a false image formed by our thought does not deceive us, without the truth of the substance. This is how the ancient people thought about the spirits of the dead (manes) and the demigods, and that thought deceived them.
But it cannot be denied that it exists, and that it is, as it were, a kind of fountain of all goods. There can be no denying that it exists and that it is the source of all good.
For everything
that is called imperfect, by a diminution of the perfect

that is said to be imperfect … The imperfect is always called imperfect because of a lack of the complete. From this it follows that if something seems to be imperfect in any kind of thing, there must also be something perfect in that kind. Therefore it is necessary that if something lacking exists, there is also something complete of the same kind. That is an argument from the part to the whole.

For if perfection is taken away, no one can even imagine where the thing called imperfect would have come from. Put the other way, if the complete does not exist, no one needs to think about the lacking. An argument from the whole to the part.
For the nature of things did not take its beginning from diminished

and unfinished. For the nature of all things did not take its beginning from deficient and incomplete things. But proceeding from whole and perfect things, it slides down into these lowest and exhausted things. Rather, beginning from whole and full things, it slid downward afterward until it came to these last things and to these powerless things. From the delights of paradise man came to the miseries of this world. From immortality he came to mortality. From the likeness of God he became like the senseless beasts. But if there is a certain imperfect happiness [?] of fragile good, as we showed a little before, it cannot be doubted that there is also some solid and perfect happiness. If there is incomplete happiness, then there is no doubt at all that there is also full and whole happiness.
"That has been concluded most firmly and most truly," I said.
"You have established it very firmly and very truly," I said. "What can be firmer or truer than when one supports the whole with the part, or the part with the whole?"

WHERE THE HIGHEST GOOD IS. "Consider where it dwells," she said, "in this way." "Where it is," she said, "work that out for yourself as follows." The common understanding of human minds proves that God, the ruler of all things, is good. That God, the lord of all things, is good is something every person's mind admits. For since nothing better than God can be conceived, who would doubt that the thing than which nothing is better is good? Since no one can think of anything better than God, whatever has nothing better than itself must be good. The highest is necessarily high, the greatest is necessarily great, the best is necessarily good.

That is an argument from the greater to the lesser. Reason shows that God is good in such a way that it also proves that the perfect good is in him. This argument confirms that God is good in such a way that perfect good is in him. Since nothing is better than he is, he is not merely a good thing but perfectly good. For if he were not such, he could not be the ruler of all things. If he is not perfectly good, then he is not the highest lord of things. For then there would be something more excellent than he, possessing the perfect good, which would seem to be prior to him and older than he. For then there would be another, more lordly, having perfect good, which would be earlier and worthier than he. For it has been made clear that all perfect things are prior to less complete ones. For I said a little while ago that all perfect things come before deficient ones.

PREMISE. "Therefore, lest the reasoning proceed to infinity, it must be acknowledged that the highest God is most full of the highest and perfect good." Therefore it must be admitted, so that the argument does not become too long, that the foremost God is full of the foremost and perfect good.
PREMISE. But we have established that the perfect good is true happiness. Now it has been shown that the perfect good is true happiness.

INFERENCE. Therefore true happiness must be located in the highest God. Therefore true happiness is necessarily in God. The syllogism is constructed like this: In God is the highest good. Thus all is one: the highest good

and happiness. Because that is so, happiness is where the highest good is. "I accept it," I said. "I understand it well," I said. "Nor is there any way it can be contradicted." And no one can dispute it.

ON THE PREDICATIVE AND THE CONDITIONAL SYLLOGISM. Here two premises (sumpta) produce one inference (illatio), because this is a predicative syllogism, just as in the conditional syllogism the proposition and the assumption produce the conclusion. What are premises (sumpta) but things conceded (concessa), that is, in our language, admissions? When someone admits two things from which a third follows by necessity, even without his admitting it, that third is rightly called an inference (illatio), because it is "brought in" (illatum) from two premises, or from three if that happens to be the case. That means it is thrown in along with them, whether he likes it or not. But what is a proposition (propositio)

but the first test, which reaches further, with which one first challenges the man and probes further what he will admit? In the same way, the assumption (assumptio) is what is taken up in addition (assumptum), to probe his admission a second time. Because these two produce the third, by which the man is caught so that he cannot get away, it is called the conclusion (conclusio), that is, the "lock." The conditional syllogism gets its name from the fact that it speaks with conditions and with "if": if this is so, and this, then that is so. Therefore "conditional" means "spoken with conditions." But "predicative" means "spoken plainly," because it says openly, without conditions and without "if": this is so, and this.

Therefore it is so. The members of both of them are called in common predications, or proloquia, or propositions, or enunciations. These four words we may interpret equally and in common as 'statement'. Since an enunciation is, as Aristotle says in the Peri Hermeneias, a speech that is true or false, and a predication is the same thing, and a proposition, and a proloquium, what then are lies and truths but statements? But a syllogism must always have two statements of such a kind that they support the third. That cannot be otherwise than that the first two are so joined to each other that the second has half of the first, either the subject part

or the declarative part (the predicate). And because the second repeats half of the first, whatever is left over unrepeated in each of them, when it is predicative, makes the third. Whoever wishes to recognize this in other syllogisms, let him learn it here. One statement is: 'The highest good is in God.' 'The highest good', that is the subject; 'is in God', that is the declarative part. The second is: 'The highest good is blessedness.' There the subject part of the first is repeated. The third is: 'Blessedness is in God.' That was left over from the first two, because from the one came 'blessedness', and from the other came 'is in God'.

That is how it goes in the predicative syllogism. In the conditional it goes nearly the same way. If we say: 'If the sun is above the earth, it is day', that is the proposition. The assumption takes half of it, thus: 'But it is day.' What then still remains unrepeated in the proposition makes the conclusion, thus: 'Therefore the sun is above the earth.' The subject is that in the proloquium about which something is said; but what is said about it, that is the declarative part. Without this law no syllogism comes about. As long as she taught him with arguments and with examples, the discourse was easier; because she now wants to give him stronger remedies, she has therefore now undertaken with him, in addition to the arguments,
syllogisms, which are the most powerful both in disputing dialectically and in persuading rhetorically.

THAT GOD IS IN HIS SUBSTANCE THE HIGHEST GOOD AND BLESSEDNESS, BECAUSE THERE IS NO DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THEM. "But I ask you," she said, "see how reverently and how firmly you prove what we said: that the highest God is completely full of the highest good." "Now I ask you," she said, "see how devoutly and how worthily you consider what I said: that the sovereign God is full of the most glorious good." "In what way?" I said. "What do you mean?" said I.

"Do not suppose that this Father of all things either received from outside that highest good of which he is said to be full, or has it by nature in such a way that you might think the substance of God, who has it, is different from the substance of the blessedness that he has."

Never think that the Lord of all things has received the good of which he is full, or that he has it from himself in such a way as if the substance of God who has it and of the happiness that he has were not one. Neither of these two is the case: he has not received it, nor does it separate itself from his substance. For if you should think it was received from outside, you could judge that what gave it is more excellent than what received it. If you think he received his highest good from somewhere else, then you could consider the giver superior to the one who received it.
But that he is the most excellent of all things…

…we most worthily confess. But you know that we rightly declare him the highest of all things. But if it is indeed present in him by nature, yet differs from him in its essence, since we are speaking of God, the prince of things, let whoever can, imagine
who joined these different things together. Now he has not received it [from another].

But if he has it from himself, and it is still in any way unlike him, then let someone try to guess, since we have judged God to be the highest of things, who joined them together, I mean God and his good, things so unlike. Finally, what is different from any thing is not that thing from which it is understood to be different. To put it most strictly: what is unlike another is also something other than that which it is unlike. That is an argument from the dissimilar. Things that are dissimilar cannot be one.
Therefore, what is different from the highest good

by its own nature is not the highest good. From this it follows necessarily that a God who is by nature in any way unlike the highest good is not the highest good. But it is wicked to think this of him, than whom it is agreed that nothing is more excellent.

"It is impious to think this of that God than whom nothing is superior. For no thing at all can have a nature better than its origin. No nature can be better than its origin. This is an argument from the efficient cause: the effect is necessarily such as its efficient cause is. That is why the proverb says: 'As the root, so also the branches.' How then can the highest good be better than God, who is its origin? He is its origin, but in such a way that he himself is it. Therefore, by the truest reasoning, I would conclude that what is the origin of all things is also, in its substance, the highest good. Therefore I can establish by true reasoning that God, who is the origin of all goods, is the highest good in his substance."

"Most rightly," I said. "Very rightly," said I, "have you established it," that is, because your arguments are true. "But it has been granted that the highest good is happiness." "So it was judged earlier," she said, "that the highest good is happiness." "It is so," I said. "So it is," said I. "Therefore," she said, "that God is happiness

must be confessed." "So it is also necessary," she said, "that God is not only a highest good but also happiness." That is the fitting conclusion. "Nor," I said, "can I oppose the premises put forward, and I see that this inference follows from them." "I cannot oppose the earlier statements," said I, "and I see that these later ones follow from them by necessity."
LIKEWISE A SUBTLER ARGUMENT: THAT THINGS WHICH ARE DIFFERENT ARE NOT HIGHEST GOODS, AND THAT THINGS WHICH ARE HIGHEST ARE NOT DIFFERENT.
"Consider," she said, "whether the same thing may be proved more firmly from this as well:
that two goods which are different from each other cannot be highest." "Now consider for yourself whether it will also be proved by these arguments that two unlike goods cannot be the highest."
PREMISE. "For it is clear that goods which differ are not such that the one is what the other is." "I have shown before that dissimilar goods cannot be one."
PREMISE. "Therefore neither of them can be perfect, since the one is lacking to the other." "Therefore neither is a full good, since neither is together with the other."
INFERENCE. But that what is not perfect

is not the highest is manifest. What is not complete cannot be the foremost. The syllogism is constructed thus: Unlike goods are not one. Things that are not one are both deficient. What is deficient never becomes the foremost. Which are the unlike goods? Riches and glory. How are they deficient? In that each of them lacks the share [?] of the others. Because that is so, that which lacks anything cannot be the foremost.
LIKEWISE A PREMISE. "In no way, therefore, can those goods that are highest be different." "Those, on the other hand, which are the highest are not unlike."
PREMISE. "But we have concluded that both happiness and God are the highest good." "Now I have shown before that God and happiness are the highest."

INFERENCE. "Therefore it is necessary that whatever is the highest divinity is itself the highest happiness." Therefore it is necessary that the divinity which is prince of all things is the princely happiness. This syllogism too is constructed thus: The highest goods are not unlike each other; God and happiness are the highest goods. Because each of them is what the other also is, I mean, because each of them is the highest good, therefore they are one.
"Nothing," I said, "truer in substance than this,
nor firmer in reasoning, nor more worthy of God can be concluded." "Now," said I, "nothing can be established that is truer, or more reasonable, or more fitting to God."
THE PRESENTATION OF A GIFT FOR WELL-UNDERSTOOD REASONINGS. "In addition to these things," she said, "just as geometers are accustomed

after demonstrating their propositions, to infer something which they themselves call porismata, so I too will give you a kind of corollary." When I had answered her thus, she said: "Geometers have the custom," she said, "after demonstrating their questions, of giving their students something extra that was not asked; this addition they call questum [gain]. So I give you as a gain what I now tell you unasked, just as if I were giving you a corollary.
For since people become happy by attaining happiness, and happiness itself is divinity,
it is clear that they become happy by attaining divinity.

Since people become blessed by attaining blessedness, and God is blessedness, whoever attains God is blessed. An argument from the efficient cause. Because God and blessedness are one, they therefore make people blessed. An argument of this kind holds between a cause and its effect, in the manner of a syllogism, for it says: if this and this are so, then that is so. "But just as people become just by attaining justice, and wise by attaining wisdom, so by the same reasoning those who have attained divinity must become gods." Now further: just as people become just by attaining justice, and wise by attaining wisdom, so they must also become gods in the same way by attaining God. An argument from likeness. Just as that attainment does,

so this one does too. That is a likeness. "Therefore every blessed person is a god." Since that is so, the blessed person is a god. Since God and blessedness are one, they also make one. That is still an argument from the efficient, that is, from the cause. "But by nature there is only one; by participation, however, nothing prevents there being very many." But note this distinction well: only one God exists by nature; many can become gods by grace, by having a share in him. With this she has presented him with a gift [?].

'And this is beautiful and precious,' I said, 'whether you prefer it to be called a porism or a corollary.' Now it is also very beautiful, said I, whether you call it a porisma or a corollarium. The common honors of victory were palms in the hands of all victors and laurel crowns on their heads. But to those who had done something very glorious in war, or also in games and in spectacles, a precious head ornament was given, which, from its likeness to a corolla, that is, a crown, was called a corollarium. Of this Suetonius speaks concerning the generosity of Caesar Augustus, in these words: 'Therefore he offered corollaries and prizes from his own means, both frequent and great, even at others' shows and games, and he attended no Greek contest at which he did not honor each of the contestants according to his merit.'
WHAT THINGS ARE ADDED TO BLESSEDNESS.

WHETHER THEY ARE TO BE CALLED ITS PARTS, OR WHETHER THEY ARE REFERRED TO ONE OF THEM. 'And yet nothing is more beautiful than this too, which reason urges us to attach to these things.' Nothing yet, she said, is more beautiful than what reason teaches us to add to this. 'What?' I said. What is that? said I.
"Since," she said, "blessedness seems to contain many things,

do all of these join together into one body of blessedness, made up of a variety of parts? Or is one of them what completes the substance of blessedness, with the others referred to it?" Since blessedness includes many things, namely the good and the five mentioned above, are these parts of blessedness, as the various limbs are parts of the body? Or is one of them blessedness, with the others looking toward it? She has already stated very precisely that the highest good is blessedness. Now she wants to say that the other five aim at the highest. "I would like you," I said, "to make this plain by going through the things themselves." "I would like you," I said, "to show me this by telling me the thing itself."
THAT BLESSEDNESS HAS NO PARTS. "Do we not consider blessedness to be the good?" she said. "Should we not consider blessedness good?" she said.
"Yes, and the highest good," I said.
"Yes, and the foremost," I said. "You may add this to all of them," she said. "You must add 'highest' to all five," she said.

For this same thing, that is, beatitude, is judged to be the highest sufficiency, the same is the highest power, and also reverence, renown and pleasure. Just as beatitude is the highest good, so it is also the highest sufficiency, and the highest power; it is also the highest reverence, and renown, and pleasure.
What then?

Are all these, good, sufficiency, power and the rest, like certain members of beatitude? What do you think? Are all these, I mean good, and sufficiency, and power, and the others, like limbs of beatitude? Or are they all referred to the good as to a summit? Or do they all aim at the good, as if it were their head?
I understand, I said, what you propose for investigation.

But I want to hear what you decide. I understand well, I said, what you give me to work out; but how you explain it, that I long to hear. Take the distinction of this matter as follows. Now listen, she said, I will teach you to distinguish it! I will teach you how they aim at the good, and do not make up that same good as parts. If all these were members of beatitude, they would also differ from one another. Thus you should follow it step by step through argument: if the good and the other five were limbs of beatitude, they would be unlike one another. That is an argument from adjuncts: dissimilarity is always joined to members. For this is the nature of parts, that diverse things make up one body. Such is always the nature of parts, that unlike things make one body. But yet,
all these have been shown to be the same.

Now these have been shown to be one thing. Therefore they are by no means members. Therefore they are not members. Because they are one, therefore they are not diverse. That is an argument from incompatibles, for being one and being diverse are incompatible. Because they are also not diverse, therefore they are not members. That is, as I just said, from adjuncts. Otherwise beatitude will seem to be joined together from a single member, which cannot happen. Otherwise beatitude would have to be made out of one limb, which cannot be. No composition can come about from one thing. That again is an argument from incompatibles, for being simple and being composite are incompatible.
"That indeed," I said, "is not in doubt." "There is no doubt about that," I said. "But I am waiting for what remains." "Next I am waiting for what is still to come."

THAT THE THINGS WHICH BELONG TO BEATITUDE ARE REFERRED TO ONE. But it is plain that the other things are referred to the good. The other five, which are one together with the good, are sought for the sake of the good, because people want to reach the good through them.

For sufficiency is sought because it is judged to be good. People desire sufficiency because it is considered good. Power is sought for this reason, because it too is believed to be good. That is why power is also dear,

because it seems good to people. One may conjecture the same about reverence, renown and pleasantness. I can say the same about the other three. Therefore the good is the sum and the cause of all things that are sought. Therefore the good is always the head and the purpose of everything that people desire.
For whatever holds in itself no good, either in reality or in appearance,
cannot be sought in any way. But whatever is not good

…nor like the good: no one desires that. And on the other hand, things that are not good by nature are still sought as if they were truly good, if they seem to be good. Therefore, on the other side, things that are not good at all, if they are only like the good, people desire them even for that reason, as if they were good. Hence it comes about

that goodness is rightly believed to be the chief hinge and cause of all things that are sought. Therefore one should believe that goodness is always the innermost hinge and the foremost impulse of all desiring.
But that for whose sake something is sought seems to be what is most desired.

For whatever reason a thing is desired, that reason is what one chiefly aims at in it. For example, if someone wants to ride for the sake of his health, he does not so much desire the motion of riding as the effect of health. So the man who rides for his health is not aiming at how he stirs himself by riding, but at becoming healthier.
Since, therefore, all things are sought for the sake of the good,
it is not those things but the good itself that all people desire. From this it is clear that whatever anyone desires for the sake of the good, he does not desire that thing but the good.
LIKEWISE. But we granted that happiness is that for whose sake other things are desired. But the good, for whose sake everything was desired, I said was happiness.
So in this way too, happiness alone is sought.

Therefore in this way too, I mean by seeking the one good, happiness alone is sought. From this it is plainly evident that the substance of the good itself and of happiness is one and the same. From this it is openly clear that good and happiness are one thing.
I see no reason why anyone could disagree. "I know of nothing there that anyone could argue against," I said.
AGAIN. But we have shown that God and true happiness are one and the same. "Now I have shown," she said, "that God and blessedness are one."

"That is so," I said. "That is so," I said. Therefore we may safely conclude that his substance too lies in the good itself and nowhere else. "Therefore," she said, "I may boldly affirm that God's own substance lies in the good."
AN INVITATION TO HAPPINESS. Come here together, all you captives. Come here together, all who are in distress.
whom deceitful desire, dwelling in (that is, possessing) earthly minds, binds with wicked chains. You whom evil lusts, which possess your minds, bind with strong chains.
This will be your rest from your labours.
Here you will find rest: a house of refuge.

open to the wretched. This alone is the asylum of the guilty, which always stands open to the wretched. This is more certain than the one the descendants of Hercules made at Athens, who feared for their lives because of his guilt; or the one Romulus made at Rome as a refuge for fugitives.
Whatever the Tagus gives with its golden sands,
or the Hermus with its glowing red bank,
or the Indus, which lies near the hot part of the world,
mixing green stones with white ones,

does not light up the sight. Whatever the Tagus, a river of Spain, gives in its golden gravel, and the Hermus, a river of Asia Minor, on its gold-coloured bank, or the Indus, which is nearest of all to the eastern sun, mixing green gems, such as the emerald, with white ones, such as pearls, none of these opens the eyes of a man's mind.
Rather, they hide blind minds in their own, that is, their accustomed, darkness. Instead, they push blind minds further into their familiar darkness.
Whatever pleases here and stirs minds,
the earth has nourished in its inmost caverns. Whatever of this pleases a man or stirs his mind, the earth breeds in its bosom.
The splendour by which heaven is ruled and has its strength
shuns the dark shadows of the mind. But the radiance of God's wisdom, which rules heaven and makes it firm, shuns the dim darkness of the mind.
Whoever is able to perceive this light
will deny that the rays of Phoebus are bright. Whoever is able to see that light will not say that the sun has bright radiance.

THAT THE ONE AND THE GOOD ARE THE SAME. I agree, I said. I affirm it, I said. For everything holds together, linked by the firmest reasons. All your arguments are certain and strengthened by firm reasoning. They are made fast with arguments and syllogisms. Then she said:
How highly will you value it if you come to know what the good itself is? "Well then," she said, "how precious does it seem to you
if you consider what the good itself is?" "Infinitely," I said. "Beyond measure precious," I said, "if it is also granted to me to know God, who is the good. If I may also come to know God by it."
who is good. Yet, she said, I will make this plain by the truest reasoning. Truly, she said, I will reveal it to you with very true argument. Only let what was concluded a little earlier stand.

Only keep in your memory the things that were established before. They will stand. They do, I said. Did we not show, she said, that the things most people seek are not true and perfect goods, because they differ from one another? Have I not shown you by argument, she said, that the goods many people desire are therefore neither true nor perfect, because they are separated? And that since each one lacked what another had, it could not bring full and absolute good? And that since each lacks another, it cannot by itself give full good, nor complete good?
But that they become the true good when they are gathered, as it were, into one form and one working, so that what is sufficiency is also power, reverence,

renown, and pleasure? And again, that they become true good when they gather together, as into one form and one working, so that what one of the five is, the others are the same? If there were five highest goods, there would also be five kinds of happiness, and there would also be five workings, because each would make a person happy by itself. Unless they are all one and the same, they have nothing by which they could be counted among the things worth seeking. And did I not show you that unless they are one, they have nothing worth desiring, because one can do nothing without the others?
It has been shown, I said. "It has been shown," I said. Nor can it be doubted in any way. There is no doubt about it at all.

PREMISE TAKEN. So then, things that are not good at all when they are at odds, but become good when they begin to be one: is it not by gaining unity that they come to be good? "Those things," she said, "that are not good while they are at odds, but become good when united: did they not become good because unity came to them?"
"So it seems," I said. "That is how it seems to me," I said.

PREMISE. But do you grant that everything that is good is good by participating in the good, or not? And everything that is good, she said, as the five are once they are no longer separate: do you grant that it is good by participating in the good, which is the One, or do you not grant it? It is so. That is so: it is good, I said.

CONCLUSION. By similar reasoning, then, you must grant that one and good are the same. By the same reasoning, she said, you must necessarily grant that one and good are not separate. If you grant two things, you must necessarily grant the third. The syllogism is made like this: what is not good becomes good from the One. So then it has become good from the good! I mean from the One. Therefore one and good are not separate. For things whose effect is not by nature different have the same substance. Things whose action is not separate must have a substance that is not separate. Goodness makes a thing good by its participation in itself, and so does the One. Therefore they have one action. I cannot deny it, I said. I can never deny that, I said.

THAT THE ONE GIVES SUBSISTENCE TO ALL THINGS. One [?]. Do you know, then, she said, that everything that exists remains and subsists as long as it is one? Do you not know, she said, that every thing lasts and endures as long as it is one? But that it perishes and is dissolved likewise
and has ceased to be one? And that it falls apart and perishes when it is not one?

"In what way?" "How so?" I said. "Is that really so?" "As," she said, "in living things: when soul and body come together into one and remain so, that is called a living creature." "As you can see," she said, "in all living things: when soul and body come together."
