Afterward they held them by the river Alpheus in Arcadia, where it runs between two cities, Elis and Pisa, because there are beautiful fields there. The festival was established so that there would be a public testing of all virtues there. For that reason the testing was called in Greek pancratium. And there was no one in all Greece who undertook any glorious deed by which he wished to win glory who did not show it there at the Olympiad. If he undertook wrestling, he was called in Greek palaestricator; if he undertook fighting with the club, he was called pugil; or with the sword, he was called gladiator; or with the caestus,

which we call [fighting] with cudgels, he was called agonitheta, that is, decertator. If he wished to compete in a contest on his chariot, that was called curule certamen. If he wished to show how he could [move] aloft, he did so by walking over the rope, which was called funambulum. If he also wished to show his swiftness, he did so by running in the stadium, as those did at the tomb of Anchises, of whom Virgil tells. Stadium was the name of the very course that they were to run, named in Greek from exercise. It was one hundred and twenty-five paces, that is, the ninth part of a mile. To all of these their reward was given there in return from the public. The reward was called in Greek brabeion, in Latin bravium.
ON THE CERTAIN PUNISHMENT OF THE WICKED. Since these things are so, no wise man can doubt the inseparable punishment of the wicked as well.

Accordingly, let no wise man doubt that the wicked too are never without punishment. For since good and evil, and likewise punishment and reward, stand opposed face to face, the things we see happen in the reward of the good
must necessarily have their counterpart on the opposite side in the punishment of the wicked.

Since good and evil, reward and punishment, are opposed to each other, it must be that what happens in the reward of the good and in the punishment of the evil is also opposed. What is that? Therefore, just as for the upright their uprightness itself becomes their reward, so for the wicked their wickedness itself is their punishment. That is what you can learn here: just as the reward of the good is their goodness, so the torment of the evil is their evil itself.
Now whoever is afflicted with punishment does not doubt that he is afflicted with an evil. I think that whoever suffers any punishment

acknowledges that what he suffers is evil. If, then, they are willing to judge themselves, can they consider themselves free of punishment, when wickedness, the worst of all evils, not only affects them, that is, afflicts them, but also deeply infects them, that is, corrupts them? Therefore, how can they suppose themselves to be without punishment, if they are willing to think about themselves, that is, if they are willing to perceive anything about themselves at all, when wickedness, the greatest of all evil, not only torments them but even corrupts them? This is an argument from effect: because they are infected, it is clear from that how severely they are afflicted.
But see, on the side opposite to the good, what punishment accompanies the wicked. Look also, from the side of the good,
what punishment there is upon the wicked. For you learned a little while ago that everything that is, is one, and that the one itself is good.

from which it follows that everything that is should also be seen to be good. I taught you this syllogism before: that everything that is [?], and that the one is good; these are two premises, and from them the conclusion necessarily follows that everything that is, is good. In this way, therefore, whatever falls away from the good ceases to be. To that conclusion, however, this one is attached: whatever is not good, is not. When one conclusion follows from another, that is called in Latin, as Martianus says, 'confinis conclusio' (adjoining conclusion), and in Greek 'symperasma'.

WHAT THOSE GIVEN OVER TO VARIOUS VICES ARE TO BE CONSIDERED. Hence it comes about that the wicked cease to be what they had been, that is, men. From this it follows that the wicked are not the men that they were when they were not wicked. But that they were men is still shown by the remaining appearance of the human body itself. But that they were men is shown by the human form itself, which is still on them.
Therefore, turned to wickedness, they have also lost their human nature. Therefore, turned to evil
they lost their human nature. But since goodness alone can raise anyone above men, it must be that those whom wickedness has cast down from the human condition

it thrusts down below what a man deserves. But since goodness alone can raise anyone above men, so that he becomes a god, it must be that those whom their wickedness throws down from manhood are at once made lower than men. It follows, then, that you cannot consider a man someone you see transformed by vices. Hence you cannot take for a man someone you see changed by vices.
He burns with avarice, a violent robber of others' wealth [? the text reads 'apum', 'bees'];
you would call him like a wolf. Sometimes he becomes greedy and a violent seizer of other people's property.
then he is like a wolf. Is he fierce and restless, exercising his tongue in quarrels? You will compare him to a dog. One who is fierce with his tongue and never stops quarrelling is like a dog.
A hidden plotter, he rejoices in having stolen by frauds!
Let him be likened to little foxes.

So it is: whoever lies in wait secretly to gain something by treachery is called a fox. Is he immoderate in anger, and does he rage? Let him be thought to carry the spirit of a lion. So it is: whoever cannot control his anger and is always raging carries the spirit of a lion.
Is he timid and quick to run, afraid of things that should not be feared?
Let him be thought like the deer. If he is needlessly fearful and quick to run, he should seem to you like a deer.
Is he lazy and dull, and sunk in sluggishness?
He lives the life of an ass. Whoever is sluggish and lazy, and shrinks from hard work, lives like an ass. Is he fickle and unsteady, always changing his interests?
He is no different from the birds. Whoever is light-minded and unsteady in what he takes up is like a bird.
Is he sunk in foul and unclean lusts?

He is held fast by the pleasure of a filthy sow. One who gives himself over to shameful and unclean lusts is like a sow that has wallowed in the mire. So it comes about that one who abandons goodness and ceases to be a man, since he cannot pass into the divine condition, is turned into a beast. So it happens that one who has given up goodness is not a man, and since he cannot attain to the dignity of God, he becomes a beast.
THAT IT IS NOT SO HARMFUL FOR THE BODY TO BE TURNED INTO A BEAST AS TO BE CLOTHED WITH A BEAST'S MIND. The sails of the Neritian leader, that is, Ulysses, whose homeland was the island of Neritus,
and his ships wandering on the sea
the east wind drove to the island
where the beautiful goddess dwelling there,
born of the seed of the Sun,
mixes for her new guests, that is, those who have just arrived,

cups touched with a spell. I can remind you of a great horror, which is still not equal to this horror. What is it? When Ulysses was returning from Troy, he wandered far over the sea, and he traveled from Sicily toward Italy. Then the wind drove him out with his ships to the island that is called Aeaea. There the beautiful Circe, daughter of the Sun, who dwelt there, poured bewitched drink for these same guests.
When the hand powerful in herbs turned them into various shapes,
the face of a boar covers this one;
that one, a Marmaric lion, that is, from the province of Africa, Marmarica,
grows teeth and claws;
this one, newly added to the wolves,
howls when he means to weep;
that one, like an Indian tiger, walks tamely around the house.

So when the magic hand changed them into various forms, one was like a boar, one like the lion; and one who had also become a wolf stood and howled when he wanted to weep. And one also went around the house, made like a tiger.
But although the divinity of the winged Arcadian,
pitying the leader beset by various ills,
freed him from the plague of his hostess,
yet the oarsmen had already drunk the evil cups.

And yet Mercury, flying like a bird, who was raised on Mount Cyllene in Arcadia, out of pity freed the distressed leader from the poison of his hostess; yet the companions had already drunk the evil drink. Mercury is painted 'alatis talariis', that is, with feathered shoes, which the Greeks call 'petasi'. He warned Ulysses to avoid Circe. But when it happened that he came there against his will, and she poured drink for the others, which he would not drink, then Mercury gave him a remedy for it
with his staff,
which was called the caduceus, and which was healing against all things. 'Already the swine had exchanged the food of Ceres for acorns.' And having become swine, they exchanged bread for acorns.
And nothing remains whole,
voice and body being lost. And they were completely lost, in limbs and in voice.
Only the mind, unchanged, groans
over the monstrous things it suffers.
Only the mind stood firm, grieving over the horror that had happened to it. O hand far too weak,
nor the power of herbs,
which, though they can change the limbs,
cannot change the hearts. Indeed, how weighty that was! What could the herbs and the poisoning hand achieve, which harmed the limbs but could not harm the mind?
Within lies the strength of men,
hidden away in a secret citadel. The power lies within. There the strengths of man are deeply hidden.
These poisons, that is, vices,
drag a man away from himself more powerfully. The poisons I speak of make a man less master of himself.
Which pass dreadfully deep within,
and do not harm the body,
but rage with a wound to the mind. These strike deeper in. They do not harm the limbs, but attack the mind.

THAT THE WICKED WOULD BE LESS WRETCHED IF THEY WERE NOT PERMITTED TO SIN. Then I said: "I admit it, and I see that it is not wrong to say that the vicious, though they keep the outward form of the body, are still changed into beasts by the nature of their minds." "I grant you that," I said then, "and I know that I rightly call the wicked beasts, since they have beastly minds, although in their bodies they are like men."
"But those whose savage and wicked mind rages for the destruction of the good: I would not have wished that very thing to be permitted to them."

But that those whose minds are so perverse and so evil should be allowed to persecute the good, that is what I would not wish. "Nor are they allowed," she said. "No," she said, "they are not allowed." "As will be shown in the proper place." You will learn this well when I bring you to that point.

"But if the very thing they are believed to be allowed to do were taken away, the punishment of wicked men would be lightened in great part." But if the very thing you think they are allowed to do were taken from them, their punishment would be lightened by it.

PROPOSITION. For, though it may perhaps seem unbelievable to someone, the wicked are necessarily more unhappy when they have accomplished what they desired than if they could not fulfill what they desire.
Truly, though many do not believe it can happen, the wicked are the more unhappy for doing their will than if they could not do it.

ASSUMPTION. For if it is wretched to have willed wicked things, it is more wretched to have been able to do them. If willing evil is wretched, being able to do evil is more wretched still. Without this ability, the effect of a wretched will would languish. For an evil will could not show itself without it.
CONCLUSION. Therefore, since each has its own misery,
those whom you see willing a crime must be oppressed by a threefold misfortune:

to be able, to accomplish. Therefore they are necessarily unhappy in three ways, since there are three miseries: I mean willing, being able, and doing what is evil. That is a rhetorical syllogism, because it is more diffuse. A dialectical one is more contracted, because it scarcely has [anything beyond] the subject part and the declarative part in each proposition. 'I grant it,' I said. 'I grant you that,' said I.

THAT THE WICKED WOULD BE MOST UNHAPPY EVEN IF THEY NEVER DIED. "But I earnestly wish that they may soon be free of this misfortune, deprived of the power to commit crime. May God grant that they lose the power to do evil and so be rid of that unhappiness very soon."
"They will be free of it," she said, "sooner than you perhaps wish, or than they think they will be free of it.

"That is what happens," she said. They lose it even sooner than you might wish it to happen, or than they themselves expect. "For nothing within such short limits (that is, spans) of life is so late that an immortal mind especially (that is, a wise one) would think it long to wait for." Even within the span of this short life, nothing is so slow that any eternal mind would think it too long to wait for. The wise man, who knows eternity, counts temporal things as nothing.
"Their great hope

and lofty machinery of crimes is often destroyed by a sudden and unexpected end." Their powerful hope, and the lofty scaffolding they built for evil, is often struck down suddenly and unexpectedly by death. "And this indeed sets a limit to their misery." Yet this sets a limit to their misery.

"For if wickedness makes men wretched, then whoever is wicked for longer must be more wretched." For if evil makes men wretched, then the longer someone is evil, the more wretched he must be. That is an argument from the lesser to the greater. Since even wickedness that is only beginning makes men wretched, wickedness that is growing does so all the more, I say.
I would judge them the most unhappy of all, if at least death in the end did not finish their malice.

I would call them the most wretched of all if death did not at least put an end to their evil. That again is an argument from the lesser. Since someone who has been wicked for a long time is more unhappy than someone who is only beginning to be wicked, someone who was wicked forever would be the most unhappy of all. That is why she then says: "For if we have reached a true conclusion about the misfortune of depravity, it is clear that misery known to be eternal is infinite." If what I said earlier is true, that if wickedness makes men wretched, then whoever is wicked for longer must be more wretched, then it is certain that the misery that is eternal is infinite, and therefore the most unhappy. If long-lasting depravity is more wretched than brief depravity, then everlasting depravity must be both everlasting and infinite.

and most unhappy. She confirms this statement so carefully because she worries that he might doubt it. Who can easily believe that the wicked, always living and always unpunished, can be most unhappy and most wretched from sheer injustice? Therefore hear his answer. Then I said: I answered her. "Wonderful indeed," I said, "and a conclusion hard to grant." That is a wondrous conclusion, I said, and hard to believe. "But I recognize that it agrees all too well with what was granted earlier." But I do see clearly that it agrees with the earlier admissions.
"You judge rightly," she said.

It seems right to you, she said. "But whoever thinks it hard to accept the conclusion, it is fair that he demonstrate either that something false came before, or show that the arrangement of the propositions does not produce a necessary conclusion." But whoever is unwilling to believe this conclusion, let him point out the falsehood that stands before it, with which I supported it, or let him say that those same statements, though they may also be true, are not arranged so that they produce this conclusion. "Otherwise, once the preceding points are granted, there is nothing at all to object to in the inference." Otherwise, if he simply admits the preceding argument, he cannot deny the conclusion. She says this because the preceding statement is often false, as this one is:

"No wise man despises riches," and so it does not support the conclusion, which is: "Therefore Socrates, because he despised riches, was not wise." Often the two preceding statements are true, as these are: "Every wise man despises riches. Yet many wise men are rich." But they are not arranged so that they support this third: "Socrates, if he were wise, would be rich." Everything that can make syllogisms and arguments go wrong lies in these two faults, and therefore the arguments in which they are found are called sophistical. Whoever wants fuller examples of these deceptive syllogisms, let him take them from Cicero in the Rhetorics.
THAT THE WICKED WHO ARE HANDED OVER TO JUST PUNISHMENTS AT DEATH ARE HAPPIER THAN IF THEY REMAINED UNPUNISHED.

For this too, which I shall say, seems no less marvelous, but from the things that have been assumed, that is, granted, it is equally necessary. 'What I shall tell you next,' she said, 'will seem to you just as great a wonder, and yet it follows necessarily from what was admitted earlier.' 'What is that?' I said. 'Which?' said I.
"That the wicked are happier," she said, "when they pay penalties than if no penalty of justice restrained them." The wicked who suffer just punishment are happier
than they would be if they did not suffer it.
"Nor am I now attempting what might occur to anyone, that depraved morals are corrected by punishment and brought back to the right path by fear of penalty.

I am not saying that evil habits are punished and corrected by penalty, as someone might suppose. He need not suppose it, for that is not what I mean. "Nor that it serves as an example to others to avoid blameworthy things," that is, an example to others, so that they avoid guilt and do not do the same. "But I hold that the wicked are happier when punished in some other way, even if no account is taken of correction and no regard is given to example." Rather, I consider it in another way: that the wicked are the happier for paying for their sins, even though it is neither a correction for them nor an example to others.
"And what other way will there be," I said, "besides these?"
"What other way can there be," I said, "besides these?" And she said: "Have we not granted that the good are happy

but the wicked are wretched?" "Did we not agree," she said, "that the good are happy and the wicked wretched?" "So it is," I said. "That is so," I said. "If then," she said, "some good is added to someone's wretchedness,

is he not happier than the one whose misery is pure and unmixed, without the admixture of any good?" If, then, good is added to the wretchedness of either of them, is that one not happier than the one whose wretchedness has no good mixed into it? "So it seems," I said. It seems so to me, I said. "What if another evil is added to that same wretched man who lacks all goods,
besides those through which he is wretched? Must he not be judged much unhappier than the one whose misfortune is relieved by a share in some good?"

And if some other wretchedness were added to the wretched man who lacks every good, besides the wretchedness that already makes him wretched, would he then not be much more unhappy than the man whose wretchedness is lightened by a mixture of some good? This is an argument from the contrary. For if anyone is made happy by an added good, then he is necessarily also made unhappy by an added evil. "Why not?" I said. "How could it be otherwise?" I said.
"So when the wicked are punished, they do have something good attached to them, namely the punishment itself,

which is good by reason of justice." So she said: when the wicked are being punished, they have some good mixed in with them. I mean the punishment itself, which is good because it is just. "And when the same people escape punishment, there is something more of evil in them: the impunity itself, which you have admitted is evil because of its injustice." And while they are without punishment, they have in them, besides their wickedness, another evil: the impunity itself, which is evil because it is unjust.
I cannot deny it.
"I cannot deny that," I said. "The wicked, therefore, are much more unhappy when they are granted unjust impunity than when they are punished with just retribution."

"Therefore," she said, "the wicked are more unhappy when they are let off with unjust impunity than when they are justly punished. But it is clear that it is just for the wicked to be punished and unjust for them to escape unpunished. So it is plainly right that the wicked pay for their wickedness, and plainly wrong that they go unpunished for it." "Who would deny that?" I said. "Who can deny that?"
"But no one," she said, "will deny this either: that everything that is just is good,

and, on the contrary, that what is unjust is evil." "No one will deny this either," she said, "that what is just is good and what is unjust is evil." Then I answered her: "These things follow from what was concluded a little earlier. These things," I said, "follow necessarily from what was established in the earlier chapter." This chapter agrees with that one. For if the wicked would be most unhappy, as she said earlier, if they always had to remain unpunished, then they necessarily become happier when they are punished.

QUESTION. "But I ask you," I said, "do you allow (that is, grant) no punishments of souls after the body has been ended by death?" "Now, God protect [us] [?]," I said, "is there any punishment of souls after death?"

ANSWER. "Yes, great ones," she said. "Mighty ones," she said. "I think some of them are carried out with penal severity, and others with purifying mercy. I know that some of them come as vengeance, leading to damnation, and others as mercy, leading to purification.
But it is not my plan to discuss these now. I have no wish to speak about that now.

A RECAPITULATION OF WHAT HAS BEEN SAID FROM THE BEGINNING OF THIS BOOK UP TO HERE. Up to now we have argued this, so that you would recognize that the power of the wicked, which seemed to you most unworthy, is nothing. I pursued this up to here, she said, so that you would recognize that the power of the wicked, which grieved you so much, is nothing. And those whom you complained of as unpunished,

you would see that they never lack the punishments for their wickedness. And you saw that the people you said went unpunished for their wickedness are never without punishment. You would learn that the license you prayed might quickly end does not last long either.

And you learned that the license you prayed might soon come to an end [?] is not long. You learned that it would be more unhappy if it lasted longer, and most unhappy if it were eternal. And you knew it would be the more unhappy if it lasted long, and unhappy beyond all things if it were eternal. After this, you learned that the wicked are more wretched when they are let go with unjust impunity than when they are punished with just retribution. Those who go unpunished for their wickedness are more wretched than those who are punished.

From this conclusion it follows that they are pressed by heavier punishments precisely when they are believed to go unpunished. From this it necessarily follows that they suffer the sharpest punishments when people think them unpunished for what they do. Then I said: Then I answered her.
"When I consider your reasoning," I said, "I think that nothing truer could be said.

But if I turn back to the judgments of men, who is there who would find these things not only believable but even worth hearing? When I examine your argument," I said, "I consider nothing truer. But if I think about people's opinion, who is there who would believe it, or even be willing to hear it?"

THE LIGHT OF REASON DOES NOT SHINE FOR DARKENED MINDS. It is so, she said. It is so, she said. For they cannot lift eyes accustomed to darkness to the light of clear truth. They cannot lift their eyes, accustomed to the darkness, up to the light. And they are like birds whose sight the night lights up and the day blinds. And they are like the birds that the day blinds and the night makes able to see, such as eagle-owls, screech-owls, and the night-raven. For since they look not at the order of things but at their own desires, they think that licence
or impunity for crimes is happy.

Since they look to their own will, and not to the order that reason gives to things, they think that the license to sin and impunity are blessed. But see what the eternal, that is, divine, law ordains. Look and see how God's law means it.
If you have shaped your mind to better things, there is no need for a judge to give the reward.
You yourself have joined yourself to the more excellent. If you have turned your efforts toward worse things, do not look outside yourself for an avenger.

You yourself have thrust yourself into worse things. By taking up the better, you have honored yourself; there need be no examiner to thank you for it. But if you turn yourself to evil, do not think about who else should avenge it: you yourself have harmed yourself. Just as if you were to look in turn at the filthy ground and at the sky,

with nothing else outside acting, by the very act of looking you would seem to be now in the mud, now among the stars. It is just as if you looked in turn up to heaven and down to the earth, and with no one else's doing, simply by your own looking, you were for one while in heaven and for another while in the mire.
But the common people do not consider these things. But the people know nothing of this. What then? What shall we do, then?
Shall we side with these, whom we have shown to be like beasts?

Shall we, because of that, attach ourselves to those whom we said were like animals? What if someone, having entirely lost his sight, should even forget that he had ever had the power of seeing, and should think that nothing was lacking to him for human perfection?

Would we, seeing the same things, i.e. the loss of his eyes, think we were blind? What if he whose eyes have been taken away forgot that he once had them, and maintained that he was whole in every way? Should we then, who saw him eyeless, be counted blind?
HE WHO INFLICTS INJURY IS MORE WRETCHED THAN HE WHO SUFFERS IT. For they will not even agree to this, which rests equally on strong foundations

[?] of reasons, that those who do injury are more unhappy than those who suffer it. Nor do they admit this, which firm reasoning shows to be just as certain: that the one who does wrong to another is more wretched than the one who suffers it.
"I would like," I said, "to hear these very reasons."

"I would like," I said, "to hear the reasoning by which I might know that." "Do you deny," she said, "that every wicked person deserves punishment?" "Will you deny," she said, "that the wicked man deserves punishment?" "Not at all." "No," I said. "Moreover, it is clear in many ways that those who are wicked

are unhappy." "Now it is clear in many ways," she said, "that those who are evil are unhappy." "So it is," I said. "So it is," I said. "Then you do not doubt that those who deserve punishment are wretched." "You know," she said, "that those who deserve punishment are wretched."
"Agreed," I said.

"That is fitting," I said. "If, then," she said, "you sat as judge, on whom would you think punishment should be inflicted: on the one who had done the injury, or on the one who had suffered it?" "If you were a judge sitting in court," she said, "which would you think deserved the punishment: the one who did the wrong, or the one who endured it?"

"Nor do I doubt," I said, "that I would make amends to the one who suffered through the pain of the one who did it." "I would not doubt at all," I said, "that I should give satisfaction to the one who suffered it through the other's punishment."
"Then the one who inflicts injury would seem to you more wretched

than the one who receives it." "Then," she said, "the one who did wrong would seem to you more wretched than the one who endured it." "It follows," I said. "It comes to that," I said. "Hence, then, it is clear from other reasons resting on the same root, the principle that wickedness by its own nature makes people wretched,

that an injury done to anyone is the misery not of the one who receives it but of the one who inflicts it." "So," I said again, "from this reasoning, and from other reasons rooted in the same principle, that shameful deeds make people wretched in themselves, it also becomes clear, as you say, that wretchedness belongs to the one who does the wrong, not to the one who suffers it." This is an argument from the efficient cause. Wickedness is the efficient cause of the wretched, just as, on the other hand, honestas, that is, virtue, is the efficient cause of the blessed. Wickedness is the common name of all vices, just as honestas is the common name of all virtues.
WHO IS MORE WRETCHED.
RATHER OF THIS ONE. "And yet now," she said, "the orators do the opposite."

The opposite: IS TO BE PITIED. "The advocates now do the opposite," she said. "For they try to arouse the judges' pity for those who have suffered something grievous and bitter. They are always urging the judges to have pity on those to whom great harm has been done, when a juster pity is owed rather to those who commit the wrong. Pity would be more needed by those who do it."
These people ought to be brought to judgment like the sick to a physician, not by angry accusers but rather by kindly and compassionate ones,

so that they might cut away the diseases of guilt by punishment. Their accusers ought to bring them to court the way one brings the sick to a physician: not out of hatred, but out of mercy and compassion, so that they might do them good there by cutting out the gall of their sins. That is an argument from likeness (argumentum a simili). For just as the body needs medicine, so also does the soul. In this way the whole work of defenders would grow cold. Or, if they preferred to help people, it would be turned into the form, that is, the manner, of accusation. In that case the efforts of the advocates would be given up. Or, if they wished to help anyone, they would do it by accusing him instead of defending him.

The wicked themselves too, if they were allowed to glimpse through some small crack the virtue they had abandoned, and saw that they would put off the filth of their vices through the torments of punishment,

in exchange for the goodness they would gain, would not count these torments as torments. If the wicked themselves could look out at all at the virtue they have cast away, even as if through a crack, and saw that they would be washed clean of their sins by the severity of the punishment, in return for gaining goodness, would they then count it as punishment? They would also reject the work of their defenders and give themselves over entirely to their accusers and judges.

They would not ask for the help of advocates. Instead they would give themselves over to their accusers and also to the judges, so that these might chastise them. So it comes about that among the wise no place at all is left for hatred. If they act in this way, there is no path that could lead the wise to hatred. For who but the greatest fool would hate the good? And to hate the wicked makes no sense. As you can see from these arguments: Who would hate the good, except the worst of creatures? That is an argument from contraries (argumentum a contrariis), for the foolish and malicious are the opposite of the good. And that anyone should hate the wicked, what sense is there in that? That is an argument from incompatibles (a repugnantibus), for unjust hatred is incompatible with reason.
For if viciousness is a kind of disease of souls, just as sickness is of bodies, and since we judge that those who are sick in body by no means deserve hatred,

but rather with pity; much more are they not to be pursued (that is, with death) but to be pitied, whose minds are oppressed by wickedness, which is more savage than any sickness. If lack of virtue is a sickness of the mind, just as corruption of the body is the body's sickness, and those who are sick in their bodies do not seem to us to deserve hatred but pity, then those whose minds are stifled by wickedness, the most grievous of all diseases, are not to be persecuted; rather, pity is to be had on them.
WHY WOULD ANYONE KILL THOSE WHO ARE GOING TO DIE OF THEIR OWN ACCORD? What good is it to stir up such great commotions and to provoke
fate with your own hand? Why do you desire to show such great wrath, and to bring on death with your hand?
If you seek death, it draws near of its own accord!
nor does it hold back its swift horses.
If you desire it, it comes uninvited, of its own will, and it does not delay its journey. Those whom the serpent, the lion, the tiger, the bear, the boar
attack with their teeth, these same people nevertheless attack themselves with the sword. Those whom all the animals pursue slay themselves needlessly on top of that with weapons.
Or is it because their ways differ and disagree
that they set unjust battle lines and savage wars in motion,
and wish to perish by each other's weapons?

That is not a just enough reason for cruelty. Because their customs differ and do not agree, do they draw up troops against each other over that, and fight over that? That is no just reason at all for such severity!
Do you wish to give deserts a fitting return?
Love the good, as is right, and have pity on the bad. Do you wish to reward each person according to his deserts? Then do this: love the good, as is right, and have mercy on the wicked.
WHY THINGS ARE MIXED AS IF BY CHANCE EVENTS, SO THAT EVIL BEFALLS THE GOOD AND GOOD BEFALLS THE WICKED. At this I said: Then I said: I see what happiness is
or misery [heading continues: BEFALL] is established in the very deserts of the upright and of the wicked,
but I judge that there is some good or evil in this common fortune itself.

"I see well what happiness or what misery lies in the merits of both kinds, the good and the wicked. Yet I still find that there is good and evil in this very fortune of the people as well. For none of the wise would rather be an exile, poor and disgraced, than be strong in wealth, revered for honour,
mighty in power, and flourish while remaining in his own city.

That is clear from the choice of the wise: none of them would as gladly be an exile [?], and poor, and despised [?], as be at home, rich, honoured, powerful and in every comfort. In this way the office of wisdom is carried out more clearly and with better witness, when the happiness of the rulers is in some way poured out over the peoples near them. So they carry out the office of their wisdom more visibly and with better testimony if their happiness, while they rule the people, becomes known even among outsiders.
Especially since prison, law,
and the other torments of legal penalties ought rather to fall on harmful citizens, since it was for them that these were established.
So why are these turned the other way round, so that punishments for crimes weigh down the good and the wicked seize the rewards of virtue?

I wonder at it greatly. And since [?] prison, the law-book and all the punishments laid down by law ought to fall on the harmful, for whose sake they were established, why is there such a reversal, so that suffering weighs on the good instead of the wicked, and the wicked snatch away the honour of the good? At this I wonder greatly. And I want to learn from you what reason there seems to be for so unjust a confusion. And I would gladly learn from you what reason there is for such an unjust mixing-up. For I would wonder less
if I believed that all things were thrown together by chance events. I would not wonder at it at all if I believed that all things wavered in uncertain happenings.
Now God the ruler heaps up my astonishment.

But God is the ruler, and he makes my astonishment great. Since he often gives pleasant things to the good and harsh things to the wicked, and on the other hand gives hard things to the good and grants the wicked what they wish,

then unless the cause is found, what is there that seems to set this apart [?] from chance events? Since he is such that he often gives delight to the good and hardship to the wicked, and then on the contrary hardship to the good and pleasure to the wicked, I can find no reason for it. How then can it seem to me to differ from fickle chance events?" "It is no wonder," she said,
"if something is believed to be random and confused when the reason for its order is unknown."

"It is no wonder," she said, "if people think something is disordered and confused when they have not learned the reason for its order. But although you do not know the cause of so great an arrangement, do not doubt that all things are done rightly, since a good ruler governs the world. But although you do not know the purpose of so mighty a governance, the one who governs the world is a good ruler. So do not doubt it, but trust that everything is rightly ordered. For it must be that the righteous one acts righteously." These two terms are paired, so this is called an argument from paired terms (argumentum a coniugatis).
THINGS WHOSE REASON IS NOT KNOWN RIGHTLY SEEM WONDROUS.
If anyone does not know that the stars of Arcturus, that is, the star called Arcturus,
glide near the highest pole. And if anyone does not know
why slow Boötes gathers, that is, follows, the Wagon, that is, slow to set,
and plunges his late flames into the sea,
while he unfolds his risings all too swiftly,
he will be astonished at the law of the high heaven.

Whoever does not know [what] stands here near the north pole of heaven, and why the constellation of Bootes, in which Arcturus stands, slowly follows the Wagon, goes slowly to its setting, and yet rises quickly, must necessarily wonder how this comes about up above us in heaven. Because the north pole is above the earth, just as the south pole is below the earth, the signs that hover nearest to it do not set, as the Arcti do, which people call the Wagon. Those that stand somewhat farther off, as Bootes does, set for a while, so that they make a short journey under the earth compared with the one they make above the earth. Whoever does not know this may well wonder at it. Duae arcti, that is, duae ursae (the two Bears).

...Helix and Cynosura. Helix is the name of the greater one [the Great Bear]. On it one sees seven bright stars, which are called Septentrio. Boötes follows it, because he goes behind it, and wherever it turns its hind parts, there one sees Boötes. Why the horns of the full moon grow pale, tinged (that is, darkened) by the limits of the dark night (that is, by its nightly courses), and why Phoebe, confounded (that is, obscured), uncovers the stars (that is, by failing)
which she had covered with her shining face.

It may also be a wonder to them why the full moon, when an eclipse of the moon happens in the middle of the night, suddenly grows altogether dark and lets the lesser stars shine, which it covered before, as long as it had to shine brightly. It is plain that the moon has no light of its own, and that the sun makes it bright by shining on it, and that it is always moving either away from the sun or toward the sun. Therefore it happens that when, at full moon, it goes so far that it stands directly opposite the sun on the other side of the heaven, and the earth is between them, its light fails it in that place, until it moves further on, to where the sun can shine on it. That failing is called an eclipse of the moon.
The public error (that is, the common error) stirs up the peoples. Then the people are alarmed at something about which they are all in error. They wonder what it means.
And they weary the air with frequent beatings (that is, with people asking). And then they keep asking about it, until the heaven itself may grow weary of their asking.
No one marvels at the blasts of Corus [the northwest wind]
beating the shore with roaring wave. But on the other hand no one marvels at it when the wind blows and the wave strikes the shore.
Nor that the mass of snow, hard with cold,
is loosened by the burning heat of Phoebus. Nor that the ice melts from the heat of the sun. Why is that?
For here it is easy to discern the causes. Because these causes are easy to understand.
There hidden ones (that is, causes) trouble hearts. But those causes are hard to understand, because they hide themselves.
Everything that a rare age brings forth. Everything that happens rarely.
And the fickle crowd is astonished at sudden things. And at which the common people are alarmed when it happens suddenly. Let it yield to ignorance
that is, if the clouded error of ignorance should yield. If they are instructed about it,
"Then surely they cease to seem marvellous." Then there is at once an end to wondering. "So it is," I said. "It is so," said I.

REQUEST, AND HOW DIFFICULT THE THINGS ASKED FOR ARE TO SUPPLY. But since it is your office to unfold the causes of hidden things and to explain reasons veiled in darkness, I ask that you determine and explain from this, since this marvel disturbs me most of all. But since it is yours alone to tell what all things each mean, and to explain hidden reasoning, why that is which I asked about, because so heavy a wonder grips me, I pray that you tell me and set me right about it. Then she, smiling a little, said: 'You call me to the greatest of all matters to inquire into, for which scarcely anything, even when exhausted, is enough.' She then, laughing a little at me,

Then she said: "You are pointing me to the greatest of all questions, one that can never be answered fully." For the matter is such that when one doubt is cut away, countless others grow up like the heads of the Hydra. It has to be answered in this way, and the matter is of such a kind that when one doubt is removed, many come in its place. That is what happened to Hercules when he had to kill the serpent that is called hydra in Greek and excedra [?] in Latin. When he struck off one of its heads, three grew in its place, and from those that were struck off, many more grew. Nor would there be any limit, unless someone holds them in check with the liveliest fire of the mind. Nor will there be any limit to them unless they are subdued with the lively fire of the mind. That is what Hercules did to the Lernaean marsh, from which this fable arose. Because he could not cover it over and stop it up, and it kept breaking out again, he attacked it with fire.

With that he destroyed [?] it. For in this matter, people usually ask about the simplicity of providence. Here we must ask about God's simple providence. It is simple and single, and unlike human providence, because it sees everything together and at a single glance. A human being sees only some things, and sees even those things at separate times, as she teaches later in the fifth book. Therefore human providence is what we call forethought and precaution. But God's providence is the all-at-once overview, which is not divided by times and places, and by which present things are grasped all together.

the past and the future, the higher and the lower, are all grasped together. But because his providentia is sometimes used in place of praescientia, it is also rendered as foreknowledge or foresight. This is not its proper sense. It follows the pattern of human foresight and foreknowing. With God, all of it is a looking-upon and an overseeing. "About the chain of fate": about the onward sequence of God's will. "About sudden chance events": about sudden happenings. "About divine knowledge and predestination": about God's knowing and appointing. "About freedom of choice": about self-choice. Here it should be understood that, for convenience, we translate liberum arbitrium as "selbwala" (self-choice),

as if it meant liberam electionem (free choice). But Boethius teaches us in the third book of the second edition of his commentary on the Peri Hermeneias that we should say liberum arbitrium with the word voluntatis understood, that is, liberum voluntatis arbitrium (free choice of the will). God has made us arbiters and judges of our own wills, whether they are good or evil. That is why it says liberum voluntatis arbitrium, the self-governing choosing of the will. But if we say that liberum arbitrium means libera voluntas (free will), we aim at the same thing, and we then have three words captured in two. We ought to render those two as "willewaltigi" (power over one's own will), except that in our language this word has the meaning that liberalitas has among the Latins. So Terence says: "serviebas liberaliter" (you served as a free man would). We put it this way: "You served willingly." "How heavy these matters are, you weigh for yourself." How heavy that is, you know.
"But since to know these things too
is a certain part of your medicine, although within a narrow limit,

that is, within the path of the time allotted [?], we will nevertheless try to settle, that is, to define, something." "But because this too serves your healing, if you can grasp it, I will still undertake to speak of it, though there is too little time before the end of this book." "But if the delights of music, that is, of metrical song, please you, you must put off this pleasure for a little while, until I weave together in order arguments that are linked to one another." "If you long for verse, wait for it for a while, until I weave together for you, in order, the arguments that hold together."
"As you please," I said.
"As you wish," said I. Then she spoke as follows, as if starting from another beginning. She then spoke thus, as though starting out on another path.

ON PROVIDENCE AND FATE. It receives its forms, that is, what kind of thing it is, from the stability of the divine mind. The coming-into-being of all things, that is, of living things, and every advance of changeable natures, that is, the way the seasons are,

and whatever is moved in any way, such as the sun and the moon, [receives] its causes, that is, why it is, and its order, that is, how it is. The birth of all things, the course of all changeable things, and everything that moves in any way all receive from the stability of God's wisdom why they are, how they are, and what kind they are. This, that is, this stability,

established (that is, placed) in the citadel (that is, the dignity) of its simplicity, sets up a manifold way of ruling things. It sits in its majesty, simple in itself, and directs other things in manifold ways.
When this way is beheld in the very purity of the divine intelligence, it is called providence;

"But when it is considered in relation to the things that it moves and arranges, the ancients called it fate." This same way of ruling has two names. One applies when we think of it in God's own pure wisdom; then it is called providence. The other applies when we look at the things that it drives and orders; then it is called fate in the old writings. In the same way, our own work has two modes: in one it is in the mind, all at once, arranging; in the other it is done piece by piece with the hands, bringing about.
"That these are different will easily become clear if one considers the power of each in the mind." Whoever considers them both easily sees that they are distinct.

"For providence is that divine reason itself, established in the highest ruler of all things, which arranges all things." For providence is the very reason that resides in God, which establishes each thing.
Fate, however, is an ordering that inheres in movable things,
through which providence binds each thing into its own orders.

So fate is the very ordering that clings to all changeable things, by which providence compels each thing into its order. For providence embraces all things alike, however diverse, however infinite. Providence grasps things together, however various they may be, and however endless their number. But fate sets individual things in motion, distributed by places, forms and times. Fate directs them one by one in their course, divided here and there.

[?] in such and such ways, at those times, and in those [?]. So that this unfolding of the temporal order, united in the foresight of the divine mind, is providence; but the same unity, distributed and unfolded in time, is called fate. In this way: the ordering that follows the order of time, uniting itself in the foresight of God's mind, is called providentia; and when it is unfolded instead at separate times [?]

it is called fatum. Although these are different, one still depends on the other. For the order of fate proceeds from the simplicity of providence. Although the two are not one, still the one hangs on the other, because fate comes from providence.
For just as a craftsman, grasping in his mind the form of the thing to be made, sets the work in motion, and what he had foreseen simply and as present to him,

he carries out through the orders of time, so God's providence disposes, singly and stably, the things that are to be done, but through fate it administers these very things it has disposed in many ways and in time. Just as the carpenter first shapes in his mind what he means to do, and afterwards works it; and what he conceived in the unified presence of his mind, he carries out piece by piece: so it happens that God's providence, in steadfast oneness, determines what is to be done, and afterwards he accomplishes it through fate in manifold ways and in due order. Whether, then, fate is carried out
by certain divine spirits serving providence, or by the soul, or by the whole of nature serving it, or by the heavenly motions of the stars, or by the power of angels,

Whether the chain of fate is woven by the varied skill of demons, or by some of these, or by all of them, this at least is clear: providence is the unmoving and simple form of the things to be done, while fate is the moving connection and the temporal order of those things that the divine simplicity has arranged to be done. By whichever of these fate is brought about,

by God's own sevenfold Spirit serving providence, or by the soul serving it, or by both soul and body, or by the sun and moon, or by angels, or by the devil's cunning, or by some of these serving, or even by all of them serving, and the course of fate is guided by them, this much is always certain: that providence is the still and single shaping of the things that are to happen, but fate is the moving bond and temporal ordering of those things that God's simplicity shaped to be done.
SPIRITUAL CREATURES ARE SUBJECT TO PROVIDENCE, BODILY CREATURES TO FATE. From this it follows that all things that are under fate are also subject to providence, to which fate itself is also subject.

But some things which are placed under providence surpass the chain of fate. For this reason it is so arranged that the things subject to fate are subject to providence, to which fate itself is also subject. And yet some things subject to providence rise above fate. These are the things which, firmly fixed close to the first divinity, go beyond the order of fate's changeableness. Those are the things which, set firm together with God, do not suffer the orders of running fate, because they are near to him. Those things are subject to providence which are steadfast in their nature, but those things are subject to fate which are driven by it. So fate too is subject to providence, because providence comes first, in God's will, and fate follows that will and carries it out.

For just as, of the circles turning around the same pivot, the one that is innermost comes close to the simplicity of the centre (Suspension of the voice.) Just as, of the many rings that turn on the wheel around one axle-pin, the one that is innermost of all is nearest to the pin. and is, for the others placed outside it, a kind of pivot around which they turn. (And here.) And it too, for the others running outside around it, because of its nearness to the pin,
is itself like a pin. But the outermost, turned with a wider circuit, is spread out over wider spaces the further it moves away from the indivisible centre point.

And here: the outermost circle, which has the larger circuit, spreads itself wider the farther it is from the narrowness of the point there in the middle. But whatever joins and attaches itself to that middle is drawn together into simplicity and stops spreading and flowing outward. And here: what holds to the middle draws itself together, unspread and undispersed. In the same way, whatever moves farther from the first mind is entangled in greater bonds of fate, and a thing is free from fate to the extent that it comes nearer to that hinge of things. Depositio [?]. In the same way, it is wound about with more bonds.

…of fate, whatever is moved farther from the foregoing will, that is, God's providence. And each thing is so much the more unbound from fate the nearer it is moved to the innermost hinge. If you ask what the fetters, bonds and knots are: they are the causes of all things, which hold fast to themselves the very things whose causes they are. This is how it goes when God's anger comes about because of sins, and from that comes bad weather, and from bad weather diseases, and from diseases death. Each of these holds on to the next. "But if it clings to the firmness of the supreme mind, lacking motion, it also rises above the necessity of fate." If it also holds closely to the firmness of God's providence, then it is freed from change, and so it is without the necessity of fate.

The things that undergo change are earthly things. But what changes do heavenly things undergo? Heavenly messengers do travel from place to place, but they do so in a way that is not bound to place, because they have no front and back, right and left, above and below, as bodily things have. Inwardly they are always unchanged from God's presence. But those who are so close to God that they do not change their place or carry out messenger service, as the scriptures say of the cherubim and seraphim, what changes can we say that they undergo? "Therefore, as reasoning is to understanding, as what comes into being is to what is, as time is to eternity, as the circle is to its centre point, so the moving series of fate is

to the stable simplicity of providence." Fate stands in the same relation to providence as reasoning does to understanding. When we infer one thing from others, as Aristotle taught, that is reasoning. Human wisdom has discovered these methods. They are made useless when people's eyes are opened to heavenly things and their minds are drawn up to know what no philosophical reasoning knows. That is where understanding lies. For example, we know that God is above all, and that he is in the world in such a way that he contains it, not it him. He is in it in such a way that he is encompassed in it [?]. Human reason does not know how this can be; divine understanding teaches it. We will come to this question again in the fifth book. Fate is also to providence as what comes into being is to what is.

What comes into being also passes away and changes for as long as it lasts. Or, if it is not to pass away, it is still changeable until God makes it unchangeable, as he did with the good angels at the fall of the evil ones. But God, who is, cannot pass away and cannot change. Fate is also to providence as time is to eternity. Time runs through three tenses: present, past and future. Eternity always stands fixed in the present. And fate is to providence as the circle is to the point that stands in its middle. The circle has its course around, and its measure and its breadth. The point has no size, and therefore it is without measure
and without parts. It is an indivisible thing.

HOW MUCH FATE CAN DO. This chain moves the heavens and the stars. This course of fate drives the heavens around, together with the stars. The ancients, as Servius says, called fate 'the voice of Jove', as though he had decreed by his speech what must happen to each person. For this reason many interpret fatum as 'destiny'. But when God's will is to be carried out in certain events, and his inner ordering is to be revealed in his outer ordering: the outer ordering, as was said before, is called fate, just as the inner one is called providence. The sequence that is in it

and the order from beginning to end is called series, from serere ('to sow'), after the sowing of the farmer, who sows along the length of the furrow until he reaches the end. It blends the elements with one another and transforms them by alternating change. It measures out the elements and brings them into harmony with one another, although they are contrary to each other, and gives them forms that change back and forth. For people made from earth become earth again, and then people again. But birds made from water do not become water again; they become earth. The same chain renews all things that are born and die through similar successions of offspring and seeds. That same course of fate, that is, of God's outer ordering, renews and replaces all perishable things, which at one time come into being

and meanwhile pass away, with like increase of their seed and of their offspring. This also binds the deeds and fortunes of men by an indissoluble connection of causes. This also constrains the deeds of men and their fortunes with the firm bond of causes. Nothing happens by chance. It always happens from some source, as death comes from sickness or from wounds. That from which it happens is its cause; that is its seed, that is its making, that is its explanation, which binds it fast to itself.
Since it proceeds from the beginnings of unmoving providence, it too must be unchangeable. This ordering must necessarily be unchangeable, because it comes from there, from the steadfast providence.

For things are best governed in this way: if the simplicity that abides in the divine mind brings forth an unswerving order of causes. Thus he governs it all best, if the simplicity of his mind gives an unchanging order to the seeds [causes] that bring about each thing.
But this order is to restrain changeable things by its own unchangeableness,

things that would otherwise drift about at random. This outer order, which has come from the inner one, must constrain with its unchangeableness the changeable things, which would otherwise waver in disorder. Hence it is that although to you, who are quite unable to consider this order, all things seem confused and disturbed, nonetheless its own measure, directing them toward the good, disposes all things. Hence it is that however much all things seem confused and disordered to you who do not recognize this order, his way, aiming at the good, nonetheless orders all things none the less for that.
For there is nothing that is done for the sake of evil, not even by the wicked themselves,
whom, while they are seeking the good, perverse error has turned aside, as has been most amply shown!

Much less would an order proceeding from the hinge of the highest good turn aside anywhere from its beginning. No one does anything for the sake of evil, not even the evil themselves, whom error turns aside while they are striving toward the good, as I have said sufficiently. How then could an order that has come from God move in any other way than according to him?
THAT WHAT SUITS THE GOOD AND THE WICKED IS DISPENSED FROM THE HIDDEN COUNSELS OF PROVIDENCE, AND THAT PEOPLE WONDER AT THIS.
But, you will say, what confusion could be more unjust than that there should befall the good

now adversity, now prosperity, and the wicked likewise now what they desire, now what they hate? So you say: what lack of distinction could be more unjust than that pleasant and painful things should befall the good and the wicked alike?
Do men, then, live with such soundness of mind that those whom they have judged good

or bad must necessarily also be as they think? Are people, then, of such sound mind that those whom they consider good or bad must necessarily be as they consider them? And yet in this the judgments of men conflict, and those whom some think worthy of reward, others think worthy of punishment. Truly, people always disagree about this: those who seem to some to deserve good seem to others to deserve evil. But let us grant that someone could tell the good from the bad. Now let us nevertheless say that someone could discern who is good
or bad. Will he then be able to see into that inmost temperament, that is, the mixture, of souls, as is usually said of bodies

namely by physicians? Can he also know the inner nature of the mind, as physicians say of bodies that they know it? For it is no different a marvel to someone who does not know why, among healthy bodies, sweet things suit some and bitter things suit others, and why, among the sick, some are helped by gentle remedies and others by sharp ones. It may seem just as great a wonder to someone who does not know it why, among healthy bodies, sweet things agree with some and bitter things with others; and why some sick people are healed with sour things and others with mild ones.

But the physician, who knows the measure and balance of health itself and of sickness, does not wonder at this at all. But the physician, who knows the measure and the balance of sickness and of health, is not seized by any wonder at this.
But what else does the health of souls seem to be than goodness,

and what their sickness than vices? And who else is the preserver of the good or the driver-out of evils than God, the ruler and healer of minds? What else can the health of the mind be but goodness? And what can its sickness be but vices? And who is it that keeps the good within and drives the evil out, except God, the ruler and also the healer of human minds?
When he has looked out from the high watchtower of providence, he recognizes what suits each one, and he assigns what he knows to be suitable.

When he looks down here from the watchtower of his providence and perceives what befits each one, he then gives him what he recognizes to befit him. Here now occurs that remarkable wonder of the order of fate, when one who knows does what astonishes those who do not know. So then comes about the singular wonder of fate proceeding in rightness: that God knowingly does what startles the unknowing.

THAT MEN AND PROVIDENCE DO NOT JUDGE ALIKE. For, to touch briefly on a few things about the divine depth that human reason is able to grasp: concerning this man whom you think most just and most careful to observe what is fair,

…seems otherwise to the all-knowing providence. So that I may still give you some grounding in the divine matter, as much as a man is capable of: the one you consider most just and most equitable of all seems otherwise to the all-knowing providence. And indeed our friend Lucan reminded us that the victorious cause pleased the gods, but the vanquished one pleased Cato. And that is what my dear Lucan told you: that the cause that won the victory pleased the gods, but the cause that lost pleased Cato. If Caesar's cause had not pleased them, they would not have helped him to victory! And if Pompey's cause, even without victory, had not pleased Cato well, it would not have seemed better to him to kill himself than to surrender to Caesar.
Here, therefore, whatever you see happen contrary to your hope, there is indeed right order in the things themselves, but a perverse confusion in your opinion.

Know, therefore, that whatever you see happen here in the world contrary to your hope is all right ordering for the things themselves, but wrong confusion for your opinion. With this she has answered his question, though she will still show him the same thing point by point.

THE VARIETY OF DISPENSATION TOWARD THE GOOD. But suppose someone is so well-mannered that divine and human judgment agree about him alike. Now suppose there is someone so upright in conduct that God and man value him alike. But he is weak in strength of mind. He may happen to be soft-hearted.

If anything adverse befalls him, he will perhaps stop cultivating the innocence through which he could not keep his fortune. If anything grievous befalls him, he will perhaps stop holding fast to righteousness, since it brought him no good fortune.
Therefore wise dispensation spares the one whom adversity could make worse,

so that he does not allow one whom it does not suit to suffer hardship. God's measured governance spares him and does not thrust him into hardships, because they do not suit him and would make him worse.
Another is perfect in all virtues, holy and very close to God.
Providence judges it wrong for him to be touched by any adversities at all, so much so that it does not let him be troubled even by bodily illnesses. Likewise, someone is full of all virtues,

holy and godly. God judges him unworthy of any trouble, so much so that he does not even let him become sick. For, as someone more excellent than I said, virtues have built (that is, fortified) the body of a holy man: andros de ieras daumasa aliteres icodomeson [? garbled Greek]. For, as someone wiser than I said, virtues have so fortified the body of a holy man that nothing can harm it. She says "wiser." Who can be wiser than Wisdom herself? Yet by speaking this way she teaches us humility.
But it often happens
that the supreme government of affairs is entrusted to the good,

so that overflowing wickedness may be beaten back. It also often happens that power comes into the hands of the good, for this reason: that evil that has grown great may be suppressed by them. To others he allots a certain mixture according to the quality of their souls. To some God lets both kinds of things befall, troublesome ones and agreeable ones, according to the character of their minds.
Some he stings, so that they do not grow wanton through long good fortune.

Some he afflicts for a while, so that they do not grow foolish and proud from long ease. Others he allows to be harassed by hardships, so that they may strengthen the virtues of the mind by the use and exercise of patience. Some he wants to be tried with hardships, so that they may gain virtuous minds by hardening themselves and growing used to patience.
Some fear more than is right what they are able to bear; others despise more than is right what they are not able to bear.
These he leads through sorrows to a testing of themselves.

Some are frightened, needlessly, of what they could well endure; others trust themselves too far. Both of these he brings into fear, so that they may come to know themselves. Some have purchased a name revered by the world at the price of a glorious death. Some have won a renowned name in the world through a glorious death, like Judas Maccabeus. Certain others, namely the martyrs, unconquered by tortures, have set before the rest an example that virtue cannot be conquered by evils. Some, tormented for the sake of righteousness and yet not overcome by it, gave others the example that true virtue is not overcome by woes.
How rightly and in what good order these things are done…

and for the good of those to whom they seem to happen, there is no doubt. How rightly and how orderly all these things happen is also certain from the very blessedness of those to whom they have happened.

HOW VARIOUSLY THE WICKED TOO ARE DEALT WITH. For the fact that sometimes sad things and sometimes desired things come to the wicked also arises from the same causes. That both sorrow and joy befall the wicked also comes from the same source, divine providence. And no one wonders at the sad things, because everyone thinks they have deserved ill. No one wonders that sorrow befalls them, because to everyone they seem deserving of evil.
Their punishments both deter others from crimes

and correct the very ones on whom they are inflicted. Their punishment does two good things: it turns others away from wrongdoing, and it draws back from wrongdoing those on whom it is inflicted. But the happy things speak to the good as a strong proof of what they ought to judge about happiness of this kind, which they often see serving the wicked. But the fact that joy comes to the wicked teaches the good exactly what they should take that happiness to be, which attaches itself even to the wicked.

In this matter I believe this too is arranged: that perhaps someone's nature is so headlong and restless that lack of means might rather drive him to crimes. Here I also think God intends this: that some people's nature is so rash and so restless that they would go wrong because of poverty. Providence heals this man's sickness with the remedy of money bestowed on him. Providence calms his wickedness with the gift of treasure.
This man, looking at his conscience stained with shameful deeds and comparing himself with his fortune, perhaps becomes afraid that losing what he enjoys using may be painful.
So he will change his ways, and while he fears to lose his fortune,

...abandons wickedness. A certain man recognizes how he has acted, and when he measures his good fortune against that, he is afraid that he may lose such joy, lest it then go hard with him [?]. So he changes his life and, fearing misfortune, gives up wickedness. Others an undeservedly increased good fortune has thrown headlong into deserved ruin. For some it turned out that their unjustly won good fortune hurled them into the ruin they deserved. To some the right of punishing has been permitted, so that it might be a cause of training for the good and of punishment for the wicked. To some power was granted to torment people: for the good as a hardening trial, for the wicked as retribution.
For just as there is no bond between the upright and the wicked,

so the wicked themselves cannot agree among themselves. You need not wonder at all that one wicked man torments another. For just as there is no common mind between the good and the wicked, so there is not full concord among the wicked themselves either. Why not, since each disagrees with himself, while his vices tear his conscience apart? How could it be otherwise, since each of them strives even with himself, his conscience torn apart by his vices? And they often do things that, once done, they judge should not have been done. And they often do what their conscience tells them is not to be done! Yet they do it. When their conscience grieves them, they strive with themselves.
From this that highest providence has often brought forth a remarkable miracle: that bad men made bad men good.

From this God's providence has often brought forth that singular sign: that bad men make good men out of bad ones. For when some see themselves suffering injustice from the worst men, they burn with hatred of the guilty and return to the fruit of virtue, while they strive to be unlike those whom they hated. That is the wonder I speak of. When unrighteous men see that they are made to suffer by other unrighteous men, they conceive hatred for them and turn to goodness, hastening to be unlike those whom they hate.
THAT THERE IS NO EVIL ANYWHERE. For it is the divine power alone

to whom even evils are good, since by using them fittingly he draws out the effect of some good. Only God's power is such that even evil is good to him, because by using it fittingly he turns it to good.
For a certain order embraces all things.

so that whatever departs from the assigned, that is, the fixed, plan of the order falls back into it, even if into another order, so that nothing in the realm of providence may be left to random chance.

The order of God's providence embraces all things. If anything turns aside from the sure direction of its order, it is at once turned into another order, so that nothing wrong is ever allowed in God's kingdom. Whatever will not keep to its right way is nevertheless always brought back onto the way. The envy of Joseph's eleven brothers, in which they had abandoned the right way, God brought back onto the way: He used that same envy as the occasion to raise Joseph above them, and He humbled them before the one they thought they had crushed. Most mighty God in the world. Argalthon demetauta theonos omnia peregit panta gopiin [? garbled Greek]. The mighty God always did in the world all that He wished. For it is not permitted to man either to grasp with his intellect
or to set forth in speech
all the workings of the divine design. Nor is it granted to humans to know or to tell all of God's contrivances.

Let it be enough to have seen this much: that God, the producer (that is, the one who brings forth) of all natures, also directs them toward the good and orders all things. Only let this be well understood: that God, the creator of all natures, sets all things in order, always turning them toward good.
And while He hastens to keep the things He brought forth in His own likeness,

He banishes all evil from the borders of His commonwealth through the chain of fated necessity. And by drawing the things He created toward His likeness, He drives every kind of evil out of His kingdom through the binding order of fate, because He wills that the things that came from good should be good.
Whence it comes about
that if you look at the providence that orders all things, you will judge that there is nothing evil anywhere,

that is, of the evils that are believed to abound on earth. From this it follows that if you look to God's reckoning, you will consider that there is nowhere anything of any evil at all, though people think the world is full of it. But I see that you have long been burdened by the weight of the question and wearied by the length of the argument, and are waiting for some sweetness of song. Now I see that the heaviness of this laborious question and the toil of the long answer have left you longing for sweet song again.
Take, then, a draught, so that, refreshed by it, you may press on more firmly to what lies further.
Now drink what I give you, so that with this refreshment you may go further.
That by God's providence all things are bound together by love, so that they are not dissolved.
If you wish, with skill and with a pure mind, to discern the laws of the Thunderer on high,
look at the heights of the highest heaven. There the stars keep their ancient peace
by the just covenant of things. If you wish to know thoroughly how firm God's law is, then look into heaven.
There the stars still firmly keep the harmony that they have always kept according to their ordering.
The sun, driven onward with its ruddy fire, does not
hinder the cold axle of Phoebe. As is evident there, the hot sun does not hinder the cold moon in its course.
Nor does the Bear, which turns its swift courses at the highest summit of the world,
seeing the other stars sink into the western ocean,

never desires, washed in the deep, to dip her flames. Nor does Helice, which turns her swift course around near the summit of heaven, seeing all the signs go down to their setting, ever desire to bathe in the sea-water.
Vesper announces the late shadows,
and Lucifer always brings back the kindly day, in equal turns of time. The evening star always announces the night, and in answer the morning star brings us the day just as many times.
So mutual love renews the eternal courses;
so discordant war is banished from the star-bearing regions. So love in alternation renews the untiring courses, and quarrelsome discord flees from heaven.
This concord tempers the warring elements in equal measures. This concord unites the opposing elements in like ways,
so that wet things yield in turn to dry,
and cold things keep faith with flames;
the hovering fire rises on high,

and heavy things sink down by the weight of the earth. In this way they are balanced: the dry agrees with the wet, and the cold with the hot, and the light fire presses up to the very top, and the heavy earth sinks to the very bottom.
For these reasons the flowering year breathes out its scents in the warm spring.
Burning summer dries the grain.
Autumn returns heavy with fruit.

Falling rain waters the winter. From this comes the scent of the flowers at the time of year when it is spring. From this the grain ripens in summertime. Autumn comes laden with fruit, and winter wet with rain.
This tempering nourishes and brings forth
whatever breathes life in the world. This moderation gives life to and nourishes whatever is living anywhere in the world.
The same, snatching away,
hides and takes away what has come into being, sinking it in final death. And again, as it changes, it gives and it takes all things that have come into being, sinking them into death.
Meanwhile the Creator sits on high
and, ruling, guides the reins of things,
king and lord, fountain and origin,

law and wise judge of what is just. Meanwhile the Creator sits above, and, ruling, he turns the bridle of the world: lord and king, beginning and source, the law itself, and wise judge of what is right.
And the things he stirs by motion to go,

he draws back and halts, and he makes firm the things that wander. And the things he sets moving on their way, he steadies by drawing the bridle toward himself, and he turns their course, for he forces them back toward himself.
For unless, calling back their straight paths,
he forced them again into curving orbits,
the things that a stable order now holds together

would be cut off from their source and fall apart. If he did not do this, and did not bend back into a circle the courses that run straight away, then the things that a sure order now holds fast would fly apart and be cut off from their origin.

This is the love common to all things. This is the love I am speaking of, which is common to all things. God himself is what they love, for he is the highest good (summum bonum), and they came from him.
And they seek again, that is, they desire, to be held by the end of the good. And so they long to be bound to the end of the good, which he is.
Because they could not last in any other way
unless the causes flow back again with their love turned back, that is, unless they join themselves to that cause
which gave them being. For they could not exist otherwise unless they hastened back, with their love turned there, to the God who bade them come into being, who is the cause of them all.
THAT ALL FORTUNE IS GOOD. Do you now see, then, what follows from all the things we have said? Do you not now perceive what necessarily follows from all these things?
"What is that?" I said. "What?" said I.
"That all fortune whatsoever," she said, "is good." Both good fortune and misfortune are good.
"And how," I said, "can that be?" "How can that be?" said I. "Pay attention," she said.

"Take note of this," said she. Since all fortune, whether pleasant or harsh, comes about for the sake either of rewarding or training the good, or of punishing or correcting the wicked, all of it is good,
since it is agreed to be either just or useful.

Then every fortune, whether pleasant or harsh, is granted so that it may reward the good or exercise them, and punish or correct the wicked. Therefore it is necessarily good, since it is either just or useful. That is an argument from the effect: from the effect it becomes clear what the efficient cause is like. "The reasoning is very true indeed," I said. It is a very true statement, I said. "And if I consider providence, which you taught a little before, or fate, the view rests on firm strength." And if I look at both, providence and fate, which you spoke about just now, then it has great strength. For what else do God's providence
