or the ordering of fate do with all fortunes except these four things: reward or punish, exercise or correct? And what can be more just, and at the same time better? "But if you please, let us count it among those which you taught a little before are unbelievable." Now let us put it, then, if it seems right to you, among the unbelievable things you spoke of before, such as this one: that the wicked who are punished are happier than those who go unpunished. "How so?" she said. How then? she said. Why should I put it among those?
"Because the common talk of people says this, and indeed often:
that some people have bad fortune." Because it is the people's way of speaking, I said, and often, that bad fortune follows certain people.
"Do you wish, then," she said, "that we draw near for a little while to the talk of the common people,

so that we do not seem to have withdrawn too far, as it were, from the usage of humankind?" "Do you wish," she said, "that I come close to the people's talk, so that I do not separate myself too sharply from the everyday talk of men? Do you wish me to speak in a way more easily believed?" "As you please," I said. "As you wish," I said.
PREMISE. "Do you not, then, judge that what is beneficial is good?" "Do you not think," she said, "that what is useful is good?"
"So it is," I said. "That it is," I said.
PREMISE. "But that which exercises or corrects is beneficial?" "The fortune that tests or improves a man," she said, "is it not useful?" "I admit it," I said. "That I confess," I said.

CONCLUSION. "Therefore it is good." "Then it is good," she said. "Why not?" "How else?" I said. In this syllogism she has drawn close to the people's talk, for although it pursues the same argument as the argument before it, its words are nevertheless more credible to people
than those were. "But this fortune belongs to those who, either established in virtue, wage war against hardships, or, turning away from vices, take up the path of virtue."

"But such fortune," she said, "which tests or improves a man, belongs to one of two kinds of people: either to those who are virtuous and struggle against hardships, or to those who are now beginning to turn from vices to virtue." "I cannot deny it," I said. "That I can never deny," I said.

THAT FOR THE GOOD ALL FORTUNE IS GOOD, AND FOR THE WICKED ALL FORTUNE IS BAD. "But what about the pleasant fortune that is given to the good as a reward?" But what about the pleasant fortune, she said, that comes to the good as a reward? "Surely the common people do not judge it to be bad?" Do the people say that this one is bad too?
"By no means, but as it is,
so they also judge it to be the best.

No, I said, but good, as it is. "What about the remaining one?" But what about the other one? she said. "Since it is harsh and restrains the wicked with just punishment, do the people think it good?" I mean the one that is harsh and chastises the wicked as justice requires: do the people consider that good?
"On the contrary," I said, "of all things that can be imagined
judges it to be most wretched. He considers it, I said, the worst of all that one can know.
See, then, that in following the opinion of the people we do not arrive at something quite incredible.

See now that, in following the opinion of the people, we do not establish something incredible. This is said by contraries, as if she said: see whether I should give way to the opinion of the people and not say what is incredible to them. "What?" I said. "What is that incredible thing?" I said. "From the things that have been granted," she said, "it follows that for those who are either in possession of virtue, or advancing in it, or attaining it,
every fortune, whatever it may be, is good; but for those who remain in wickedness, every fortune is the worst.

It truly follows of necessity, she said, from the earlier admissions, that every kind of fortune is good for those who are settled in virtue, or are striving toward it, or have at least attained it; but for those who hold fast to their wickedness, every kind of fortune is equally bad. That is true, I said, although no one would dare to admit it. That is true, I said, though no one dares to admit it, because it is so hard to believe.

WITH WHAT MIND ALL FORTUNE IS TO BE BORNE. Therefore, she said, a wise man ought not to take it badly whenever he is drawn into a struggle with fortune, just as it does not befit a brave man to be indignant whenever the noise of war has sounded. Therefore, she said, a wise man should not be troubled whenever he has to fight with fortune, just as it does not befit a bold warrior to resent it
when he hears the storm of battle. For to both of them, to the one for spreading his glory, to the other for shaping his wisdom, the difficulty itself is the material. The hardship itself

gives both of them occasion: the one to make his glory famous, the other to perfect his wisdom. From this, too, virtue gets its name, because, relying on its own strength, it is not overcome by adversities. From this strength gets its name, because it is sufficient of itself and does not yield to adversity.

"For you who are placed on the path of advancement in virtue have not come here to dissolve in delights and to wither away in pleasure." What are you thinking of? You virtuous ones, you are not directed toward growing slack and dull through indulgence in luxury and pleasures.
You join a very fierce battle with every kind of fortune. You wage hand-to-hand combat with every kind of fortune. Do not let sad fortune crush you or pleasant fortune corrupt you.

With firm strength, take hold of the middle, that is, equanimity. Hold yourselves fast to equanimity, so that grievous fortune does not weigh you down and overcome you, and pleasant fortune does not corrupt your mind so much that you no longer know who you are. Whatever either stops short below it or goes beyond it scorns happiness and does not get the reward of its labour. Whatever lets itself sink lower than equanimity, or climbs higher, loses happiness and goes without the reward.
For it lies in your own hands what kind of fortune you choose to shape for yourselves.

It is up to you what kind of fortune you wish to make for yourselves, and how evenly you wish to bear yourselves toward it. For every fortune that seems harsh punishes, unless it either trains or corrects. Whatever seems harsh does one of these things: it either toughens a person, or improves him, or punishes him.
ON THOSE WHO CONQUERED ADVERSITY BY VIRTUE. The avenging son of Atreus, having waged war for twice five years,
atoned for his brother's lost marriage-bed

with the ruins of Phrygia. Agamemnon, the son of Atreus, avenged the stolen wife of his brother Menelaus by destroying Troy, waging a ten-year siege. It is well known how Alexander Paris, the son of Priam, plundered Sparta, a city of Greece, took Helen, the wife of King Menelaus, while the king was away, and carried her home to Troy. It is also known how the Greeks went after them to take revenge and besieged Troy without stopping until they conquered it and won Helen back. He, that is, Agamemnon, while he wished to give sails, that is, winds, to the Greek fleet
and while he bought the winds, that is, appeased them, with blood, that is, his daughter's blood,
put off the father,

that is, stripped himself of the name of father, and the grieving priest, that is, Calchas, cut the wretched throat, that is, the breast, of the daughter. In this way Agamemnon became childless. Because he wanted to sail away quickly, he sacrificed his daughter Iphigenia to the winds, and Calchas pitifully slaughtered her as if she were a sacrificial animal. This showed how earnest he was: he did not even spare his daughter, so long as he could avenge his name.
The man of Ithaca wept for his lost companions,
whom savage Polyphemus, in his rage, swallowed into his monstrous belly.
But afterward, as the giant lay with blinded face, that is, countenance, in his vast cave,

Ulysses repaid his sad tears with joy. Ulysses mourned his companions, whom the giant Polyphemus furiously devoured in Sicily as Ulysses was returning from Troy. But he was compensated for his tears, because afterward the giant lay blind for a long time in his cave. Ulysses found him asleep and blinded him, and then he was consoled for his comrades, because he had avenged them.
Hard labours make Hercules famous.

Hercules was made famous by the many labours that he overcame. He tamed the proud centaurs. He subdued the centaurs, which the fables say were half men and half horses. He came to where they were playing in the water, and there he shot two of them.

He took a spoil from the savage lion. This was the lion the Greeks called the Nemean, after Nemea, a forest of the Argives. Hercules killed it at the will of King Aristeus. He took its hide and afterward wore it, claws and all, as a mark of glory.
He also shot down the birds with unerring arrows.

He also shot the birds that were called Harpies, and drove them out of the kingdom of King Alcinous, who ruled in Achaea. From there they fled to the Strophades islands, where Aeneas found them. They were the legendary hounds of Jove, named from 'rapiendo' (seizing), because 'arpo' in Greek means 'rapio' (I seize) in Latin. Ovid, however, calls them Stymphalides, from the river Stymphalus, by which Hercules fought with them, though it may be said that the Argonauts drove them away. 'He took the apples from the watching dragon.' While the dragon looked on, he took the golden apples that it guarded in the garden of the Hesperides islands, which lie beyond Mount Atlas in the western ocean. The story that golden apples grow there arose from the fact that one of these same islands is extremely fertile in every kind of produce. And because there is an estuary of the sea in it, that is to say,

a sea-inlet, which looks like a dragon to those who see it from far away, people say that a dragon lies there and guards the apples. An aestuarium is the water that flows in from the sea and moves back and forth on the shore. It is named from 'aestuando' (surging), just as 'stagnum' (a pool) is named from 'stando' (standing). So it takes its name from 'aestuando', that is, from surging, because when the sea's flood tide comes in, it surges, although it is calm when the ebb comes. 'Aestus' properly means the restlessness of the sea, which it has of itself, 'accedendo et recedendo', that is, by going out and coming in. 'His left hand heavier with the golden metal.'

that is, with the club, "he dragged Cerberus on a triple chain." And armed with a club, he dragged Cerberus out of hell on a threefold chain. Because of this it happened that when Cerberus came up here into the light of day, he became sick and spat out a foam, and from it grew aconite, the worst of herbs.
"The victor is said to have set out cruel fodder"

"for the savage four-horse team: their master." He gave the savage king Glaucus, once he had overcome him, to his own savage horses to eat. He did this because the king had earlier trained them to eat human flesh.
"The Hydra perished, its venom burned up." He destroyed the poisonous serpent, the Hydra, with fire.
"The river Achelous, disfigured on his brow,"
"plunged his shamed face into his banks."

The river Achelous, having been made hornless, hid his shamed head in the bank. Achelous changed himself into various shapes until he also became a bull and fought with Hercules. When Hercules struck off his horn and left his head maimed, he hid it afterward. All waters are horned because of the trees that stand around them. Whoever takes the trees away has made them hornless. Because Hercules also cleared the forest from the bank, he took the river's horns from it. "He laid Antaeus low on the Libyan sands." He also overcame the giant Antaeus, son of Earth and king of Libya. He could not overcome him by wrestling while Antaeus stood on the earth, because his mother Earth gave him strength. Then he lifted him up and strangled him in the air.

'Cacus satisfied Evander's wrath.' Cacus the thief, son of Vulcan, who stole Hercules' cattle, cooled the anger of King Evander by his death. When Hercules slew him, he had done what Evander wished, since Cacus had committed robberies in Evander's kingdom. 'The bristly boar flecked with foam the shoulders'
'on which the high heaven was to press.'
That is, 'which it was to press.' The boar foamed onto his shoulders, with which he was to hold up the heaven. It did this as it snorted and tossed its head, because he was carrying it alive.
The last labour.

That is, in his last labour he held up the heavens with unbending neck. In the last victory he held up the heavens with unyielding neck. That was when Jupiter defended himself against the giants and he wanted to throw the heavens down upon them.
And in turn he earned heaven, the reward of his last labour. And as a reward he himself went up to heaven, because he had held it up last.
Go now, you brave ones.

where the lofty path of a great example leads. Now take him as your example, all you virtuous ones, and go where the way that goes on high leads you. Why do you sluggards bare your backs? The earth, once overcome, gives the stars. Why should you yield like cowards and turn your backs? Despise the earth; that gives you heaven.

TO WHAT PART OF PHILOSOPHY THE QUESTIONS OF THIS FOURTH BOOK, AND OF THE FIFTH WHICH STILL FOLLOWS, BELONG. Just as in the third book the questions are moral ones, which show the happiness of the good, so are those here in the fourth.

…which show us the misery of evils, and those that follow after them, on providence and fate. But those still to come in the fifth book, on chance and free will, are different. Chance pertains to providence; therefore that question is a moral one. But whether providence and free will can exist together, which he has yet to ask Philosophy, belongs to theology, because in it the nature of God's simplicity is recognized. That is, it belongs to the kind of reasoning that concerns divine things. Because that reasoning is not human but divine, it has another name: it is called intellect. The understanding of divine things surpasses human reason.

For this reason the questions she set out for us about the reward of the good and the wicked are strengthened with arguments and syllogisms. But the hidden power that is in God's providence, which she has yet to speak of, will be understood divinely, because it is divine. Morality is spoken of in relation to morals. So if you ask what God's disposition, which is in fate and in providence, has to do with that, you should know that God's disposition is called moral by likeness to human morality. How people are mannered, or how they ought to be mannered, is called in Latin moralitas: the quality of manners. And therefore it is also called morality when God answers those same manners, both here by judging,

as was said before, and hereafter by rewarding. So the blessed Gregory morally admonishes in his homily that God would not give a drop of water to the man who did not give the poor man a crumb of bread. Therefore the Saviour said: "With the same measure that you measure, it shall be measured to you again." With this agrees the proverb: "Do evil, and do not expect better." What, then, is morality but how things go, and ought to go, in the manners of men, and how God's manner corresponds to them? HERE ENDS THE FOURTH BOOK OF BOETHIUS.

HERE BEGINS THE FIFTH BOOK OF BOETHIUS. PHILOSOPHY IS CALLED BACK FROM THE DISCUSSION SHE HAD PROPOSED. She had spoken, that is, she had completed the preceding songs that make up the end of the fourth book. This she said. And she was turning the course of her speech

to the treatment and explanation of certain other matters. "To other matters" means other than I wished. She was taking up a different discussion than I wanted. I wanted her to explain the incidental questions, but she wanted to fully explain the questions she had proposed. Here we should know what she meant to heal his sick mind with: the questions she had put before him in the first book. They are these: what man is; by what helm the world is steered; what the end of things is; that wicked men are not to be believed powerful and happy; and that the changes of fortune do not drift about without a ruler. She found him grieving over his misfortune. But when he had learned from her the reasoning of those questions, I mean, that man by participation in God

…is God; and that these are the rudders that govern the world; that prosperity and adversity happen to him; and that all the reprobate are unhappy and powerless, because they cannot attain the good toward which they strive; and that the changes of fortune he complained about are not unjust, because they come from the just God. Then he began to take comfort, and to move on from these questions to others that arose from them. She has explained some of these to him in the fourth book, that is, the causes of hidden things, the simplicity of providence, and the chain of fate. Still to come are the ones he now wants: chance, divine predestination, and freedom of choice.

Then I said: Your exhortation is indeed right. Then I said to her: That is a right exhortation, namely what you say: "Go now, you brave ones, where the lofty path of great example leads." And it is entirely worthy of your authority. And it well befits your authority. But I find in fact what you said a while ago. But now I become aware of what you said before: that the question of providence is entangled with many others. The discussion of providence is bound up with many others.

THE QUESTION OF CHANCE. For I ask whether you think chance is anything at all. I wonder whether you will hold chance to be anything. And what you think it is. And what you consider it to be. Then she said:
Then she answered: I hasten to discharge the debt of my promise. I hasten to fulfil my promise. And to open to you the way by which you may be carried back to your homeland.

And to show you the way that will bring you home. The exile of your mind has caused you grief; I wish to hasten to set it back in its place, with other discourse [?]. But although these things are very useful to know. Although these questions are also useful to know, yet they turn somewhat aside from the path of what we set out to do. They still break away somewhat from the way I am travelling. And it is to be feared that, worn out by byways, you may not have strength enough to cover the right road. And I worry that you, having grown tired on byways, may afterwards be unable to travel the right way.
"Do not fear that at all," I said. "Do not fear that," I said. "For it will serve me as rest to learn the things in which I most delight."

It is rest to me, not trouble, if I may learn what I long for. At the same time, let there be no doubt about what follows. And let there be no doubt about the later discussion. When every side of your argument has been established with undoubted certainty. That is, when the questions that have come up on the side have first been made certain. That is, so that the incidental questions that arise on the side, once they are first untangled, may lend credibility to the rest of what you have put forward.
Then she said, "I will do as you wish." "Now," she said, "I will go along with your wish." And at the same time she began like this. With that she began like this.

THAT IT IS FALSE TO CALL CHANCE SOMETHING WITHOUT A CAUSE. "If," she said, "someone should define chance as an outcome produced by random motion and with no chain of causes. If anyone calls chance an event that happened at random, without anything bringing it about, I affirm that chance is nothing at all. Then I say boldly that chance is nothing. And I judge it to be a completely empty word.

Apart from the meaning of an underlying thing. And I call it a bare name without meaning. A cause is always linked to the outcome. So when one says 'by random motion,' 'without a cause,' or 'without a chain of causes,' it is all the same. All of these mean: at random, by chance, without need, without origin, without source, without cause, without reason. Temerarius motus ('random motion') can also mean self-moving or self-raising. I mean it would be like something rising up of its own accord and coming into being of its own accord. But what is that?

We can say it, but we never find it. Temeritas is thoughtlessness, heedlessness, rashness, disorder, boldness, lack of discernment, and wrongness. A temerarius, that is, a headlong mind, is someone who does not care what he does and acts without thought on whatever occurs to him in the moment. Such a person we call a 'rágare' [?]. Temeritas comes from temnendo ('despising') by syncope, as if it were temneritas. "For what room can there be for any randomness when God constrains all things into order? Where can there be what people call 'at random,' 'by chance,' and 'without order,' when God compels all things into order?
For it is a true saying that nothing comes from nothing.

It is true, what is said: from nothing, nothing comes. No one among the ancients ever contradicted this. All our forebears affirmed it. Although they did not say this of the working principle, that is [?]. Yet they did not say it of the Beginning that works all things out of nothing. But of the material subject. Rather, of the seedful thing. Things are seedful that have seed and cannot come to be without it, as trees are, and herbs, and all living creatures. These are called subjects, because they are subject to their accidents. The four elements are the seed of them all and their matter. But this they (that is, the ancients) laid down as a kind of foundation of all reasonings about nature. And they laid that foundation and showed it

of all their reasonings and all the answers that they gave about nature. Such a manner of speaking is called hypallage: he says "foundation of reasonings" instead of "reasoning of the foundation." That is the sure reasoning of the foundation of all natures, that they said nothing comes to exist out of nothing. Natures, such as trees and herbs and all bodies, do not come into being suddenly; they have some matter from which they come to be, and that he calls the foundation. And if anything happens to them, there is some cause of it, and that too is a foundation. There is always some reason, hidden or open, as to what their foundation is, from where they come to be, or from where anything happens to them.
But if something arises from no causes, it seems to have arisen from nothing. If, however, anything comes about without an origin, it has come from nothing.
But if this cannot happen, then chance of this kind cannot exist either,

such as we defined it a little earlier. If that cannot be, then chance cannot be such as we said before either, I mean that it is an event produced by random motion. "What then?" I said. How then did I speak? "Is there nothing that can rightly be called either chance or fortuitous?" Can nothing now exist that should rightly be called chance or fortuitous?
"Or is there something to which these words apply, even though it is hidden from the common people?" Is there anything to which these names belong, even though people do not recognize it?

WHAT CHANCE IS. "My Aristotle," she said, "defined it in the Physics, with a brief argument and one close to the truth." My friend, she said, Aristotle said it in his book the Physics, briefly and convincingly.
"In what way?" I said. "How?" said I. He said:

"Whenever," he said, "something is done for the sake of some thing, and something other than what was intended happens from certain causes, it is called chance." When, he said, someone does something somewhere for the sake of something, and from some source something happens other than that for which one does it,
that is called chance. "As if someone, digging the ground in order to cultivate a field, were to find a mass of buried gold." That is as when someone, breaking the earth to work his field,

finds a pound of gold buried there long ago. "This, then, is believed to have happened by chance." People say it happened unexpectedly. "But it is not from nothing." Yet it is not from nothing at all; it has happened from some source. "For it has its own causes, whose unforeseen and unexpected concurrence seems to have produced the chance event." Their courses, coming together quietly and unexpectedly, bring about the occurrence.
"For unless the cultivator of the field had dug the ground," For if the farmer had not gone there to his field

If the one who stored the money had not buried it in that place, the gold would not have been found. (Old High German:) If the man hiding his treasure had not buried it there, it would not have been found there.

These, then, are the causes of the chance gain. These are the causes of the unexpected good fortune. It came about from causes that met and flowed together. (Old High German:) This happened to him there because two things came together, namely to produce a third. It did not come from the intention of either person who acted. Neither of the people who acted had this in mind.
"For neither the one who buried the gold nor the one who worked the field

…intended that this money should be found. For neither the man who buried the gold nor the man who ploughed the field had any thought that it would be found there. But, as I said, it came together and coincided that this man dug where that man buried. Rather, as I said: where the one buried, the other dug there; these ran together and fell together. The one could not have brought about the event without the other. We may therefore define chance as
an unexpected event. Now I must say that chance is what happens unexpectedly. From causes flowing together in these things,

namely in causes, which are done for some purpose. From things that fall together, which people do for the sake of something. But that order which descends from the fountain of providence arranges all things in their places and times. But the order, namely the order of fate, which comes from God's providence, arranges all things one by one in their place and in their time. Proceeding by an inevitable connection. Coming with a firm bond. It makes the causes run together and flow together. It makes the causes of chance events fall and run together and hold together. Providence knows things all together; fate unfolds them one by one. For where one man had earlier buried, fate joined to that the fact that another later dug there; to those two the third, the finding, was joined by necessity. When God willed those two things to happen, the third happened from them by necessity.

LIKEWISE, CHANCE SHOWN FROM THE MEETING OF RIVERS. The Tigris and the Euphrates flow from one source in the cliffs of the Achaemenian rock. The Tigris and the Euphrates spring up together in the mountains of Armenia.
There the fleeing fight, that is, the fighter in flight, shoots arrows backward into the breasts of the pursuers. There the warriors shoot behind them as they flee, at those who are chasing them.
And soon, their waters parted, they separate. And they at once part from each other in far-apart courses.
If they should come together and be called back again into one course — (the voice is held in suspense here). If after that they flow together and come into one channel,
so that what the wave of each stream carries would flow together,

And here: thus, so that what each water carries would flow together. Ships would meet, and trunks torn up by the river. And here: I mean the ships, and the tree trunks torn out of the earth by the river.

And the mingled water would entangle chance modes, that is, orders; namely, this is called chance. And the mingled water entangles the unexpected orders. These are orders: that water always runs after water. If that happens unexpectedly, the occurrence is called chance.
Yet these wandering chances are governed by the very slopes of the land

and by the downward-flowing order of the falling stream. These same occurrences, I mean those of the confluence, are caused by the slopes and by the river's course, which always sinks downward. If there were no valley, and the water did not hasten there, they would not come together. So chance submits to the reins,
though it seems to drift with loosened reins.

So chance goes under constraint, though it seems to you to go unconstrained. And it proceeds by its own law. And it does not go without law. The causes that make chance constrain it; they set a law for it. Therefore chance, accident and unexpected event are what the causes make, whether open or hidden.
WHETHER THE HUMAN WILL IS CONSTRAINED BY FATE.
I see it, I said. I understand it well. And I agree that it is so, as you say.

And I see that it is so, as you say. But is there no freedom of our will in this series of causes that cohere with one another? Is there now no self-determination of our will in this chain of causes that hold together? Or does the chain of fate constrain even the motions of human minds? Does fate also compel human thoughts, as it does other events?
"There is," she said, "free will." "There is," she said. "Nor could there be any rational nature that did not also have freedom of will.
No creature has reason without free will. The angels in heaven and men on earth have both.

THAT JUDGMENT COMES FROM REASON AND CHOICE FROM FREEDOM. For whatever can naturally use reason has judgment. Whoever has been granted understanding and its use has also been granted choice, by which he can tell each thing apart: whether it ought to be done or not. Between these two he is under no compulsion. This freedom from compulsion is called libertas (freedom). Reason teaches him what he should do; freedom lets him do whichever of the two he wishes. So by itself it recognizes what should be avoided and what should be desired. He knows of himself what he should shun and what he should love. Reason teaches him this.
Whatever someone judges to be desirable, he seeks; he flees what he thinks should be avoided. What he thinks is good,

he wants; what he thinks is evil, he shuns. Free will allows him this. Therefore those in whom there is reason also have the freedom to will and not to will. So those who have been granted the knowledge of evil and good have been granted power over their will. But I do not hold, that is, I do not admit, that this freedom is equal in everyone. I do not say that it is the same in all.
in all who have it. For clear-sighted judgment, uncorrupted will, and effective power to obtain what they desire are present to the higher, divine substances.

For the angels have been granted true knowledge, right will, and effective power to carry out their will. God gave these three things as a reward to the good angels after the fall of the evil ones, who turned their free will to evil while they still had it. Now they do not have it. Even though they recognize what is good to do, they do not want to do it, nor can they. Man, however, before his transgression, had power over both, understanding and will. Through the transgression both were so confused that, when he chooses, he often takes a lie for the truth, and when he wills, he wills evil in place of good. Moreover, his will does not succeed, even when he wills well, unless the grace of God brings it about.
HE SPEAKS FROM THE OPINION OF THE PHILOSOPHERS. But human souls must be freer when they keep themselves in the contemplation of the divine mind.

Human souls are necessarily freer while they have the sight of God in heaven. There neither error nor the difficulty of judging or of choosing weighs on them. There, before they come here, they know what is good for them, and they also want it. But they are less free when they slip down into bodies. Coming here into bodies, they become less free. And they are less free still when they are bound to earthly limbs. They also become less free when they take up their dwelling and are fastened to the earthly limbs. But the utmost slavery is when, given over to vices,
they have lost possession of their own reason. That is the most extreme slavery, when they are given over to sins and turn away from their wisdom.

For when they have cast their eyes (that is, the eyes of the mind) down from the light of the highest truth to lower and dark things, this is how they are enslaved: when they let their mind sink down from what is above to what is below. Soon they are darkened by a cloud of ignorance. Then they at once become ignorant.
They are troubled by harmful passions.

They become bound by ruinous desires. By drawing near to these and consenting to them, by giving in to them and following them, they strengthen the slavery that they brought on themselves. They support the slavery that they let take hold of them. In a way, they are prisoners of their own freedom. And then they are exiled and cut off from their freedom.

Yet that gaze of providence, looking out on all things from eternity, sees these things. The foreseeing eye still looks on it, knowing all things in advance. And it arranges each predestined thing according to its merits, that is, those whom he predestined, these he also rewards.
And it shapes the things it has named in advance according to their deserts. [Greek:] "It sees all things and hears all things." That eye sees everything and knows everything.
HOW MUCH MORE PENETRATING THE GAZE OF GOD IS THAN THE RAY OF THE SUN. Homer of the honey-sweet mouth
sings of Phoebus as bright with pure light.
Homer, sweetly speaking, calls the sun bright
and clear. Which nevertheless is not able to break through all the inner parts of the earth
or of the sea
with the weak light of its rays. Which nevertheless cannot shine through the earth and the sea, because of the weakness of its beams.
Not so the founder of the great world. God is not so powerless.
To him, beholding all things from on high,
the earth does not resist with any mass. Against his eyes, which look over all things, no thickness of the earth stands.
Night with its black clouds does not obstruct him. Nor does any darkness of the night.
In a single glance of the mind he sees what is, what has been, and what is to come. With one look he sees what was before, what is now, and what is still to come.
Him you may call the true sun, because he alone beholds all things. Him you can call the true sun! For he alone looks upon everything.

QUESTION: SINCE WHAT IS FORESEEN MUST NECESSARILY HAPPEN, HOW CAN FREE WILL STAND? Then I said. Then I answered her: "Look, I am confounded again by an even harder uncertainty. Now I am stuck in still greater doubt."
She said: What is this? Which is that doubt? For I already guess by what things you are troubled.

I can well guess, she said, what troubles you. I said: They seem very much to oppose and fight against each other. It seems to me, I said, that these two struggle and are against one another: that God foreknows all things, and that there is any free choice of will.

That God knows everything beforehand, and yet it rests in man's will. For if God foresees all things and cannot be deceived in any way, then what providence has foreseen as future must necessarily come about. For if God knows everything beforehand, and his knowledge cannot deceive him, then what he knows to be coming must necessarily happen.
That is true. Therefore, if he foreknows from eternity not only the deeds of men but also their plans and wills, there will be no freedom of choice.

This is false. For if he always knows beforehand not only people's deeds but also their wills, then free will is gone. For no deed and no will at all will be able to exist except what divine providence, which cannot be deceived, has foreseen. Nothing can happen, in deed or in will, that God's eye does not see, and no one can deceive that eye. That is true.
For if things can be turned aside to happen otherwise than they were foreseen, there will no longer be firm foreknowledge of the future,
but rather uncertain opinion, which I judge it impious to believe of God.
If any of them can turn out otherwise, then it cannot be called certain knowledge, only uncertain opinion, and no one may accuse God of that.

THE ARGUMENT BY WHICH SOME THINK THEY SOLVE THE QUESTION IS REFUTED. For I do not approve of the reasoning by which some believe they can untie this knot of the question. Nor do I praise the argument with which some think they have answered this difficulty. For they say
that something will not come about because providence has foreseen that it will be, but, they say, the reverse: because something is going to be,

…but rather that it cannot be hidden from divine providence. They say: it does not happen because God foresees it; rather, because it happens, he therefore foresees it. And in this way they think this necessity slips back to the opposite side. And so they think that this necessity of future events turns back the other way.
For they hold that it is not necessary for the things that are foreseen to happen, but that it is necessary for things

that are going to happen to be foreseen. Nor do they think that the things God foresees happen of necessity. They think instead that the things which are going to happen are of necessity foreseen. Through this reversal they think that the event causes the foresight, not that the foresight causes the event. As if the real labor were to find out which is the cause of which: whether foreknowledge is the cause of the necessity of future things, or future things are the cause of the necessity of providence. It is as if I were struggling over which of them is the cause of the other: whether foresight is what causes the necessity of future things, or future things are what cause the necessity of foresight. But let us strive to show this: that the outcome of things foreknown is necessary, however the order of causes may stand. And let there be nothing more for me to show than that the outcome of things foreknown is necessary, however the order of the causes may be — namely, because it always seems to me that through this necessity free will is taken away.
Even if foreknowledge does not seem to impose on future things the necessity of coming about. Even though foresight does not lay necessity on future things.

The argument of those who are in error is shown by another line of reasoning. TAKEN FROM ARISTOTLE'S CATEGORIES. For if someone is sitting, the opinion that supposes he is sitting must be true; and conversely, if the opinion about someone that he is sitting is true,
it is necessary that he sit. What they think is like this case: If anyone believes that a sitting man is sitting, that belief does not deceive him. If the belief does not deceive him,

then the man is sitting. So there is necessity in both: in the one, the necessity of sitting, and in the other, the necessity of truth. Both carry necessity: the sitting, and the belief's freedom from deception.

But no one sits because the opinion is true. A true belief does not make anyone sit. Rather, the opinion is true because someone's sitting came first. Rather, the sitting that comes first makes the belief true.
So, although the cause of the truth comes from one side, there is still a necessity common to both. So it happens that the cause of the truth is on one side only, but the necessity is on both sides.
It is clear that one may reason in the same way about providence and future things.

This is how the argument about God's providence and about future things is made, that is, as it has been understood by those who go wrong on it. For if things are foreseen because they are going to happen, they still do not come about because they are foreseen. For even if God foresees things because they are going to happen, as these people think, the things still do not happen because he foresees them.
Nevertheless it is necessary either that future things be foreseen by God

and that things foreseen come to pass. Now there is necessity on both counts: both that God foresees future things and that things foreseen happen. So here too, as they think, causation runs in one direction, but necessity runs in both. And this alone is enough to destroy freedom of will. At this point that is enough to destroy free will, because necessity takes away the power of choice.
THE FALSE SUPPOSITION about foreknowledge IS RIDICULED. But now how backwards it is

to say that the outcome of temporal things is the cause of eternal [foreknowledge]. How completely upside down it is for anyone to say that these temporal events are the cause of God's eternal knowledge.
But what else is it to think

that God foresees future things because they are going to happen, than to suppose that things which happened long ago are the cause of that highest providence? What else is it? Whoever wants to believe that God knows future things because they are going to happen, of him I say that he believes events are the cause of God's knowledge.

IT IS PROPOSED AGAIN THAT FOREKNOWLEDGE CANNOT BE AVOIDED; OTHERWISE IT WOULD RATHER BE OPINION. To this must be added: this too must be added to it: just as, when I know that something is, it must necessarily be, so, when I know that something will be, it must necessarily be going to be. Just as it is necessarily so if I know something in the present, so too what I know as future necessarily happens afterwards. So it comes about
that the outcome of a foreknown thing cannot be avoided. So it always happens that a thing known beforehand cannot fail to take place.
Finally, if anyone should judge something to be otherwise than it actually is: but if anyone judges the thing otherwise,

than that it is [?]. That is not only not knowledge, but a false opinion, far removed from the truth of knowledge. That is not just a lack of knowledge, but a false belief, far separated from the truth of knowledge.

Therefore, if anything is going to happen in such a way that its outcome is not certain and necessary. Therefore, if any thing is going to happen in such a way that its coming is neither certain nor necessary,
how could it be known beforehand that it will happen? How can anyone know beforehand that it is going to happen?
For just as knowledge itself is unmixed with falsehood,

so what is conceived by it cannot be otherwise than as it is conceived. Nothing happens otherwise because of this. Just as knowledge does not mix itself with falsehoods, so nothing it holds in its grasp can turn out otherwise than as it is in its grasp. The events lie contained in that knowledge, and as they lie there, so they come about by necessity.

For the reason knowledge is free of falsehood is that each thing must be just as knowledge understands it to be. Therefore knowledge is without falsehood, because each thing must be as knowledge has found it to be.
that it is. What then? What now?
In what way does God foreknow these uncertain future things? The things that are uncertain: in what way does God know them beforehand?
For if he judges that things will inevitably happen
…which it is also possible may not happen, he is deceived. If he thinks that future things cannot fail to happen, when they can in fact fail to happen,

then his opinion deceives him. "It is wicked not only to think this but even to say it aloud." It is wicked to say it, not only to think it. "But if it decides that they will be in the future just as they are!"

so that he knows equally that they can either happen or not happen. But if he determines that they will come about just as they are, I mean, that he knows equally that they can happen and not happen, what kind of foreknowledge is this, which grasps nothing certain and nothing stable? What kind of knowledge is that, which holds nothing certain or stable in it?

Or how does this differ from that ridiculous prophecy of Tiresias: "Whatever I say will either be or not be"? Or how much more certain is it than the laughable prophecy of the Sibyl, the priestess of Apollo, when she said: "What I say is either true or false"?
For in what would divine providence surpass human opinion if, like men, it judges uncertain things

whose outcome is uncertain? How then does God's wisdom surpass men's supposition, if he doubts doubtful things just as they do? But if with him, the most certain source of all things, nothing can be uncertain: but if with him, the source of all things, nothing is doubtful, then the outcome of those things which he has firmly foreknown as future is certain. Then the things which he certainly knows to be future also happen without doubt.

Therefore there is no freedom in human counsels and actions, which the divine mind, foreseeing all things, binds and constrains to one outcome. Therefore man has no power over his deeds, good or evil, since God, who foreknows everything, compels him to that one outcome. That is a false conclusion.

IF FREE WILL TOO IS TAKEN AWAY BY THE NECESSITY OF FUTURE THINGS, THE WHOLE ORDER OF HUMAN LIFE IS OVERTURNED. Once this is accepted, it is clear how great a ruin of human affairs follows. If that is so, then there is no doubt how completely human affairs will fall to ruin.
For rewards and punishments are set before

to the good and the wicked. In vain, then, are rewards and punishments promised to the good and to the wicked, which no free and voluntary movement of minds has earned. Since neither of them can earn them by its unfree and not self-governed will. And that will seem the most unjust of all which now seems most just. And then the most unjust of all things will be what is now most just: either that the wicked are punished or that the good are rewarded. I mean, repaying the good with favour and the wicked with punishment, whom their own will does not send to either. Whom their will does not lead there. But the necessity of what is to come compels them. Rather, the necessity of the future compels them.
Neither vices nor virtues, therefore, will have been anything at all.
but rather a mixed and undistinguished confusion of all merits.

Then there are no vices and no virtues, but an equal and undivided mixture of all deserts. And nothing more wicked than this can be imagined: since the whole order of things is derived from providence, And this is the most dangerous of all things to take into one's thoughts: since providence orders all future things, and nothing is left to human counsels, And as long as nothing at all depends on human will, it follows that even our vices are traced back to the author of all good things.

Then there is no other course except that our sins are smeared onto God, who gives all good. Therefore there is no reason either to hope for anything or to pray for anything. No one can give any account of hope or of entreaty, or say what either is for! For what should anyone hope for, or even pray to avert, when an unbending chain of events links together everything that might be wished for? What should one hope for or entreat, when the unturnable straight course, that is, of fate, binds all desirable things together indissolubly, like a chain? If all things are held fast in their order as they were appointed, then whatever is to come to each person comes to him without entreaty.
Therefore that one unique exchange will be taken away, namely between God and men, that of hoping and praying. If it is to go so,

then that one exchange between God and men is hindered, and the bargain which rests entirely on hope and on supplications. For indeed by the price of just humility, namely that which is in prayers, we earn the inestimable return of divine grace. For with the value of true humility, which is what prayers are, we buy from him the precious payment of his grace. We can carry on no other trade with him.

Which is the only way by which men may be seen to be able to converse with God. That is the one way in which people can speak with God. And by the very means of supplication to be joined to that inaccessible light, even before they obtain [what they ask]. And by praying to draw near to the invisible light, even before they obtain anything.
And if, once the necessity of future things is accepted, these are believed to have no power,

If now, because of the necessity imposed on future things, hope is to avail nothing, what will there be by which we can be joined to that highest ruler of things and hold fast to him? By what thing, then, can we hold ourselves to God, the lord of all things?
Therefore the human race, cut off and separated from its source, will necessarily fail.

as you sang a little while ago. Then, as you sang midway through the work in the verses "si vis celsi iura tonantis", the race of men must crack apart like clay, broken off and separated from the true spring from which it came.

WHAT HOLDS HIM BACK FROM UNDERSTANDING THIS QUESTION. HE HIMSELF INVESTIGATES. What discordant cause loosens the bonds of things? What discord disturbs the agreements of two things, namely of God and of man,
or of foreknowledge and free will?
O God, who has set such great wars between two truths? What god has given such strife to two truths? What things are truer than they are?
So that the things which stand firm singly, each on its own,

refuse to be yoked together when joined? That the things which exist separately, each by itself, will not go together? What necessity can separate God's providence and man's free will, so that they are not together in every deed of man?
Or is there no discord between truths? Or is there no discord among true things? The true and the false flee each other; two truths love each other.
And do certain things always cohere with one another? And do the certain things, that is, those that are certain through themselves, always hold together?
But the mind, that is, the soul, overwhelmed by the blind limbs of the body, cannot know the fine connections of things.
by the fire of its smothered light.

But the fault is not theirs; rather, the human soul, because of its dullness, cannot know their hidden bonds, which you, however, know, Philosophy, and which I wish to learn from you. That is as if he said: Free will is entirely certain to us, because it is evident in the deeds of men. God's providence is equally certain in the other creatures, which do not have free will. But in man's deeds the two cannot exist together. Or if they can, then the reason how that may be is very hidden. That reason is hard for him to work out "by the fire of smothered light," that is, by the keenness of a weighed-down mind, with the confused understanding of the mind. The body makes the soul lose power over its understanding, which it had before it came to the body. It always strives toward it, but it succeeds poorly.
But why does it burn with such great love
to find the hidden signs of truth? Why then is it so urgent for it to discover the hidden word-signs of truth? Does it know
what it anxiously longs to know? Does it know what it wants to know?
But who labors to know what is already known? But who would ask about something
that he knows? But if it does not know, what does it blindly seek? And if it is so blind that it does not know it, what then does it want?
For who would desire anything without knowing it? Who is there who would want what he does not know?
Or who could pursue things unknown?
or where would he find it?

Or who can seek what he neither knows nor recognizes? Or how could he succeed in discovering it? Who, being ignorant, could recognize the form once it was found? And who can recognize what is unknown to him, even when he finds it?
Or when it, namely the soul, beheld the high mind, that is, God,
did it know the whole and the particulars equally? Or should we believe that it knew both, the particular things and the whole together, for as long as it looked upon God?
Now, hidden by the cloud of the bodily limbs,
has not wholly forgotten itself. Now indeed, though darkened in the limbs,

it still has some of it, yet has not forgotten everything. And it holds the sum, while losing the particulars. And the gist it knows; the particulars it does not know. No one is so mindful that he remembers all the particulars as well as the gist.
Therefore whoever seeks the truth
is in neither state. Whoever asks after the truth, as I am doing now in this question, is in neither state. For he does not know [m ?]
and yet he is not wholly ignorant of everything. He neither knows all of it nor is ignorant of all of it.
But the whole, which he keeps and remembers,
it consults. Rather, the gist, which he holds in memory, that he examines, retracing things seen on high, thinking deeply on what he saw.

So that it may add the forgotten parts to those it has preserved. So that by means of the things remembered he may arrive at the forgotten ones. Like someone who had thoroughly learned a book and now remembers only the outer sum of it, and often turns his mind to that, so that from it he recalls the rest as well. What a 'summa' is, Cicero teaches us in the Rhetoric, saying: 'The summa of the deed is: he committed homicide.'

The particulars, however, are these: what was done before the matter, what after the matter, what in the matter itself, or what around the matter. Suppose someone says to us: "Is it necessary that what is foreseen comes to pass?" We say: "It is necessary." He says again: "And will free will stand?" We say: "It will stand." He also says: "How will something be free that is necessary? Necessity and freedom cannot belong to one and the same thing. Or if they can, by what bonds are things bound together that are opposed to each other?" What do we say then? If those bonds are unknown to us, then we cannot answer this question fully. Then we know only the main point; the particulars we do not know. We shall learn the particulars later from Philosophy herself.
FIRST RESPONSE.

THAT UNDERSTANDING, NOT REASON, MAKES THEOLOGIANS. Then she said. Then she answered me: This is the old complaint about providence. This is the old complaint about God's providence: that it hinders free will (liberum). It was vigorously pursued by Marcus Tullius when he divided divination. And it was discussed at length by Cicero, where he divided divination, namely into three parts: haruspicy, divination by lightning, and divination by birds. Haruspicy was taken from the livers of sacrificial animals; divination by lightning from the lightning flashes; divination by birds from the cries of birds.

And it is a question that you yourself have long and thoroughly pursued. And it is for you (that means by you) a matter very diligently sought. But until now it has by no means been resolved carefully or firmly enough.

…by any of you. But it has never yet been truly or certainly explained by any of you. The cause of this darkness is this. That the motion, i.e., the effort, of human reason cannot be brought near to the simplicity of divine foreknowledge. That a person's reason, however hard it strives for it, cannot reach the simplicity of God's foreknowledge. If it could in any way be conceived, namely at least by the intellect, since it cannot be by reason. If anyone can know it by rising above reason, nothing doubtful will remain. For that person there is no doubt about this question. God's foreknowledge is simple, for he knows all things

and knows them all at once, as present. He does not remember them behind him or think ahead to them before him. Whoever recognizes this has no doubt that the deeds of free will are also necessarily in his knowledge, but not in foreknowledge. They can exist together in the same way that our knowledge exists together with the deeds of people, which are free. How does our knowing their deeds hinder their freedom? I will try at last to make this plain and resolve it in this way, if I first weigh the things that trouble you. I will then try to reveal and explain that simplicity to you, once I have first set you right and examined what weighs on you and makes you doubt free will.

WHY SHE DOES NOT ACCEPT THE ARGUMENT BY WHICH OTHERS THINK THEY SOLVE THE QUESTION. For I ask why you think less effective that argument of those who solve it. Now I ask you why you do not think useful the argument of those who solve the question, that is, as they think they do. It holds that the freedom of choice is in no way hindered by foreknowledge. That argument holds, i.e., contends, that free will is not hindered by foreknowledge. Because it judges that foreknowledge is not a cause of necessity for future things. Because it does not impose necessity on future things, i.e., on the things to come, i.e., in their opinion. Here let us remember that he did not find fault with this opinion earlier, nor should he have, for it is correct. What he found fault with was their saying that the outcome of future things was the cause of God's foreknowledge.
For do you draw the argument for the necessity of future things from anywhere else?

From what else do you also infer that future things must happen by necessity? Except that the things that are foreknown cannot fail to happen? Except that the things that are foreknown cannot fail to come about? Here again we must consider how true that argument is. Everyone who wrestles with this question gets stuck here. What God foresees, they say, cannot fail to happen. That is true. What cannot fail to happen happens by necessity. That is also true. If these two truths are understood without a distinction, the conclusion follows that there is no free will. She teaches us that distinction later on. She teaches us that people's deeds can indeed fail to happen.

…insofar as it depends on their own nature. On that side there is no necessity in them at all, and yet, with God looking on them, they cannot fail to happen. It is the same when we look on and see a man sitting: his sitting cannot then be left undone, even though, as far as he was concerned, it could well have been left undone, because he could have refrained from it. From this comes the question whether his sitting gives us and God knowledge of his sitting. It is answered thus: it gives that knowledge to us when it happens, not before. But God's knowledge does not wait for the event. To him it is present before it happens, and this presence makes him know it. So the solution of this question is this: what God foresees is necessary, because he looks upon it.
In the same way it is necessary that when we see someone doing something, he is doing it, even though the doer does not do it of necessity.

BECAUSE PROVIDENCE DOES NOT COMPEL FUTURE THINGS, FREEDOM THEREFORE STANDS. If, then, foreknowledge adds no necessity to future things, as you yourself admitted a little earlier: If foreknowledge imposes no necessity on future things, as you also fully admitted before. What is it by which the voluntary outcomes of things are forced toward a fixed result? By what, then, are the self-determined courses of human deeds forced toward a fixed outcome? Because they are free of compulsion, free will therefore stands. For let us suppose, for the sake of argument, that is, by way of example, that there is no foreknowledge, so that you may notice what follows. Now let us just say, for the sake of discussion, that foreknowledge does not exist, so that you may see

how things would then turn out. Are the things that come from free choice then forced into necessity, as far as this goes, that is, as far as this line of reasoning goes? Does any necessity then compel, on that account, the deeds that come from the will? Not at all. It does not.
Let us suppose again that it exists. Now let us say again that it exists, but that it imposes no necessity on things, and yet does no necessity to the deeds.
The same freedom of the will will remain, I think,
whole and absolute. Even then, I think, the same freedom of the will stands firm.
EVEN IF PROVIDENCE IS A SIGN OF FUTURE THINGS, IT IS STILL NOT THEIR CAUSE.

But, you will say, now you will say again: Although foreknowledge does not make it necessary for future things to happen, even if foreknowledge is no compulsion on future things, it is still a sign that they will necessarily come. It is still a sign that they must come by necessity.

In this way, then, it would be established that the outcomes of future things are necessary, even if there had been no foreknowledge. It would then be just as certain that future things must necessarily happen, even if the foreknowledge of them did not exist.
For every sign shows only what is,

which it signifies; it does not bring it about. A sign shows only what the thing is of which it is the sign; it does not make it. Just as the red dawns signify a storm and yet do not make it. Therefore it must first be demonstrated, namely by you, that nothing happens otherwise than by necessity, that is, except by necessity. You must first show us that all things happen by necessity, so that it may be clear that foreknowledge is a sign of this necessity, so that we may then believe that foreknowledge is a sign of the necessity.
Otherwise, if this does not exist. But if it does not exist, namely necessity,
Not even that will be able to be a sign of a thing that does not exist.

So foreknowledge cannot be its sign any more than that. "But now it is established": we know well. "That a proof supported by firm reason," the sure confirmation of anything, "is not to be drawn from signs," is not to be taken from a sign, as you do, "nor from arguments sought from outside," nor from far-fetched inferences, as you want to infer necessity from far-fetched signs, "but from fitting and necessary causes," but from things that lead to it and that create necessity, so that the argument rests on fitting and necessary things.

The first man is not begotten, because he had no father or mother. Or this: you are fasting, because today you have neither eaten nor drunk. But that, on the other hand, is taken from outside (extrinsecus): "Our fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge." For the parents are one thing and the children another. But being fasting is nothing other than not having eaten and not having drunk, and being unbegotten is nothing other than not having a father or mother.

THINGS FORESEEN MUST NECESSARILY COME TO PASS; YET NO NECESSITY IS IN THEM. But how can it be that the things foreseen as future do not come to pass? But how can it be that the things which God knows are coming do not happen?
As if we actually believed that the things which God's providence foreknows to be future will not come to pass! As if I doubted that the things God foresees must happen.
And let us not rather suppose that.

So that it rather does not strengthen that. Although they happen. Though they happen. Yet they have no necessity by their own nature that they should happen. They have in themselves no necessity by which they happen. Which you may easily judge from this.

Which you can easily perceive from this. For we behold many things placed before our eyes while they are being done. We see plenty of things that are before our eyes while someone is doing them. Such as the things charioteers are seen to do in guiding and turning their four-horse chariots. Such as what we see the chariot-drivers do, turning, namely in the chariot race, and also giving the chariots free rein as they will. And other things of this kind. And other works besides.
Does any necessity, then, compel any of those things to be done in this way?

Does any necessity compel any of them to it, against a person's will? Not at all. It does not do that. For the work of art would be in vain. One could do that in vain. If all things moved under compulsion. If they moved that way against a person's will.
Therefore the things that lack necessity while they are being done. Those that are without necessity in the doing.
These same were future without necessity

before they happen. They too are, before they come to be, future without necessity. Wherefore there are certain things that are going to come about whose outcome is free from all necessity. From this it is clear that some things are to happen whose happening and whose course is unbound from all necessity.

For I think no one will say this: I do not think anyone will want to say that: That the things which now happen were not going to happen before they happened. That those things were not future before they came to be, which now come to be.
These things, then, even though foreknown, have free outcomes.

Even when foreknown, those things kept their free occurrence. For just as knowledge of present things imposes no necessity on the things that are happening, so foreknowledge of future things imposes no necessity on the things that are going to happen. Just as knowledge does not compel present things, so their foreknowledge does not compel future things either.

THAT GOD HAS NO MERE OPINION OF FUTURE THINGS, ALTHOUGH THEY DO NOT HAPPEN UNDER COMPULSION, AND WHAT DECEIVES US IN THESE THINGS. But you say. So you say. This very thing is in doubt: whether there can be any foreknowledge of those things.

that do not have necessary outcomes. There is doubt about this very thing: whether there can be any foreknowledge of the things that do not happen by necessity. For they seem to be in conflict: for they seem to you to disagree. And you think that if they are foreseen, necessity follows: and you think that if they are foreknown, they must necessarily happen. That if necessity is absent, they are not foreknown at all: that if there is no necessity about them, there is no foreknowledge of them. And that nothing can be grasped by knowledge unless it is certain: and you think there is knowledge of nothing except what is certain.

For if those things whose outcomes are uncertain are foreseen as if they were certain. So if things are foreseen as certain which are nevertheless uncertain as to how they will turn out. That is the darkness of opinion, not the truth of knowledge. You would call that opinion, not knowledge.

For you believe that thinking a thing is otherwise than it actually is cannot be part of whole and perfect knowledge. You do not dare to ascribe to complete knowledge a belief that differs from how the thing is.

The cause of this error is the following. This is what causes the error: each person thinks that all things are known only from the power and nature of the things that are known. People think that each and every thing is known from its own nature. But the whole matter is the opposite. It is all the other way round. For everything that is known is grasped not according to its own power, but rather according to the capacity of those who know it. It is not known according to its own power; rather, it is apprehended according to the ability of the knowers. God does not see future things according to their power, but according to the power of his own ability. That they are future is so in themselves, because they have not yet come; to him they are present, without any coming. Whatever anyone does in our presence is not necessary as far as the doer is concerned; yet it is necessarily so

as we see it. The things that God looks upon are also necessary, in the way that he looks upon them; but whoever is still to do them in the future does them without necessity. Philosophy now begins to teach us this at length with examples.

SHE TRIES TO LEAD US FROM HUMAN KNOWLEDGE TO DIVINE KNOWLEDGE, BEGINNING FROM THE OUTER SENSE. To make this clear with a short example, listen now, so that it may quickly give you an illustration of it. Sight recognizes the roundness of the same body in one way, and touch recognizes it in another. If you are to perceive a round body, the eye perceives its roundness differently from the finger. Sight stays at a distance, sends out its rays, and looks at the whole at once. The eye shoots its gaze from far away and perceives the shape all together. But touch clings to the sphere
and is joined to it, and as it moves around the circumference itself, it grasps the roundness part by part. The finger, laid on it and moving all around it, explores it all piece by piece.

THE OUTER SENSE AND THE OTHER, INNER WAYS OF CONSIDERING THINGS DIFFER FROM ONE ANOTHER. Man himself, too, is regarded in one way by sense, in another by imagination, in another by reason, and in another by intelligence. These four faculties just named do not perceive the human being himself in the same way. For sense judges the shape as it exists in its underlying matter. The outer sense, such as sight, perceives the shape as it exists in some material thing. But imagination judges the shape alone, without matter. The inner sense

The faculty called imaginatio (imagination) sees the image alone, without the matter in which it saw it before. Ratio vero hanc transcendit: But the faculty called ratio (reason) goes beyond imagination. Et perpendit ipsam speciem quae singularibus inest universali consideratione: Therefore it recognizes as a general whole the form that shows itself in each individual thing, wherever it appears. In the noun "homo" (man) we understand as a whole what is seen singly and individually in Plato, Cicero and Socrates, and what also comes into the mind separately, without them. Intellegentiae vero celsior oculus existit: The eye of intellegentia (understanding) looks out over these three faculties. Supergressa namque ambitum universitatis:

For, going beyond the compass of the universal that reason grasps, contuetur ipsam illam simplicem formam pura acie mentis: with a clear eye it sees the simple form of God. That form is simple because it is [not?] in subject matter [?] in the way that nothing else is. Understanding also sees in man the deeds that are certain to God, though they are uncertain to the man himself. They happen of necessity from the side of God's foreknowledge, but not of necessity from the side of man. With the outer senses we perceive outer things, that is, bodies, which he calls matter. In bodies, or together with bodies, we perceive the bodily qualities, that is, their accidents. For example, in bodies there are colors and shapes,

and together with them their actions. Imaginatio follows the senses. It is the mind's forming of images, without the bodies, just as the eyes saw them on the bodies or the ears heard them. It might be that a person saw before a three-cornered shape, or a four-cornered one, or a round one, or the shape of a man, or of a bird. Or he saw a race, or wrestling, or white, or black. If the same likeness comes to a person in a dream, that is called phantasma and illusio. If he forms it in his mind in this way, that is called imaginatio. Beasts have these two in common with us,

that is, sensus (sense) and imaginatio (imagination). Ratio is the power of the mind that man alone has. It lets him know what he never saw and what no image can be formed of. It teaches him to tell true from false and good from evil, and to infer one thing from another. In this way he infers secondary substances from primary ones, the part from the whole, and also the whole from the part, present things from past ones, and future things from present ones. The pagan philosophers could understand nothing beyond where reason led them. Therefore they held that only those things should be believed that were supported by reason, in this form: "If this is, that is," or "If these are,"

…that will be. Then Aristotle said in the Categories that privation cannot be changed into possession, so that a toothless man gets teeth again, or a forehead becomes covered with hair again after baldness, because he knew of no reason by which this could come about. From this it happened to some people, when heavenly wisdom came and invited them to divine understanding, and told them to believe in the resurrection of the dead and that all things are possible to God, that they rejected it there. And so they were darkened by the very thing that should have enlightened them. You may say: wherever there is reason, there is also understanding. That is entirely true. Where there is human reason, there is also human understanding. But divine understanding and divine contemplation

is simple and spiritual, because God himself is a simple spirit. Whoever knows this shares in that same understanding. It teaches him that God is substance beyond substance, and form without form, without place, without time. He makes the world without matter, has a Son without otherness, and has the Spirit proceeding from him without motion. Those who looked for human reason in these things became heretics.

THAT THE LOWER IS COMPREHENDED BY THE HIGHER, NOT THE HIGHER BY THE LOWER. In this matter, this is what must be considered most carefully. For the higher power of comprehending embraces the lower. I mean that the higher faculty grasps the lower.
But the lower in no way rises up to the higher. The lower does not reach up to the higher.

For sense has no power outside matter. Sense has no working without a body, as imagination does. We must of necessity see and touch the accidents of bodies on the bodies themselves. Nor does imagination behold universal species. The mind's image-making can form the single image that it saw, but it cannot form the general image, because it never saw it. How then could it perceive it? Nor does reason grasp the simple form. Reason does not reach the simple form of God. It can only lead us to the forms that lie in substances. Those forms are not substances themselves but accidents. But God's form is form through itself: supersubstantial substance, that is, prior to the substances that stand under accidents.
But intelligence, as if looking down from above, having conceived the form,

discerns also all things that lie beneath it. But the intellect, as if standing higher and looking upon the form known to it, discerns the lower things through and through. But in the same way in which it comprehends the form itself, which could be known to no other. It sees the lower things in the same manner in which it sees the form, which none of the lower powers sees. What is that manner?
For it knows both the universal of reason and the figure of the imagination,

and the sensible material, using neither reason nor imagination nor the senses. It knows what reason and imagination and sense know, yet without guiding itself by any of them. But beholding all things with that single stroke of the mind formally, so to speak. Rather, in one glance it knows them all in its own manner, in the manner in which it knows the form. Just as Benedict saw this whole world all at once with a godlike eye.
Reason also comprehends imaginable things

or sensible things, using neither imagination nor the senses, when it considers something universal. Reason too knows what the lower powers know, yet without guiding itself by their powers, in order to see the universal.
For it is reason that defines the universal of its conception thus. This is the power that shows the generality it has grasped, with these words:
Man is a two-footed animal,
rational. Man is a living thing, two-legged, rational. And since this notion is universal,

yet no one is unaware that it is a thing that can be imagined and perceived by the senses. Although the knowledge is universal, who does not know that it can also be pictured and seen? Reason does not consider this in imagination or sense, but in rational conception. It knows this nevertheless not by picturing or seeing, but by thinking rationally. Imagination also, although it took from the senses its starting point for seeing and forming figures, (although the power of forming images arises from the five senses), nevertheless, when sense is absent, surveys all sensible things. It still explores all visible images without sense.
not by a sensible way of judging, but by an imaginative one.

Yet not with the skill of the sense, but with its own skill. Do you see then, O Boethius, how all things in knowing use their own faculty rather than that of the things that are known? Do you not now see how all the senses know more by their own power than by the power of the things being known?

And not wrongly. And rightly, too. For since every judgment must exist as the act of the one who judges. For it is very necessary, since the judging is the act of the one who judges, that each should accomplish his own work not by another's force but by his own power. That each one always carries out his deed with his own strength, not with another's strength.
WHETHER THE STOICS ARE TO BE BELIEVED, WHO SAY THAT EMPTY MINDS ARE AFFECTED BY EXTERNAL BODIES. Once the Porch, that is, at Athens, brought forth, that is, had,
exceedingly obscure old men. The Porch: the great hall at Athens.

[?] formerly, the very deep-thinking old men, that is, the Stoic philosophers. Plato, the Athenian philosopher, lived at Athens in the villa Academia, which was his own property, and taught his disciples there until his death. After his death they split up. Some stayed there and were called Academics. Some began to walk about and were called Peripatetics. Some went into the city of Athens and were called Stoics. They got that name from the stoa, that is, the portico, where they sat and thought about their wisdom. "Who believe," that is, who believed, that sensations and images are impressed on minds
from external bodies. They held that these are impressed on every person's mind:
…senses and images.

…from the external bodies. People and trees, mountains and rivers, and all the bodies outside us make us perceive in five ways. What would we perceive if they did not exist? What could we see or touch without bodies? And if their images did not exist, what would we then picture in our minds?

Coming from the bodies, they press into the mind. They have a path there through the senses. How are they impressed on our minds? They do it in such a way that we are acted on by them, not they by us, and they are impressed on us, not we on them. They give us sight and hearing, even though people say that we see them
and hear them.

"As it was once the custom to fix pressed letters with a quick stylus on the surface of a page that has no marks on it." That is, as letters are scratched with a stylus on a blank tablet. The tablet is like the mind, the stylus like the bodies, and the letters like the image.
[Heading:] THAT THE MIND EXERCISES ITS OWN POWER, YET IS OFTEN STIRRED FROM OUTSIDE, AND THEN MIXES THE INNER FORMS [WITH THE OUTER ONES]. "But if the mind unfolds nothing
by the vigor of its own motions" [Heading continued:] WITH THE OUTER ONES. But if the mind has no power and does nothing by its own activity,
"but only lies there passive," and it merely lies idle,
"subject to the marks of bodies," that is, subject to the images of the bodies that come upon it,
"and like a mirror gives back empty images of things," that is, like a mirror it reflects back the images of the bodies, copying them, if it can do nothing more:
"Where does this awareness that discerns all things get its power in minds?" That is, where then does the mind's knowledge, which perceives all things, come from?
"What power looks at individual things?" That is, which of its powers observes each thing separately so exactly?
"Or what power divides the things it knows,

and what power gathers again the things it has divided?" That is, which power divides the genera it knows into species, and then gathers them back into the groups of their genera? If the mind knows nothing more than visible things, how then does it know genera and species, which are not visible?
"And taking each path in turn,
it now raises its head to the highest things,
