now comes down to the lowest." That is, taking a journey that alternates back and forth, is it at one time among heavenly things and at another among earthly things? It deals in turn with physical and theological questions. Reason makes people natural philosophers; understanding makes them theologians.
"Then, turning back to itself,
it refutes false things with true ones." That is, it then examines itself and puts out false arguments with true ones.
"This cause is more effective
and far more powerful." That is, this power is more effective and much mightier
"than that cause
which receives the marks pressed upon it!

in the manner of matter. Then the power of the mind, which bears the images imprinted on it, just like wax, or water, or mirror-glass, in which the images appear. Yet an affection takes place first in the living body,
stirring and moving the powers of the mind.
Now something from outside still meets the senses first, stirring and rousing the powers of the mind. When is that?
When light strikes the eyes,
or a voice sounds in the ears. That is, when someone sees or hears something.
Then the vigor of the mind, aroused… Then at once the power of the mind, stirred…
…summoning the forms that it holds within to similar movements.
applies them to the outward marks. It brings the inner images out toward certain motions [?], offers them, and moves them toward those same signs. And it mixes the images
with the forms stored away within.

And it mixes those that come from outside with the images kept inside it. The soul has all natural melodies and all modes within itself. When it hears them sung, they please it, because they are like it. It gladly admits to itself the proportions out of which it is joined together, as is written in the books on music. And by offering them toward the outward ones, it mixes two like things into one. Thus, because the tyrant of Babylon also had some image of the deity in his mind, he said when he looked at the outward image: "I see a man like the son of God." And the magicians in Egypt, because they had some knowledge of God, recognized the finger of God in the miracles of Moses.
AS IS THE JUDGMENT OF OUR MIND, SO ALSO IS THE JUDGMENT OF THE DIVINE MIND.

NOT FROM THE POWER [heading, continued below:] But if the mind is not marked, that is, instructed, by passion in perceiving BELONGING TO ANOTHER [end of heading] bodies; if, I say, it is not marked by passion in perceiving bodies: If, then, a person's mind, when it perceives bodies, is not taught by their impact, judging the bodies themselves by means of their images; but judges by its own power the passion that is subjected to the body, that is, the image placed before the senses of its body: but rather judges by its own power the things that come before its eyes and its ears. Now an interposed argument comes in. Although qualities presented from outside affect the instruments of the senses: Although the images that come from outside affect the eyes and the ears, with which we see and hear.

and an affection of the body, that is, of the bodily senses, comes before the vigour of the active mind, — and the impact on its senses comes before the power of its mind, which works through itself, — which calls forth the act of the mind in itself, — this impact rouses the act of the mind in itself, — and stirs up the forms that rest within in the meantime. — and stirs up the images inside it that until then still lay hidden. The inserted reasoning goes up to this point.
How much more do those beings that are free from all affections of bodies

not follow objects presented from outside when they discern, but carry out the act of their own mind. How much more is this true of the heavenly substances, which are free from all impact of bodies? In them it is evident that they do not follow outward things when they discern, but show the power of their own understanding.
THE DISTRIBUTION OF THE KINDS OF KNOWING. In this way, then, the many kinds of knowing have been allotted to diverse and different substances. In this way the various senses

are allotted to various substances. Thus they have divided themselves among them. For sense alone, without the other kinds of knowledge, has fallen to unmoving living things. Sense alone, without the other three faculties, is allotted to those animals that stay fixed fast in one place. Such are the shellfish of the sea and other things that are nourished while clinging to rocks. This is what the sea mussels do, and other such creatures that cling to the stones. These perceive only by it [?].
But imagination belongs to beasts that can move.

To other living things, those that move about, imagination is also allotted. These already seem to have the impulse to flee or to seek. I mean those that have desire and aversion. That is why the ape imitates what it sees humans do. If it had not first formed an image of it in its mind, it could not imitate it. But reason belongs only to the human race, just as understanding belongs only to the divine. Reason is allotted only to humans,

just as understanding belongs to God alone. So this knowledge surpasses the others. Therefore understanding must rank highest. By its own nature it knows not only its proper object, that is, not only itself, but also the objects of the other kinds of knowledge, that is, also the three lower ones.

THAT TWO KINDS OF KNOWING CANNOT CONTEND WITH THE THIRD. What, then, if sense and imagination oppose reasoning? What if the two lower faculties begin to contend with reason, saying that the universal is nothing
which reason thinks it perceives.

by saying that the universal, which reason thinks it knows, does not exist. For what can be sensed or imagined cannot be universal. That is, by saying that what one can see or imagine as individual things cannot come together into one shared whole. For Socrates and Plato and Demosthenes never together acquire one common image that could be seen. So either the judgment of reason is true and nothing can be sensed. That is, by saying that one of the two must necessarily be the case: either what seems true to reason is true, or else reason is deceived about the visible.

Or, because it knows well that many things are subject to the senses and to imagination, that is, because the things that can be seen and imagined are well known to them, the conception of reason is empty.
Then reason's opinion would be deceived. Reason considers what can be sensed and is individual as if it were something universal. Reason believes that

what can be seen and is individual is universal. Suppose reason answers this in reply. It would say that it does indeed perceive, in its grasp of the universal, what can be sensed and what can be imagined. It would say that, in reasoning about the universal, it knows well what both of them know. But they cannot rise to knowledge of the universal. Neither of them knows the universal itself.
For their knowledge cannot go beyond bodily shapes.

Because they cannot step beyond the outward images. But it must rather be believed that, concerning the knowledge of things, the firmer and more perfect judgment [is to be followed]. Therefore, where one argues about their three kinds of knowing, one should rather believe the more certain and more complete judgment. In a dispute of this kind, then, would we not rather approve the cause of reason, we in whom there is the power of reasoning as well as of imagining, and also of sensing? Would we not stand by reason in this dispute, we who are able to do both: to reason, and also to see and to form images? As it itself knows.

THE THIRD MUST ALSO BE JUDGED UNEQUAL TO THE FOURTH. It is similar, too, that human reason thinks the divine intelligence does not behold future things except: It is just the same when human reason supposes that God's mind knows future things in no other way than as reason itself knows them.
For thus you argue: For this is how you reason. If some things do not seem to have certain and necessary outcomes, they cannot be foreknown as certainly going to happen. Whatever things uncertainly

and without necessity are to come cannot be foreknown as certainly coming. Therefore there is no foreknowledge of these things: And you say that there is no foreknowledge of such things. And if we believe that it does exist, there will be nothing that does not come about by necessity: And if we are to believe in it, then nothing happens without necessity.
Therefore, if we could have the judgment of the divine mind, just as we are partakers of reason. If we could have the discernment of the divine mind, just as we are rational beings.
We would think it most just that human reason should submit itself to the divine mind, just as we judged that imagination and sense ought to yield to reason.

Then it would seem equally right to us that our reason should yield to God's mind, as we judged that sense and imagination must yield to reason. Therefore, if we can, let us be raised up to the summit of that highest intelligence. Therefore let us try to lift ourselves up, if we can, to that height of the foremost intelligence. For there reason will see what it cannot behold in itself. Then reason will find there

what it does not have in itself. And this is it. I mean this: in what way foreknowledge sees as certain and definite even those things that have no certain outcomes; how God's foreknowledge holds as certain and precisely determined those things that in themselves have no certain outcome. And [it will see] that this is not opinion; and that it is no supposition. But rather the simplicity of the highest knowledge, enclosed by no limits; rather, simple knowledge, having no measure and bounded by no borders.
THAT A MAN WHO HAS AN UPRIGHT BODY OUGHT ALSO TO BE RAISED UP IN MIND. In what varied shapes living creatures move across the lands! Of how many shapes
are the animals that travel about the world. For some have bodies stretched out and sweep the dust. Some move by stretching themselves out
and wiping the earth. And they draw a continuous furrow, driven on by the force of their breast. And they make an unbroken track, going on their breasts.
There are some whose roaming lightness of wings
both beats the winds and swims through the spaces of the vast ether in liquid flight. There are others that beat the wind with their wings and glide far and wide in the clear air.
These rejoice to have pressed their footprints on the ground. Some tread the earth with their feet. And they rejoice either to cross the green fields with their steps
or to go into the woods. So they wander about on foot, in wood and in field.
Though you may see all these differ in their various forms.

Though you see all these differ from one another in their shape. Yet their downward-bent face can weigh down their dull senses. But their head, hanging down, makes them have dull wits. In this they are not different from one another.
Only the human race lifts its lofty head higher.
Man alone lifts his head up. And he stands lightly with upright body and looks down on the earth. And he raises himself lightly all the way up, looking away from the earth.
This figure admonishes you, earthly one, unless you are foolishly witless. This image admonishes you, man, if you can understand it.
You who seek heaven with upright face and lift up your forehead,
lift your mind on high as well. You who look straight at heaven

and lift your head up, lift up your mind also. Lest, while the body is raised higher, the weighed-down mind sink lower to its ruin. Lest, with the body upright, the burdened mind sink down to perdition.

WHAT THE DIVINE STATE IS. Everything that is known is known not through its own nature but through the nature of those who comprehend it, as was shown a little earlier. That is, all known things are known not through their own nature but through the nature of the knowers, as we also said before.
Let us now consider, as far as is permitted,

what the state of the divine substance is: So let us now see, as far as we are permitted, what state God's substance has. So that we may also come to know what his knowledge is: So that we may also perceive
what his knowledge is like. It is the common judgment of all who live by reason that God is eternal. That God is eternal is the common belief of all rational beings. They all agree on that.
Let us therefore consider what eternity is.
Now let us see what eternity is. For it reveals to us both the divine nature and the divine knowledge. Through it, eternity teaches us to recognize God's nature and God's knowledge.
Eternity, then, is

the whole, simultaneous and perfect possession of unending life. Eternity is the full and simultaneous possession of endless life. This becomes clearer when it is compared with things in time. That is, it appears more plainly from comparison with temporal things.

THAT WHICH RUNS IN TIME, EVEN IF IT IS INFINITE, IS NOT ETERNAL. For whatever lives in time moves on as a present into the future. Because what lives in time runs from the present into the future. And nothing set in time can embrace the whole span of its life all at once. Nor is there any non-eternal thing that can grasp all its life at once.
But it has not yet reached tomorrow, and it has already lost yesterday.

Rather, tomorrow is still ahead of it, and yesterday has gone from it. In today's life too. And in today's life as well, which lies between yesterday's and tomorrow's, you live no more. You live no more than in that moving and passing moment. Than in the unstable and passing instant. We do not live in the past, nor in the future; we are always in the present. Yet we cannot stand still even in that: as it comes, it runs away. And if anyone wants to point it out to someone else, he can barely say just once, "It is now." Straight away, the second time, he has to say, "It was now," if he is to point out the same thing. Such is our present.
Therefore, that which is subject to the condition of time. That which must always be subject to the nature of time,
even though it never began to be and never ceases,

as Aristotle thought about the world. Even though it has no beginning and no end, as Aristotle believed about this world. And even though its life extends through the infinity of time. And even though its life stretches across the endlessness of time, that is, of the past, the present and the future. Still, it is not yet the kind of thing that can rightly be believed to be eternal. It is still not such that it may rightly be called eternal.
For it does not comprehend and embrace the whole span of life all at once, even if that life is infinite. It does not grasp all at once, as eternity does,
the whole extent of its life, even though its life has no end. But it does not yet have what is to come, and it no longer has what is past. One time still lies ahead of it; the other is gone.
That, therefore, which comprehends and possesses all at once the whole fullness of endless life,

but that which possesses all at once and holds within itself the whole extent of its endless life, so that nothing of the future is absent from it and nothing of the past has flowed away: so that nothing of what is to come is absent from it, and nothing that has passed has slipped away from it. That is rightly said to be eternal: that is rightly called eternal. And it must be in possession of itself: and of that one must say that it has power over itself. And be present to itself: and be its own presence to itself. And hold as present the infinity of moving time: and hold as present all the endlessness of running time. Therefore some people think wrongly: for this reason those people think wrongly
who think, when they hear that it seemed to Plato that this world neither had a beginning in time nor will have an end: those who think this,

when they hear it said that this world did not seem to Plato to have a beginning in time, or an end, that the created world is in this way made coeternal with its Creator: that this created world is in that way equally eternal with the Creator. For it is one thing to be carried through an endless life, which Plato attributed to the world: for to have life without end, which Plato granted to the world, is one thing. It is another to have embraced all at once the whole presence of endless life: it is another to have grasped all at once the whole presence of the ever-enduring life. This is clearly proper to the divine mind: this is plainly proper to the mind of God.
Nor should God be thought older than created things by quantity of time,
nor should God seem to us to come before his creatures in age of time, but rather by the property of his simple nature: but rather in the simplicity of his nature that is proper to him.

THE LONG DURATION OF TIME IMITATES ETERNITY. For that endless motion of temporal things imitates this present state of unmoving life. This endless course of the world strives to imitate that very state of present life, of life that always stands fixed. And since it cannot reproduce it and equal it, and since it cannot imitate it or make itself equal to it, it falls away from immobility into motion. So instead it gives up steadfastness and passes into unsteadiness.
And from the simplicity of the present it shrinks into the infinite quantity of the future

and of the past. And it falls away from that simple presence into the infinite multiplicity of past and future time. And since it, that is, the motion of time, cannot possess the whole fullness of its life all at once. And since that same course cannot take in all the fullness of its life at once, as eternity does. It seems to imitate to some extent what it cannot fulfil and express, through the very fact that it never ceases to exist in some way. So, because it always endures, it seems to imitate in some part that which it can never fully equal.
Binding itself to whatever kind of presence belongs to this small and fleeting moment.

Keeping itself to the presence, such as it is [?], of this small and fleeting instant. And because this presence bears a kind of image of that abiding presence. And because it gives some picture of that presence which stands still and steadfast. That is, this same presence grants to whatever things it touches that they seem to exist. It allows the things it rests upon to seem to exist.
But because it could not stay,

because it could not stay still. It took up the infinite journey of time. It set out on the journey that has no end within time. If the journey ends, then time has ended too. And so it came about that it continued its life by going. And so it happened that it kept its life going by travelling. That is, it could not embrace the fullness of that life by staying. It could not grasp the wholeness of that life by standing still.
Therefore, if we wish to give things fitting names, following Plato — if we now wish rightly to give things fitting names according to Plato — let us indeed say that God is eternal,
but the world perpetual. Then let us say that God is eternal, and the world lasting.
HAVING SET THESE THINGS OUT, TO SOLVE THE QUESTION Since, therefore, every judgment comprehends the things subject to it

HE TURNS. according to its own nature. Because every act of judging judges what is before its eyes according to its own power. And God has always an eternal and present state. And because God has an eternal and present state, his knowledge also, surpassing every motion, that is, the course of time, remains in the simplicity of its presence. So his knowledge too must necessarily abide in that simple presentness, rising above every change of time. If that same presentness did not grasp all things together, it would not be simple. Therefore he says immediately afterwards: And embracing the infinite spans of past and future. And embracing together the endless expanses of past and future.

It considers all things in its simple knowledge, as if they were happening now. It sees all things in its simple knowing, both those that are past and those still to come, as if they were always being done in the present.

THAT IT IS MORE PROPER TO GOD TO KNOW AND TO PROVIDE THAN TO FOREKNOW AND TO FORESEE. Therefore, if you wish to consider the presence by which he discerns all things — if you will consider his presence, by which he knows it all — you will not think it to be foreknowledge, as of something future. Then you will not say that he has foreknowledge, as of things to come,

but more rightly the knowledge of a never-failing present — but rather a knowing of a presence that never fails him. Hence it is not called foresight (praevidentia) but rather providence. Therefore it is not called fore-sight, but rather a far-reaching oversight from above.

Because, set apart from the lowest things, it looks out upon all things as if from the lofty summit of things. Because it stands far from the lower things, it looks down on them all from far above, as if from the highest peak of the world.

THAT THINGS ARE NOT MADE NECESSARY BY GOD'S SEEING THEM, ANY MORE THAN BY OURS. Why then do you demand that the things lit up by the divine light become necessary? Why do you think that necessity is imposed on the things that God's eyes look upon? Since not even men make necessary the things they see? Since not even humans make necessary
the things they see?
For does your gaze add any necessity to the things

…which you perceive as present? Inno [?] Does your sight impose any necessity on the things you see? By no means. It does not. And yet, if there is a fitting comparison between the divine present and the human — indeed, if there can be any fitting comparison between the presence of man and of God — just as you see certain things in this your temporal present — just as you indeed see certain things in the presence of this transitory world —
so he perceives all things in his eternal [present]. So he sees them all

in his eternal presence. Wherefore this divine foreknowledge does not change the nature and the property of things. Therefore this foreknowledge of God does not change the nature and the property of things.
And he sees them as present before him, just as they will turn out at some time in the future. And he now sees them as present to him, just as they are still to come at some point in time.

THAT GOD SEES AND DISTINGUISHES THE NECESSARY AND THE NOT NECESSARY. Nor does it confound the judgments of things, that is, of merits — namely, according to what you said before: that once free will is lost, neither vices nor virtues are anything, but there is a mixed and undistinguished confusion of all merits. And he does not confuse his judgments, as you accuse him of doing, but he distinguishes the merits. And with one glance of his mind he discerns both the things that will come necessarily and those that will come not necessarily. And in one glance of his mind he sees the things to come by necessity and those to come without necessity. Just as you,
when you see at the same time a man walking on the earth and the sun rising in the sky. So too do you,

when you see together the man walking on the earth and the sun rising in the sky. Although both are seen at the same time, you nonetheless distinguish them. Though you see each of them together, you still distinguish them. And you judge this one to be voluntary, that one to be necessary. And you judge the one to happen by necessity, the other without necessity.
Thus, then, the divine gaze, looking down upon all things,

by no means disturbs the quality of things. So does God's eye: looking upon everything from above, it does not confuse the quality of things — things present with respect to him, but future with respect to the condition of time.

Present to him, but future as far as time is concerned. From this it follows that this is not opinion, but rather knowledge resting on truth. Therefore this is no supposition for him, but true knowledge. When he knows that something will come to be, which he likewise is not unaware lacks the necessity of existing. When he knows that it will be in the future, which can nevertheless be without necessity, that is, when it comes in the future.

IF A SYLLOGISM IS CONSTRUCTED IN THIS WAY — Here, if you should say that what God sees will happen cannot fail to happen — HOW IT IS TO BE EVADED — and that what cannot fail to happen happens of necessity,

If here you say, by way of a proposition: that what God sees as future cannot fail to happen, which is true; and, by way of an assumption: that what cannot fail to happen must happen of necessity, which is also true; and if you bind me to that name of necessity — and if you then wish to force me, by drawing the conclusion, to the name of necessity, thus: "What God sees as about to happen comes about of necessity. What God sees as future happens of necessity, since that too is true" — what do I do then? I will indeed admit it to be a matter of most solid truth. So I acknowledge this truth, made strong by the syllogism. But it is one that scarcely anyone could approach, except a contemplator of the divine.

But of such a kind that hardly anyone would understand it, except one who is a beholder of divine things. For I will answer. I say plainly: The same future thing, when it is referred to divine knowledge, is necessary; but when it is weighed in its own nature, it appears entirely free and unconstrained. One future thing is both: necessary, when one looks to God's knowledge, and free and self-determining, when one looks to its own nature. Here the question is solved; this is the hidden knot that makes two contradictory things exist together in one thing.
[Heading:] EXPLANATION OF THE SAME STATEMENT, FROM THE FACT THAT THERE ARE TWO NECESSITIES, AS IS READ IN ARISTOTLE'S PERI HERMENEIAS. For there are two necessities.

There are two necessities. One is simple. One is simple and without condition. As, for example, that all men must be mortal. Like this one: that all people are necessarily mortal. The other is of condition. The other is with an 'if' and with conditions. As, if you know that someone is walking, it is necessary that he walks. Like this one: if you know that a man is walking, then it is necessary that he walks. For what anyone knows cannot be otherwise than it is known. What one knows, how can it be otherwise than as one knows it? But this condition by no means draws that simple necessity along with it.

But this conditioned necessity does not bring the bare necessity along with it. I mean, it does not follow that if he walks willingly, he therefore also walks against his will. For it is not its own nature that makes this necessity, but the addition of a condition. For nature does not produce this necessity; it comes from adding an 'if' to it. For no necessity compels a man who walks of his own will to go. For no necessity makes the man who walks willingly walk. Although it is necessary that he goes when he walks. However great the necessity that he goes while he is walking.
GOD'S PRESENT IS TO BE UNDERSTOOD FROM OUR PRESENT. In the same way, then, if providence sees something as present, that thing must necessarily be.

In the same way, whatever the present foresight looks upon must necessarily be so. Although it has no necessity of nature. Even though it has no natural necessity. But God beholds as present those future things that come about from freedom of choice. Indeed, God sees as present the things that are still to come from free will.

AGAIN IT IS REPEATED THAT THE NATURE OF FUTURE THINGS IS NECESSARY FROM ONE SIDE AND ABSOLUTE FROM THE OTHER. These things, then (that is, future things), when referred to the divine gaze, [The Latin text and the heading are interwoven in the source; the text sentence continues in the next passage.]
become necessary through the condition of divine knowledge.

The crux of the matter about these things is this: they become necessary with respect to God's seeing, according to the condition of God's knowledge, because his knowledge is constituted in this way. But considered in themselves, they do not depart from the absolute freedom of their nature. But considered by themselves, they do not lose the self-determining freedom of their nature. Therefore all the things that God knows will come to be do come to pass without doubt. Now the things that God foreknows as future indeed happen without doubt. But some of them proceed from free will. Even so, some of them come from free will.

And although they come about by coming into existence, And however much they happen by coming to be, they still do not lose their own nature, by which they could also have failed to come about before they happened. By which they could also have remained undone before they happened.

AGAIN, ON THE DISTINCTION OF THE TWO NECESSITIES. What difference does it make, then, that they, that is, things foreknown as future, are not necessary? What then sets them apart, in that they are not necessary? Since they come about in every way like necessity, because of the condition of divine knowledge. Since they happen in every respect in the manner of necessity, as it stands in God's knowledge?

Because of that condition they happen by necessity. This, namely, makes the difference. That sets them apart. That those things make the difference. That those set them apart. Which I set forth a little earlier. Which I gave earlier as an example. Which are they? The rising sun and the walking man. The rising sun and the walking man. Which, while they are happening,

cannot fail to happen. Those two cannot be left undone while they are happening. Yet of these, one had to exist of necessity before it happened, but the other not at all. The one had to come about of necessity before it came about; the other not of necessity.

So also, without doubt, those things will come to be which God has as present. So are those things, without doubt, which God has in His presence. But of these, the one kind comes down from the necessity of things;
the other, however, from the power of those who do them.

But some of them come from necessity, some from the power of the one who acts. "Therefore we did not speak wrongly." Therefore we said rightly: "These things are necessary if they are referred to divine knowledge." These things are necessary when one looks to God's knowledge. "If they are considered in themselves, they are free from the bonds of necessity." But when one considers them in themselves, they are unbound and not necessary. "Just as everything that is evident to the senses is universal if you refer it to reason." So every thing that one can see and touch is universal if one looks to reason.

"If you look at the things themselves, it is singular." And yet it is individual if you pay attention to that. The things that we look at are always single and individual, as Plato is, and Cicero, and all individuals. Each one of these same things is also universal, because it is a man, or an ox, or a horse, or wood, or stone. Because "this man" is also "man," he is therefore both, singular and universal. The eye sees "this man"; reason knows only "man." Aristotle teaches this in the Categories.
WHETHER A CHANGED WILL COULD EVADE [PROVIDENCE]. But you will say — now it can happen, you say — if PROVIDENCE … it lies in my power to change my purpose,
I will make providence empty. If it lies in my power to change my plan, then I overturn the foresight, when I perhaps change what it foreknows. When I perhaps alter what it knows beforehand.
I will reply. To that I answer: that you can indeed turn aside your purpose. That you can well change your will.
But you cannot avoid divine foreknowledge.

But you cannot escape God's knowledge, nor get away from it. For the present truth of providence sees that you are able to do this. Because the present truth of foresight sees that you are able to do this. And whether you do it. And whether you do it. And in which direction you turn. And what you decide on. Just as you could not escape the gaze of an eye that is present. Just as you also cannot escape the gaze of the eyes of a man who is present. Although you turn yourself by free will to various actions. Even though you turn yourself, by the turnings of your will, to various deeds.
WHETHER FOREKNOWLEDGE CAN CHANGE AS THE WILL CHANGES.
"What then," you will say. How do you say now? "Will divine knowledge be changed by my disposition?" Does God's knowledge now waver according to my plan, which arises in me in the meantime?

So that when I will now this, now something else, it too seems to alternate its ways of knowing? So that it could make alternations of knowing along with me, according as I sometimes will one thing, sometimes another? Not at all. It does not do that.

For the divine gaze runs ahead of everything future. God's eye anticipates all that is to come. And it turns it back and recalls it to the presence of its own knowing. And he turns it and directs it to the presence of his knowing. Nor does it alternate, as you suppose, in turns of foreknowing,
"now this,"

"now that." Nor does he alternate in his knowing, now this, now this, now that. "But, remaining as he is, he anticipates and embraces your changes in a single stroke." Instead, always standing still, he grasps your changes beforehand and encompasses them in a single stroke.
THAT GOD'S PROVIDENCE COMES FROM HIS SIMPLICITY, NOT FROM THE OUTCOME OF THINGS. This presence of comprehending and seeing all things

God did not obtain from the outcome of future things. That ever-presence of his beholding and encompassing all things he did not gain from what will happen in the future. But from his own simplicity. Rather, from his own simplicity, which understanding (intellectus) teaches us, not reason (ratio).
By this, that point is also resolved

which you raised a little earlier. By this, what you said before is also answered: that it is unworthy if our future things are said to provide the cause of God's knowledge. It would be unseemly if anyone thought that our future things (futura) account for God's knowledge.
For this power of knowledge, this same power of his knowledge, embracing all things in its present knowing, embracing all things with its present cognition,
itself establishes the mode for all things.
It gives manner to all things, not they to it. And it owes nothing to later things. Nor does it have those that come after to thank, as though it had learned it from them.

THAT FREE WILL STANDS, AND THAT REWARDS ARE DISPENSED ACCORDING TO MERITS. "Since these things are so, the freedom of the will remains unviolated for mortals." Because all this is so, their free will is not taken away from human beings.
Nor do the laws unjustly offer rewards and punishments to wills

freed from all necessity. And rightly do the law books promise rewards and penalties to free wills. There also remains above, as beholder of all things, the foreknowing God. And God is above, the one who sees all and knows beforehand. And the ever-present eternity of his vision accords with the future character of our actions. And the eternal presence of his sight accords with the future character of our works. Dispensing rewards to the good, punishments to the wicked.

Dispensing good to the good and evil to the evil. Nor are hopes and prayers placed in God in vain. Nor are hopes and supplications placed upon God to no purpose. Which, when they are right, cannot be ineffective. They are effective when they are right.

EPILOGUE. Therefore turn away from vices. Therefore loathe the vices. Cultivate virtues. Love virtues. Lift up your mind to right hopes. Set your minds on right hope. Offer humble prayers on high. Send humble prayers up to heaven.

A great necessity of uprightness has been laid upon you, if you do not wish to pretend otherwise. Great need compels you to goodness, if you are willing to admit it. For you act before the eyes of a judge who discerns all things. For your deeds are watched over by the judge who sees everything. Here we can see that after this fifth book Boethius was cut off by death, so that he could not hear from Philosophy what she had promised him she would tell later. HERE ENDS THE FIFTH BOOK OF BOETHIUS THE CONSUL.
